protocol_intelligence.meaning: Adjacency stuck negotiating the DB-descriptor exchange; it never reaches FULL.
protocol_intelligence.likely_cause: Interface MTU mismatch between the neighbors (the classic cause); also blocked unicast (ACL/NAT) or a duplicate OSPF router-id.
protocol_intelligence.remediation: Match the IP MTU on both interfaces (or `ip ospf mtu-ignore` as a stopgap); verify unicast reachability and unique router-ids.
protocol_intelligence.confidence: observed state = fact; likely cause = Inferred (Cisco doctrine)

items.title: Undefined acl '7'
items.why: Referenced (ip nat inside source list 7 pool MIGRATE_POOL overload) but never defined — it silently does nothing (e.g. an ACL/route-map that matches nothing).
commands: ! Option A — DEFINE the missing acl '7' with the intended rules, e.g.:
!   acl 7
! Option B — REMOVE the dangling reference at: ip nat inside source list 7 pool MIGRATE_POOL overload
!   (negate the referencing line with its 'no' form)
items.caution: Decide define-vs-remove from intent; a wrong 'no' can drop a security/routing control.

items.title: Undefined route-map 'OSPF_TO_BGP'
items.why: Referenced (router bgp 65001) but never defined — it silently does nothing (e.g. an ACL/route-map that matches nothing).
commands: ! Option A — DEFINE the missing route-map 'OSPF_TO_BGP' with the intended rules, e.g.:
!   route-map OSPF_TO_BGP
! Option B — REMOVE the dangling reference at: router bgp 65001
!   (negate the referencing line with its 'no' form)
items.caution: Decide define-vs-remove from intent; a wrong 'no' can drop a security/routing control.

core1.title: Undefined acl '7'
core1.why: Referenced (ip nat inside source list 7 pool MIGRATE_POOL overload) but never defined — it silently does nothing (e.g. an ACL/route-map that matches nothing).
commands: ! Option A — DEFINE the missing acl '7' with the intended rules, e.g.:
!   acl 7
! Option B — REMOVE the dangling reference at: ip nat inside source list 7 pool MIGRATE_POOL overload
!   (negate the referencing line with its 'no' form)
core1.caution: Decide define-vs-remove from intent; a wrong 'no' can drop a security/routing control.

core1.title: Undefined route-map 'OSPF_TO_BGP'
core1.why: Referenced (router bgp 65001) but never defined — it silently does nothing (e.g. an ACL/route-map that matches nothing).
commands: ! Option A — DEFINE the missing route-map 'OSPF_TO_BGP' with the intended rules, e.g.:
!   route-map OSPF_TO_BGP
! Option B — REMOVE the dangling reference at: router bgp 65001
!   (negate the referencing line with its 'no' form)
core1.caution: Decide define-vs-remove from intent; a wrong 'no' can drop a security/routing control.

commands: ! Apply an 'access-class' ACL and a non-zero 'exec-timeout' on every VTY line.
access1.caution: CIS hardening — confirm the control suits this device's role before applying.

access1.title: Accidental root on VLAN 30
access1.why: Rooted on the default bridge priority — elected on a MAC tiebreak, so the root can move on a cutover.
commands: spanning-tree vlan 30 priority 24576
! (use 28672 for a secondary/backup root)
access1.caution: Set a DELIBERATE priority on the INTENDED root only; verify the topology before and after.

access1.title: Logging / audit trail
access1.why: no syslog / buffered logging -- no audit trail across the migration.
commands: ! Configure 'logging host' / 'logging buffered' to retain an audit trail.
access1.caution: CIS hardening — confirm the control suits this device's role before applying.

access1.title: Login banner
commands: ! Configure a 'banner login' / 'banner motd' legal-notice banner.
access1.caution: CIS hardening — confirm the control suits this device's role before applying.

access1.title: NTP time synchronization
access1.why: no NTP server -- clock drift makes logs and certificate validity untrustworthy.
commands: ! Configure an authenticated 'ntp server' so logs and certificate validity are trustworthy.
access1.caution: CIS hardening — confirm the control suits this device's role before applying.

findings.surface: Device web UI (ip http server / secure-server)
findings.label: Device web UI (ip http server / secure-server)
findings.detail: The IOS XE web UI was mass-exploited in 2023-24 (tens of thousands of devices implanted); any HTTP(S) server on a network device is standing attack surface.

advisories.note: actively exploited in the wild (web-UI privilege escalation, CVSS 10)

findings.why: The IOS XE web UI was mass-exploited in 2023-24 (tens of thousands of devices implanted); any HTTP(S) server on a network device is standing attack surface.
findings.recommendation: Disable 'ip http server' / 'ip http secure-server', or restrict them to the management network with an ACL; validate the running release with the Cisco Software Checker.

findings.label: SNMP v1/v2c read-only community
findings.detail: Cleartext community strings leak topology and credentials material, and v1/v2c packets still reach the (historically exploited) SNMP stack.

advisories.note: exploited in the wild (SNMP stack overflow -> RCE/DoS)

findings.why: Cleartext community strings leak topology and credentials material, and v1/v2c packets still reach the (historically exploited) SNMP stack.
findings.recommendation: Move to SNMPv3 auth+priv and ACL the SNMP service.

findings.label: Telnet enabled on vty lines
findings.detail: Telnet sends credentials and session content in cleartext -- one capture on any transit segment is a full management compromise.
findings.why: Telnet sends credentials and session content in cleartext -- one capture on any transit segment is a full management compromise.
findings.recommendation: Set 'transport input ssh' on all vty lines (and verify SSHv2-only).

software_risk.note: Attack-surface SCREENING from configuration evidence joined to landmark public advisories -- not a vulnerability scan. The offline toolkit carries no live advisory feed: validate every running release with the Cisco PSIRT Software Checker, and read 'exposed' as 'this surface is open', never as 'this release is vulnerable'.

punchlist.title: Native VLAN 1 on 26 inter-switch trunk(s)
punchlist.detail: 26 trunk(s) across 17 switch(es) carry the default VLAN 1 as the native (untagged) VLAN -- a hygiene and VLAN-hopping exposure.
punchlist.remediation: Set a dedicated, unused native VLAN on inter-switch trunks.

punchlist.title: No QoS configured anywhere
punchlist.detail: None of the 18 assessable device(s) has any active QoS configuration (policies attached, trust, or auto-QoS).
punchlist.remediation: The whole assessable fleet runs best-effort. Acceptable for pure data; a documented risk if voice/video/storage rides this network. Record the customer's stance as a CRD requirement before the migration.

punchlist.title: Accidental root (VLAN 30)
punchlist.detail: Rooted on the default priority -- elected on a MAC tiebreak, so it can move on a cutover.
punchlist.remediation: Set a deliberate root-bridge priority on the intended switch.

punchlist.title: Logging / audit trail

punchlist.remediation: Configure 'logging host' / 'logging buffered' to retain an audit trail.

punchlist.title: Login banner

punchlist.title: NTP time synchronization

per_group.rationale: gating checks fail (4 blocker(s)) — resolve them, then migrate in small validated waves.

playbook.pre: Resolve gating checks first; schedule single-homed (hard-cutover) switches into maintenance windows.
playbook.validate: Per wave, prove forwarding for a sample endpoint of EACH hosted class before the next wave.
playbook.rollback: A wave fails validation -> re-home that wave's uplinks to the legacy path; hold the remaining waves.

per_group.rationale: 100% of switches are dual-homed — build beside and cut leg-by-leg (make-before-break) for minimal outage.

playbook.pre: Build the new path beside the legacy one; confirm both legs of every dual-homed endpoint are up.
playbook.validate: Cut one leg, prove forwarding from a real endpoint to its gateway + a cross-VLAN service, then cut the second.
playbook.rollback: Any endpoint loses reachability on the new leg -> fail back to the legacy leg (still up); re-validate.

device_dossiers.note: Risk index = topology impact (1-10) x stacked exposure (0-10) per asset, mirroring asset-risk practice (likelihood x impact). Synthesis of already-computed axes only; an axis without evidence is 'not assessed', never red.

checks.title: Distribution/core tier present
checks.observed: 4 L3 node(s) (gateway SVI or routing adjacency) front 19 L2 access node(s).
checks.implication: A defined L3 tier bounds failure domains and gives the migration a stable anchor.
checks.recommendation: Carry the tiering into the target design; keep gateway functions at the distribution tier.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — hierarchical access/distribution/core model

checks.title: No daisy-chained access switches
checks.observed: Every observed access uplink lands on the L3 tier.
checks.implication: Failure domains stay bounded per closet.
checks.recommendation: Preserve the star topology in the target design.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — each access switch homes to the distribution layer

checks.title: Dual-homed access uplinks
checks.observed: 17 of 19 access switch(es) reach exactly ONE in-fleet neighbour: access1, access10, access11, access12, access13, access14, access15, access16, access17, access2, access3, access4 +5 more.
checks.implication: A single uplink (or single upstream switch) is a per-closet single point of failure — one optic, one linecard or one upstream chassis takes the closet down.
checks.recommendation: Dual-home each listed switch to two distribution nodes (or at minimum two linecards) as part of the migration build.
checks.reference: Cisco campus HA design — redundant uplinks from every access switch

checks.title: First-hop redundancy on every gateway
checks.observed: VLAN(s) 30 are served by a SINGLE gateway with no FHRP peer.
checks.implication: Losing that one gateway device black-holes every endpoint on the VLAN — the highest-impact availability exposure a campus carries, and a migration-readiness FAIL.
checks.recommendation: Add an FHRP peer (or move the VLAN behind a redundant gateway pair) BEFORE any migration wave touches these VLANs.
checks.reference: Cisco campus HA design — FHRP (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP) on every shared gateway

checks.title: Redundant power supplies
checks.observed: Power-supply inventory was not captured for any device.
checks.recommendation: Include 'show environment power' / inventory output in collection.
checks.reference: Cisco campus HA design — N+1 power on aggregation nodes

checks.title: No keystone single point of failure
checks.observed: Losing core1 strands 45 endpoint(s); access1 strands 42 endpoint(s); core2 strands 42 endpoint(s); access13 strands 39 endpoint(s); access14 strands 39 endpoint(s).
checks.implication: Endpoint dependency is concentrated — these devices ARE the availability budget.
checks.recommendation: Verify each keystone's redundancy (uplinks, power, supervisor) and sequence them with the most conservative cutover plan (their waves carry the widest blast radius).
checks.reference: Availability analysis — single-device blast radius

checks.title: Deterministic STP root at the distribution tier
checks.observed: Access switch(es) hold the STP root: access1 roots 1 VLAN(s); access10 roots 1 VLAN(s); access11 roots 1 VLAN(s); access12 roots 1 VLAN(s); access13 roots 1 VLAN(s); access14 roots 1 VLAN(s).
checks.implication: A root on an access closet means the L2 tree converges around the smallest box in the fabric — default (un-pinned) priorities usually caused it, and any new switch can silently steal the root.
checks.recommendation: Pin root primary/secondary priorities on the distribution pair for every VLAN.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — pin the STP root (priority) at the distribution layer

checks.title: Edge protection (BPDU Guard) on access ports
checks.observed: BPDU Guard state was not captured for the access ports.
checks.recommendation: Include 'show spanning-tree interface detail' (or run-config) in collection.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — PortFast + BPDU Guard on every edge port

checks.title: VLAN 1 not used for user traffic
checks.observed: Trunks with native VLAN 1 on 17 switch(es): access1, access10, access11, access12, access2, access3, access4, access5, access6, access7, access8, access9 +5 more.
checks.implication: Native VLAN 1 on inter-switch trunks exposes untagged control-plane crosstalk and is flagged by the hardening baseline.
checks.recommendation: Set the native VLAN to a dedicated unused VLAN on the listed trunks.
checks.reference: Cisco hardening guidance — keep user traffic and trunk native VLAN off VLAN 1

checks.title: Bounded broadcast domains
checks.observed: Largest observed VLAN carries 3 endpoint(s) — within the conventional envelope.
checks.implication: Broadcast domains are bounded.
checks.recommendation: Keep VLAN sizing within a /24-/23 of endpoints in the target design.
checks.reference: Campus design guidance — constrain broadcast domains (≈ a /23 of endpoints per VLAN)

checks.title: Trunks pruned to required VLANs
checks.observed: All 28 trunk(s) with captured lists are pruned.
checks.implication: VLAN scope stays bounded per closet.
checks.recommendation: Maintain pruning in the per-wave port maps.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — prune trunk allowed-VLAN lists to the required set

checks.title: Every access VLAN has a gateway in scope
checks.observed: All 5 access VLAN(s) terminate on an in-scope gateway SVI.
checks.implication: The L2/L3 boundary is fully accounted for.
checks.recommendation: Keep the gateway register in the LLD as the addressing source of truth.
checks.reference: Campus L3 design — every user VLAN terminates on a known, redundant gateway

checks.title: DHCP relay on endpoint-serving gateways
checks.observed: 3 endpoint-carrying VLAN(s) have a gateway with no DHCP relay configured: VLAN(s) 30, 40, 41.
checks.implication: If those clients use central DHCP, the missing helper is a silent post-cutover black hole (the classic day-1 failure); if addressing is static/local this is by design.
checks.recommendation: Confirm the addressing model per VLAN; add helpers where central DHCP is intended before the carrying wave.
checks.reference: Campus L3 design — ip helper-address on every client-serving SVI

checks.title: Single IGP, controlled redistribution
checks.observed: 3 redistribution edge(s) observed.
checks.implication: Every extra protocol and redistribution point is a loop/suboptimal-routing risk and a troubleshooting tax; migrations are when undocumented redistribution bites.
checks.recommendation: Plan convergence to a single IGP in the target design; until then, document each redistribution edge (route-map, direction, owner) in the LLD.
checks.reference: Campus L3 design — one IGP where possible; document every redistribution boundary

checks.title: FHRP active aligned with the STP root
checks.observed: No VLAN has both a known FHRP active gateway and an observed root bridge.
checks.recommendation: Collect 'show standby'/'show spanning-tree' together to enable this check.
checks.reference: Cisco campus design — co-locate the FHRP active gateway with the STP root per VLAN

checks.title: Access uplink oversubscription within 20:1
checks.observed: 19 access switch(es) measured; worst provisioned ratio 1:1.
checks.implication: Uplink capacity is within the conventional envelope.
checks.recommendation: Re-validate ratios whenever the target design changes uplink counts or speeds.
checks.reference: Cisco campus rule of thumb — ≤20:1 access→distribution, ≤4:1 distribution→core

checks.title: Port-capacity headroom for growth
checks.observed: access1 at 100.0% port utilisation; access10 at 100.0% port utilisation; access11 at 100.0% port utilisation; access12 at 100.0% port utilisation; access2 at 100.0% port utilisation; access3 at 100.0% port utilisation.
checks.implication: A full closet forces ad-hoc daisy-chaining (see HIER-2) the day a port is needed.
checks.recommendation: Size replacement hardware with ≥10% spare ports per listed closet.
checks.reference: Capacity planning — keep ~10% port headroom per closet

checks.title: No operational drift / false health
checks.observed: 1 lower-severity drift finding(s).
checks.implication: Low-grade drift compounds; the migration touch is the cheapest moment to clear it.
checks.recommendation: Fold the items into the per-wave work orders.
checks.reference: Assessment doctrine — configured is not healthy; up is not healthy

checks.title: Clean configuration hygiene
checks.observed: 2 undefined reference(s) across 1 device(s): core1.
checks.implication: A referenced-but-undefined ACL/route-map fails OPEN or CLOSED depending on platform — either way it is latent surprise during cutover.
checks.recommendation: Resolve or remove each undefined reference before its device migrates.
checks.reference: Operational hygiene — no undefined references in running configuration

checks.title: Collection confidence
checks.observed: Collection is complete across the fleet.
checks.implication: The review stands on full evidence.
checks.reference: Assessment doctrine — state collection blind spots explicitly

checks.title: Cross-domain dependencies & interoperability declared
checks.observed: The fleet spans 2 switch NOS families (22× IOS, 1× NXOS).
checks.implication: A multi-NOS estate must keep feature / CLI / automation parity across families, and any cross-family migration (e.g. IOS->NX-OS) is an explicit interoperability step, not a like-for-like swap — undeclared, it surfaces as a cutover surprise.
checks.recommendation: Declare the platform-dependency + interoperability surface in the HLD (the design interoperability footprint) and validate cross-family behaviour during NRFU.
checks.reference: Cisco Advanced Services design-review practice — declare platform dependencies & interop

checks.title: Management-plane hardening (CIS baseline)
checks.observed: 1 device(s) grade WEAK (a high-severity hardening check fails): core1; 17 more grade partial.
checks.implication: A weak management plane (open HTTP/Smart Install, missing AAA, default communities) is the attack surface that turns a migration window into an incident.
checks.recommendation: Apply the generated remediation snippets to the WEAK devices first — before any maintenance window publicises change activity.
checks.reference: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark — AAA, NTP, logging, SSHv2/VTY, SNMPv3 hardening

checks.title: Segmentation enforced at the L3 boundary
checks.observed: 1 VRF(s) in use; 2 of 9 gateway SVIs carry an ACL.
checks.implication: Partial enforcement leaves unpoliced inter-segment paths.
checks.recommendation: Close the unpoliced SVIs (or fold them into a VRF) in the target design.
checks.reference: Segmentation guidance — enforce inter-segment policy at the L3 boundary (VRF / gateway ACL)

checks.title: No hardware past end-of-support
checks.observed: 5 device(s) are past LAST-DAY-OF-SUPPORT (and 6 more past end-of-sale): access1, access10, access12, access13, access15, access16, access3, access4, access6, access7, access9.
checks.implication: Past LDoS there is NO TAC escalation path and no software fix — a fault during a migration window on these devices has no vendor backstop.
checks.recommendation: Replace (not upgrade) the LDoS devices as the first migration waves; stage spares for any that must briefly remain.
checks.reference: Cisco EoX policy — no TAC/software support past last-day-of-support

checks.title: One software image per platform
checks.observed: Every platform runs a single image.
checks.implication: Troubleshooting and rollback are uniform per model.
checks.recommendation: Pin the images as the minimum-version baseline in the LLD.
checks.reference: AS LLD convention — minimise image variance per platform

top_actions.action: Replace (not upgrade) the LDoS devices as the first migration waves; stage spares for any that must briefly remain.
Add an FHRP peer (or move the VLAN behind a redundant gateway pair) BEFORE any migration wave touches these VLANs.
Pin root primary/secondary priorities on the distribution pair for every VLAN.
Dual-home each listed switch to two distribution nodes (or at minimum two linecards) as part of the migration build.
Apply the generated remediation snippets to the WEAK devices first — before any maintenance window publicises change activity.
Set the native VLAN to a dedicated unused VLAN on the listed trunks.
Size replacement hardware with ≥10% spare ports per listed closet.
Verify each keystone's redundancy (uplinks, power, supervisor) and sequence them with the most conservative cutover plan (their waves carry the widest blast radius).
Plan convergence to a single IGP in the target design; until then, document each redistribution edge (route-map, direction, owner) in the LLD.
Resolve or remove each undefined reference before its device migrates.

summary.statement: Architecture conformance grade C (70%) — Material deviations. 8 of 22 assessable checks conform to leading practice; 2 critical and 3 material deviation(s) require remediation, concentrated in: Resiliency & availability, Layer-2 design, Security & segmentation, Lifecycle & software. 3 check(s) were not assessable from this snapshot and are listed in the review scope.

decisions.title: Enforce secure management (SSH/SNMPv3), centralized RBAC/AAA least-privilege, and retire plaintext
decisions.driver: Management-plane integrity: secure access, SNMPv3 and AAA/RBAC.

evidence.summary: 18 device(s) fail management-plane hardening (insecure-snmp, no-aaa, password-encryption, telnet-enabled, vty-hardening, weak-user-pw).

principle.title: Enforce secure management (SSH/SNMPv3), centralized RBAC/AAA least-privilege, and retire plaintext
principle.citation: CCDE Session 19 (secure management plane, SNMP versions, RBAC/AAA/least-privilege); engine CIS axis

decisions.recommended_action: Standardize SNMPv3 + SSH, disable Telnet/SNMPv1-v2c, scope SNMP views; centralize AAA (TACACS+ command-authz/accounting + RADIUS access) with RBAC/least-privilege, guarded local fallback, banners and timeouts.
decisions.alternatives: Read-only v2c restricted to a mgmt VRF with strong ACLs as an interim where v3 is unsupported; external IdP integration for larger estates; TLS-based transports (NETCONF/SSH, gRPC/TLS) for newer stacks.
decisions.tradeoffs: Confidentiality/integrity/accountability of the most-privileged plane vs the config overhead of v3 users/views, role definitions and an available AAA infrastructure; some legacy tools may only speak v2c.

decisions.title: Drive EoL/EoS hardware out of critical roles and protect against the upgrade flag-day
decisions.driver: Supportability: the target fabric must not inherit end-of-support assets.

evidence.summary: 5 device(s) are past last-day-of-support (1 more approaching LDoS) -- unsupported hardware/software in forwarding roles cannot be safely relied on in the target design.

principle.title: Drive EoL/EoS hardware out of critical roles and protect against the upgrade flag-day
principle.citation: CCDE In Depth Ch.2 Scalability (scale-out avoids the Flag Day) & Cost/TCO; engine EoL/software_risk axes

decisions.recommended_action: Prioritize refresh of EoL/EoS devices in core/critical roles; specify dual-supervisor/dual-RP (SSO/NSF) or paired-node scale-out so upgrades/swaps are non-disruptive; sequence the migration so no single change becomes a flag-day.
decisions.alternatives: ISSU on a single chassis where supported; staged maintenance-window upgrades with rollback; time-boxed risk acceptance.
decisions.tradeoffs: Investment-protection/HA vs CapEx and migration risk — refresh and scale-out cost up front but reduce long-run risk/TCO and enable hitless maintenance; deferring saves CapEx but raises outage and security exposure.

decisions.title: Clear or formally accept every CRITICAL APIC fault before freezing the migration baseline
decisions.driver: Controller-fabric health: a raised, unacknowledged critical/major APIC fault is an active service-affecting condition the fabric controller itself is reporting -- not inferred from absence.

evidence.summary: 2 raised, unacknowledged ACI fault(s) at critical/major severity (e.g. core2 F1394 critical, core2 F0321 critical). The APIC fault list is the fabric's own current broken-state inventory; a raised (lc=raised) fault that has not been acknowledged, at critical or major severity, is an active service-affecting condition -- a fabric port down, an APIC cluster degraded, a contract/programming failure. Triage each fault code against the APIC fault guide, clear the underlying condition (or explicitly acknowledge a known-accepted one), and re-pull the fault list before the fabric is accepted at cutover.

principle.title: Clear or formally accept every CRITICAL APIC fault before freezing the migration baseline
principle.citation: Cisco APIC Faults, Events, and System Messages Management Guide — Faults (severity levels, fault lifecycle soaking/raised/clearing/retaining, acknowledge vs. squelch, delegated faults, health-score impact); ACI System Messages Reference Guide — ACI F0x Messages (e.g. F0110 fltFabricNodeFailed); Address ACI fault F1394 (interface-physical-down)

decisions.recommended_action: Work the fault by its lifecycle and its delegate chain, not by silencing it. (1) Enumerate critical faults at System > Faults and per-node under Fabric > Inventory > Pod > node > Faults; record the fault code, the affected MO (dn), and the lifecycle state. (2) Follow each fault to its ROOT MO — a fault:Delegate surfaced on a parent points back to a fault:Inst on the object actually in trouble; hide delegated faults to find the true origin. (3) Look the code up in the ACI System Messages Reference and execute its documented remediation (e.g. F1394 -> verify the fabric port cabling/transceiver and that the peer is up; F0110 -> drive the node-not-active runbook; F0321/F0323/F0325 -> restore APIC cluster quorum/'Fully Fit'). (4) Remediate the underlying condition and confirm the fault transitions to raised-clearing then clears on its own. (5) Only after the real fix, if a residual is a known cosmetic/expected condition, ACKNOWLEDGE it (which deletes it immediately when retaining, or marks it expected otherwise) — and document why. Re-run the fault sweep and require zero unexplained criticals before the cutover gate.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier path is to acknowledge or squelch the fault to make the dashboard and the health score go green without fixing the cause — acknowledging an ignored fault explicitly removes it from the health-score computation, and squelching a fault code discards all instances of it fabric-wide and from logs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Acknowledging/squelching takes seconds and unblocks the gate cosmetically, but it deletes your only early warning: the underlying defect (a dead fabric link, an unreachable node, a split cluster) then surfaces as a production outage during or after cutover with no fault left to point at it.

decisions.title: Provide first-hop (gateway) redundancy on every L2-access default gateway
decisions.driver: Gateway resilience: a VLAN must survive loss of its distribution switch.

evidence.summary: 1 gateway VLAN(s) lack full first-hop redundancy: 1 single-gateway VLAN(s) (one gateway -- a per-VLAN single point of failure).

principle.title: Provide first-hop (gateway) redundancy on every L2-access default gateway
principle.citation: CCDE In Depth Ch.1 (FHRP & L2 access); Cisco Campus CVD 2024 (SVL/anycast preferred over GLBP, VRRPv3 multivendor)

decisions.recommended_action: Introduce FHRP (HSRP or VRRP) on the distribution pair for every access VLAN gateway, or — where the platform supports it — eliminate FHRP via SVL/vPC single logical gateway or VXLAN-EVPN anycast gateway. Use VRRP for multivendor; keep GLBP off stateful Internet/firewall edges.
decisions.alternatives: Routed-access design (removes FHRP need entirely); anycast gateway / fabric (EVPN, SPB, FabricPath); StackWise Virtual single logical gateway.
decisions.tradeoffs: HA vs simplicity; standards/multivendor vs feature richness — VRRP buys interop, GLBP adds per-flow load-balancing but is proprietary and polarizes at stateful edges; more FHRP groups add config. Collapsing the control plane (SVL/anycast) removes FHRP entirely but is a platform/maturity step.

decisions.title: An FTD HA pair must hold a real Active/Standby split -- FMC is the authoritative HA verdict
decisions.driver: Controller-reported firewall HA: an FTD pair FMC reports Failed/Not-Detected/split has no standby -- a single point of failure in the data path, authoritative for an FMC-managed fleet.

evidence.summary: 1 FTD HA pair(s) are degraded per FMC (e.g. core1: AJ-FTD-HA-Edge (primary Active / secondary Failed)). A pair with a node Failed / Not Detected, or split (both units the same role), has no working active/standby -- the firewall is a single point of failure, and a failover during the maintenance window would drop every stateful flow through it. For an FMC-managed fleet the controller is the authoritative HA source. Confirm the failover link, unit health and the high-availability config in FMC, and restore the standby before the firewall is on the cutover path. (An intentionally-suspended 'Disabled' pair is excluded -- re-enable it when maintenance ends.)

principle.title: An FTD HA pair must hold a real Active/Standby split -- FMC is the authoritative HA verdict
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense HA + FMC REST API (ftddevicehapairs currentStatus: Active/Standby/Failed/Not Detected/Disabled); standard stateful-HA design practice.

decisions.recommended_action: Treat the degraded pair as a cutover blocker: confirm the failover/state link, unit health and the HA config in FMC, restore the standby to Standby, and (if intentionally suspended for maintenance) re-enable HA before the firewall is on the cutover path.
decisions.alternatives: Clustering for scale + HA (more complex); an accepted-risk standalone FTD for a low-criticality edge (document the single point of failure).
decisions.tradeoffs: An HA pair doubles firewall cost and adds state-sync complexity, but removes the in-path single point of failure for a perimeter/inter-zone enforcement point.

decisions.title: Defense-in-depth via modular, layered security zones — not perimeter-only
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: A flat L2 / single-VRF posture is observable, but the target zoning needs a data-security classification (which assets must be isolated from which).

principle.title: Defense-in-depth via modular, layered security zones — not perimeter-only
principle.citation: CCDE Session 13 (defense-in-depth, zones, risk-driven controls, Private VLAN)

decisions.recommended_action: Segment into security modules/zones with layered per-module controls (edge firewall + iACL + IPS + L2 access protections + AAA), put the NMS in its own zone, run an asset/risk analysis to size controls to asset value, and use Private VLANs for intra-subnet isolation.
decisions.alternatives: Single stateful perimeter (cheaper, weaker once breached); host-based firewalls/service mesh microsegmentation; physical vs virtual (VRF/context) zone separation.
decisions.tradeoffs: Security/containment vs operational simplicity and cost — more zones/layers mean more devices and policy surface; uniform blanket controls vs risk-prioritized ones; macro- vs micro-segmentation.

decisions.title: Restore the down IPv6 routing adjacency before freezing the routing baseline
decisions.driver: IPv6 routing plane: a stuck OSPFv3 adjacency or a not-Established IPv6 BGP peer blackholes dual-stack reachability while the IPv4 plane stays Up -- a silent half-failure unless explicitly checked.

evidence.summary: 17 OSPFv3 neighbor(s) stuck in a transient (non-FULL/non-2WAY) state (e.g. access1 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART), access10 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART), access11 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART), access12 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART), access13 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART), access14 10.0.0.9 (EXSTART)); 17 IPv6 BGP peer(s) not Established (e.g. access1 2001:DB8:0:9::9, access10 2001:DB8:0:9::9, access11 2001:DB8:0:9::9, access12 2001:DB8:0:9::9, access13 2001:DB8:0:9::9, access14 2001:DB8:0:9::9). OSPFv3 settles in FULL (or 2WAY between DROTHERs); any other state is a forming/stuck adjacency, and an IPv6 BGP peer is Established only when it advertises a prefix count -- a peer in Idle/Active/Connect exchanges no IPv6 routes. The dual-stack reachability riding that adjacency is dark even while the parallel IPv4 plane is Up, so the failure is invisible to an IPv4-only check. Confirm interface MTU and IPv6 link-local reachability for OSPFv3, and update-source / AS / address-family activation for IPv6 BGP, before dual-stack is trusted at cutover.
fields: ipv6_routing.bgp_ipv6_neighbors[].state (parse_bgp_ipv6_summary / show bgp ipv6 unicast summary)

principle.title: Restore the down IPv6 routing adjacency before freezing the routing baseline
principle.citation: Cisco, 'Troubleshoot OSPF Neighbor Problems' (Doc ID 13699) and 'Troubleshoot OSPF Neighbors Stuck in Exstart/Exchange State' (Doc ID 13684), plus 'Troubleshoot BGP Neighborship Connection Issues' (Doc ID 13752); RFC 5340 (OSPFv3) for link-local-sourced adjacency

decisions.recommended_action: 1) Read the exact stuck state first — 'show ospfv3 neighbor' / 'show ipv6 ospf neighbor' or 'show bgp ipv6 unicast summary' — because the state names the failing phase (INIT/EXSTART vs Idle/Active) and points straight at the cause. 2) Confirm L1-L3 underneath: interface up, and for IPv6 that the link-local is present and NOT in DUPLICATE state (a DAD failure on fe80:: silently kills OSPFv3/EIGRPv6 adjacency); for BGP, ping the peer's IPv6 address and confirm a route to it exists. 3) For OSPFv3 stuck in EXSTART/Exchange, check MTU on both ends first (the highest-yield cause), then reconcile hello/dead intervals, area ID, area type, and authentication; verify no ACL is dropping IP protocol 89. 4) For BGP stuck in Active/Idle, test TCP/179 reachability (telnet to 179) to separate an ACL/firewall/CoPP block from a routing problem, then verify remote-AS, 'update-source' (loopback peering), 'ebgp-multihop'/TTL for multihop eBGP, and any MD5/TCP-AO password. 5) Fix the one mismatched attribute, watch the neighbor walk to FULL / Established, and confirm the expected prefixes are now installed before clearing the cutover gate. Use 'debug ipv6 ospf adj'/'debug ipv6 ospf hello' or 'debug bgp ipv6 unicast' only to confirm a hypothesis, never as the first step on a production box.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier shortcuts are to bounce the neighbor ('clear bgp ipv6 unicast *' or 'clear ipv6 ospf process') hoping it re-converges, to mask an MTU mismatch with 'ipv6 ospf mtu-ignore' so EXSTART clears without fixing the underlying MTU, or to widen an ACL / loosen authentication to get the session up. Each can flip the adjacency green in seconds, but it ships the real defect into production — mtu-ignore lets oversized LSAs be dropped and corrupts the database, a flap re-converges onto the same broken state, and a loosened ACL/auth is a posture regression.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fixing the actual mismatched parameter costs a diagnostic pass and coordination with the peer's owner, but it yields an adjacency that stays up and a route table that is genuinely complete at cutover; the bounce-and-mask alternatives buy an immediately green status at the price of a latent black-hole, a corrupted LSDB, or a weakened control-plane that surfaces under load after the window closes.

decisions.title: Use a dedicated, unused native VLAN on inter-switch trunks -- never VLAN 1
decisions.driver: L2 edge hygiene: a dedicated native VLAN on trunks closes the VLAN-hopping/double-tag vector.

evidence.summary: 26 inter-switch trunk(s) across 17 switch(es) carry VLAN 1 as the native (untagged) VLAN -- a double-tagging / VLAN-hopping exposure and a hygiene gap; the target L2 edge must use a dedicated, unused native VLAN (and prune VLAN 1).

principle.title: Use a dedicated, unused native VLAN on inter-switch trunks -- never VLAN 1
principle.citation: Cisco L2 security hardening (dedicated native VLAN, 'vlan dot1q tag native', prune VLAN 1); 802.1Q double-tagging / VLAN-hopping; CIS Cisco benchmark trunk native-VLAN guidance.

decisions.recommended_action: Assign a dedicated, unused native VLAN (not 1, not a data VLAN) on every inter-switch trunk and prune VLAN 1 from trunks; optionally enforce 'vlan dot1q tag native' so even the native VLAN is tagged. Apply it consistently on BOTH trunk ends (a native-VLAN mismatch is its own fault), and bake the chosen native VLAN into the target build template.
decisions.alternatives: Tag the native VLAN globally (vlan dot1q tag native) instead of choosing a dedicated one (closes the hop, keeps VLAN 1 plumbing); leave native as VLAN 1 and rely on access-edge controls only (weakest -- does not close the trunk-side double-tag vector).
decisions.tradeoffs: A dedicated native VLAN adds one VLAN id to the plan and a both-ends consistency requirement, but removes the untagged frame from every data segment and closes the VLAN-hopping vector.

decisions.title: Engineer a deterministic STP root at distribution, run Rapid-STP, and protect the topology (PortFast/BPDU/Root/Loop Guard, UDLD)
decisions.driver: Deterministic L2: rapid-PVST/MST, aligned roots, edge protection (BPDU-Guard), VTP off/transparent.

evidence.summary: 33 endpoint-bearing access port(s) across 20 switch(es) have no BPDU-Guard (an unprotected L2 edge) -- L2 control is not deterministic and the edge is not protected.

principle.title: Engineer a deterministic STP root at distribution, run Rapid-STP, and protect the topology (PortFast/BPDU/Root/Loop Guard, UDLD)
principle.citation: CCDE Session 16 (root at distribution, Rapid STP, BPDU/Root/Loop Guard, UDLD); engine STP parsing

decisions.recommended_action: Hard-set primary/secondary root on distribution for every VLAN/MST instance aligned to the active gateway; run Rapid-PVST/RSTP (MST at scale); enable BPDU Guard globally for PortFast edge ports, Root Guard on non-root ports, Loop Guard + UDLD on fibre (aggressive only on dual-homed).
decisions.alternatives: Routed access to remove STP from the edge entirely; MST for per-instance control at scale; UplinkFast/BackboneFast on legacy PVST.
decisions.tradeoffs: Deterministic optimal L2 paths, fast convergence and loop safety vs the discipline of explicit priorities and a small risk of err-disabling a legitimately-connected switch port or, with UDLD aggressive on a single-homed link, isolating a device with no backup path.

decisions.title: Synchronize time (hierarchical NTP), centralize severity-tuned logging, and keep a current baseline + documentation
decisions.driver: Operational baseline: an unsynchronized clock silently corrupts log correlation, certificate/Kerberos validity, and the post-cutover audit trail -- worse than absent NTP because the 'ntp server' line implies time discipline that is not actually in effect.

evidence.summary: 1 device(s) have an UNSYNCHRONIZED clock (core1 (stratum 16)) -- NTP is not locked to a reference (stratum 16 / no sync peer), even where an 'ntp server' is configured. A wrong clock makes cross-device log correlation, certificate-validity and Kerberos/802.1X checks, and post-cutover forensic reconstruction unreliable; restore reachable, authenticated NTP from a trusted stratum and confirm 'show ntp status' reports the clock synchronized before baselining.  |  also: 17 device(s) lack authenticated time sync and/or centralised logging (no-ntp/no-logging) -- without NTP-disciplined, correlated timestamps the fleet cannot be reliably troubleshot or forensically reconstructed across devices.
fields: ntp[].synchronized (parse_ntp_status / show ntp status | show ntp peer-status)

principle.title: Synchronize time (hierarchical NTP), centralize severity-tuned logging, and keep a current baseline + documentation
principle.citation: CCDE Session 19 (NTP stratum, syslog levels, baseline & documentation); engine CIS axis + baseline output

decisions.recommended_action: Deploy hierarchical authenticated NTP from trusted strata to the whole fleet; forward all logs to a central NTP-stamped syslog/SIEM with per-platform severity tuned to capture warnings/errors while suppressing chatty debug; capture and maintain a baseline + layered documentation via automated discovery.
decisions.alternatives: PTP/IEEE-1588 for sub-microsecond needs; streaming telemetry/EEM for high-value events; tiered (local+central) collectors at scale; periodic audit-and-reconcile instead of fully automated capture.
decisions.tradeoffs: Correlatable logs, reliable time-crypto, informed design and anomaly detection vs the effort to design/secure a stratum hierarchy and to keep logs and documentation current (stale docs mislead, verbose logging stresses devices); fault visibility vs log volume/storage/exposure.

decisions.title: Establish a QoS trust boundary at the edge and a coherent end-to-end policy from app requirements
decisions.driver: Application performance: real-time traffic needs a trust boundary and queuing.

evidence.summary: 18 of 18 assessable device(s) carry no QoS configuration -- there is no trust boundary at the access/voice edge and all traffic is best-effort.

principle.title: Establish a QoS trust boundary at the edge and a coherent end-to-end policy from app requirements
principle.citation: CCDE In Depth Ch.2 M&A & Applications (150ms/30ms/1%); engine compute_qos_audit; Cisco Borderless Campus QoS

decisions.recommended_action: Define a trust boundary at the access edge (trust phones/markings, re-mark untrusted ports), deploy a consistent end-to-end queuing policy sized to the app budgets, and unify divergent per-site QoS into one standard; trust access markings in the core rather than re-classifying.
decisions.alternatives: Bandwidth over-provisioning instead of QoS in a simple capacity-rich core; per-domain QoS with re-marking only at boundaries; admission control where capacity is constrained.
decisions.tradeoffs: Application performance vs simplicity — QoS adds classification/queuing to every hop; a capacity-rich core may deliberately omit it and over-provision instead. Trusting too liberally lets hosts game queues; trusting too little drops legitimate marks.

decisions.title: Harden the device baseline: disable unneeded services, lock management, protect the control plane
decisions.driver: Reduce the control-plane attack surface to a CIS-style baseline.

evidence.summary: 18 device(s) deviate from the device-hardening baseline (risky services, logging/NTP/banner, or unused/undefined config structures).

principle.title: Harden the device baseline: disable unneeded services, lock management, protect the control plane
principle.citation: CCDE Session 13 (device hardening, control plane); engine config-security/CIS axis

decisions.recommended_action: Apply the hardening baseline (disable unneeded services, SSH-only + VTY ACL, password encryption, banners, timeouts, AAA for admin) and deploy CoPP + ICMP/feature rate-limits.
decisions.alternatives: Per-platform hardening templates vs a centrally-pushed CIS profile; keep CDP/LLDP on infrastructure-facing links only; hardware-policed vs software-only CoPP.
decisions.tradeoffs: Reduced attack surface and control-plane survivability vs operational convenience (CDP aids discovery, proxy-ARP eases addressing) and the risk of dropping legitimate control traffic if CoPP policers are mistuned.

decisions.title: Engineer an explicit STP root priority on every active VLAN -- never let the root be elected by the MAC tiebreak
decisions.driver: Deterministic L2: the STP root must be explicitly placed, never left to a MAC-address tiebreak.

evidence.summary: 17 spanning-tree root election(s) across 17 switch(es) were won at the DEFAULT bridge priority (32768 + VLAN id) on the MAC tiebreak -- the root is accidental, not engineered, so a newly-introduced switch with a lower MAC can silently steal the root at cutover and move the L2 topology. Set explicit 'root primary/secondary' co-located with the active gateway.

principle.title: Engineer an explicit STP root priority on every active VLAN -- never let the root be elected by the MAC tiebreak
principle.citation: Cisco STP design (default bridge priority 32768, lowest-MAC tiebreak, explicit root primary/secondary); web-verified.

decisions.recommended_action: Configure 'spanning-tree vlan X root primary' on the intended root (priority 24576) and 'root secondary' (28672) on its peer, co-located with the active FHRP gateway, for every production VLAN; re-verify after introducing any new switch in the migration.
decisions.alternatives: Move to MST and engineer the per-instance root; or a routed-access / spine-leaf target where STP root placement stops being the failover mechanism.
decisions.tradeoffs: Deterministic, gateway-aligned L2 forwarding and a safe cutover vs a one-time priority-engineering pass across the VLANs (and keeping primary/secondary aligned with the FHRP active).

decisions.title: Enable the full IPv6 first-hop security suite at the access edge -- RA-Guard, DHCPv6-Guard, ND inspection/device-tracking, IPv6 Source Guard
decisions.driver: IPv6 access-edge security: an unguarded dual-stack segment lets a rogue RA seize the default gateway (NDP is as spoofable as ARP); RA-Guard/DHCPv6-Guard is the L2-edge countermeasure.

evidence.summary: 17 dual-stack access switch(es) have IPv6 gateways (VLAN(s) 10) but NO RA-Guard on the host-facing edge -- a single rogue or fat-fingered Router Advertisement hijacks the default gateway for the whole segment (RFC 6104 -> MITM/DoS). 17 of them also have no DHCPv6-Guard (rogue-DHCPv6 -> address theft). Enable RA-Guard + DHCPv6-Guard on every host-facing access port (trust only the real router/server uplinks), then layer ND inspection / device-tracking and IPv6 Source Guard.

principle.title: Enable the full IPv6 first-hop security suite at the access edge -- RA-Guard, DHCPv6-Guard, ND inspection/device-tracking, IPv6 Source Guard
principle.citation: Cisco IPv6 First-Hop Security (RA-Guard, DHCPv6-Guard, ND inspection, Source Guard); RFC 6104; web-verified.

decisions.recommended_action: On every host-facing access port enable RA-Guard + DHCPv6-Guard (only real uplinks trusted), enable IPv6 ND inspection / device-tracking to build the binding table, then layer IPv6 Source Guard off that table; apply even on IPv4-only segments where hosts are IPv6-capable (block rogue RAs).
decisions.alternatives: Disable IPv6 on truly IPv6-free access (rarely clean -- hosts often still process RAs); SEND (cryptographic ND) where supported and required.
decisions.tradeoffs: security (gateway-hijack / ND-spoof / address-theft prevention) vs the access-port configuration discipline (mark only real router/server uplinks trusted) and platform feature support.

decisions.title: Harden the L2 access edge: port-security, DHCP snooping, DAI, IP Source Guard, storm-control, 802.1X
decisions.driver: Access-edge integrity: a port-security shutdown is a real outage of a user/endpoint port; an unexplained violation may also be an active L2 attack (MAC flooding / rogue device).

evidence.summary: 17 access port(s) are ERR-DISABLED by a port-security violation (Port Status Secure-shutdown): access1 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access2 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access3 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access4 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access5 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access6 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access7 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099), access8 Gi0/3 (offender 0011.22aa.0099). A shutdown-mode violation drops ALL traffic on the port -- including the authorized endpoint -- so each is a live access outage with an evidenced offending MAC. Triage the violation (rogue device, MAC move, or a too-tight max), clear err-disable, and right-size port-security (sticky/MAC limits) before the migration baseline.

principle.title: Harden the L2 access edge: port-security, DHCP snooping, DAI, IP Source Guard, storm-control, 802.1X
principle.citation: CCDE Session 13/16 (L2 security suite, 802.1X/NAC); CCDE Session 15 (IPv6 RA/DHCPv6 Guard); engine CIS axis

decisions.recommended_action: Standardize the access-edge bundle (port-security, DHCP snooping + IP Source Guard + DAI with trusted uplinks, storm-control, 802.1X with MAB/guest fallback); add RA Guard/DHCPv6 Guard for IPv6.
decisions.alternatives: Private VLANs/VLAN ACLs for isolation; MAB where 802.1X is infeasible; monitor-mode/open-auth phased 802.1X rollout; static port-to-MAC for fixed assets.
decisions.tradeoffs: L2 integrity and broadcast-domain stability vs configuration/operational burden and onboarding friction (snooping trust ports, DAI bindings, port-security limits, 802.1X supplicant coverage and fail-open/closed handling).

decisions.title: Build redundancy as triangles, not squares or rings
decisions.driver: Physical redundancy: recovery should not depend on a single link or node.

evidence.summary: 17 link(s) are cut-edges (their loss partitions the topology — the worst isolates 22 node-pair(s), and 17 cut-edge(s) each isolate >=20); 19 device(s) strand endpoints with no backup path on failure.

principle.title: Build redundancy as triangles, not squares or rings
principle.citation: CCDE In Depth Ch.2 Network Topologies ('Build Triangles, Not Squares'); CCDE Switching/DC Q1

decisions.recommended_action: Re-cable to triangle/partial-mesh between distribution and core so each node has a direct alternate path; dual-home every access switch and bond uplinks (vPC/VSS/MLAG) so both forward.
decisions.alternatives: Keep the ring but add MPLS-TE FRR (protects any topology including rings); full mesh only where the demand matrix warrants the cost; spine-leaf ECMP at L3.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast-convergence/optimal-routing vs cost — more cross-links and ports cost money (full mesh is most expensive), so add just enough links to turn a ring/square into a partial mesh where demand or convergence justifies it.

decisions.title: Remediate physical-layer faults (CRC / input-errors / half-duplex / err-disable) before cutover
decisions.driver: Clean baseline: do not carry CRC/duplex/err-disable faults across the migration, or NRFU cannot certify it.

evidence.summary: 11 port(s) show physical-layer faults (11 CRC, 11 input-error, 0 late-collision, 0 output-error, 0 half-duplex, 11 err-disabled) -- a dirty L1 is migrated into the new fabric on the same cable/optic and corrupts the NRFU baseline; remediate cabling/optics/duplex/err-disable and re-baseline counters before cutover.

principle.title: Remediate physical-layer faults (CRC / input-errors / half-duplex / err-disable) before cutover
principle.citation: IEEE 802.3 auto-negotiation (duplex mismatch -> late collisions / CRC); Cisco IOS/NX-OS interface error-counter troubleshooting; NRFU/ATP clean-baseline practice.

decisions.recommended_action: Triage and clear the physical faults before the window: reseat/replace optics and cabling on CRC/input-error ports, hard-set or correct duplex/speed on half-duplex links (no auto/half mismatch), and resolve the root cause behind each err-disable (don't just recover the port). Then re-baseline error counters to zero so NRFU can certify the cutover against a clean L1.
decisions.alternatives: Carry the faults and remediate post-cutover (cheapest now, but the new fabric starts degraded and the acceptance baseline is meaningless); replace the affected hardware wholesale during the refresh (clean, but higher BoM cost).
decisions.tradeoffs: Pre-cutover L1 remediation costs field time and possibly optics/cabling spend, but is the only way to guarantee the target is born clean and the NRFU baseline is trustworthy.

decisions.title: Bound the Layer-2 failure domain: a bridged VLAN is one fault domain
decisions.driver: Bound the L2 blast radius: a bridged VLAN is one fault domain -- confine VLAN span, route between blocks, isolate any required stretch.

evidence.summary: 3 user VLAN(s) each span >= 8 switches (widest: VLAN 10 data across 19 switches;) -- a transparently-bridged VLAN is a single failure domain, so a broadcast storm, STP topology change or flood on any of these reaches every switch and endpoint in its span.

principle.title: Bound the Layer-2 failure domain: a bridged VLAN is one fault domain
principle.citation: ipSpace.net (Pepelnjak) 'A Layer-2 Network Is a Single Failure Domain' / 'The Need for Stretched VLANs'; Cisco CCDA hierarchical-design best practice (no VLAN across multiple access switches)

decisions.recommended_action: Confine each VLAN to the smallest practical span (ideally one access switch / one block); route between blocks at L3 (routed access or a distribution boundary) so an L2 event stays local; prune VLAN 1 and unused VLANs off trunks; where a stretch is unavoidable, isolate it (e.g. a controlled VXLAN/overlay segment with storm-control) rather than raw end-to-end bridging.
decisions.alternatives: Keep wide L2 with aggressive storm-control/BPDU-guard and rapid-PVST/MST hardening (accepts a large blast radius); overlay (VXLAN/EVPN) to contain bridging to the edge.
decisions.tradeoffs: Smaller failure domains add L3 boundaries/addressing and can complicate workload mobility, but bound the blast radius and improve convergence and scale.

decisions.title: Preserve dual-homed endpoints across move-groups -- move both attachment points together
decisions.driver: Preserve redundancy: a migration must not transiently collapse a dual-homed endpoint to one path.

evidence.summary: 3 dual-homed endpoint(s) (a MAC present on two switches) depend on both attachment points staying up -- the move-group plan must move both attachment switches of each in the same wave; and reconcile 1 shared-IP set(s) (FHRP VIP vs conflict), or the migration silently single-homes them during the most fragile phase.

principle.title: Preserve dual-homed endpoints across move-groups -- move both attachment points together
principle.citation: Cisco Advanced Services migration move-group methodology (preserve endpoint redundancy across waves); NIC-teaming / dual-homing dependency on both network paths.

decisions.recommended_action: Constrain the move-group/wave generator so BOTH attachment switches of each dual-homed endpoint land in the SAME wave; validate per wave that each endpoint still has two live paths after the move; and classify every shared-IP set (legitimate FHRP/anycast vs a real duplicate to renumber) before cutover.
decisions.alternatives: Move purely by switch/closet ignoring multi-homing (simplest plan, but transiently single-homes endpoints); freeze the dual-homed endpoints to a single big-bang wave (safer for them, less granular rollback for everything else).
decisions.tradeoffs: Multi-homing constraints make the wave plan less free (some waves grow to keep both legs of an endpoint together), but they preserve the very redundancy the endpoints were built with.

decisions.title: Restore the down DMVPN/NHRP spoke before treating the overlay topology as complete
decisions.driver: DMVPN WAN overlay: a tunnel peer not in UP (NHRP/IKE/down) has no overlay forwarding to that spoke/hub site -- the remote location is unreachable across the WAN.

evidence.summary: 2 DMVPN tunnel peer(s) are NOT in the UP state (e.g. core1 10.0.1.3 (NHRP), core1 10.0.1.4 (IKE)). DMVPN carries the WAN overlay over an mGRE interface with NHRP next-hop resolution and IPsec protection; UP is the only fully-established state, so a peer stuck in NHRP (next-hop unresolved), IKE (IPsec/IKE still negotiating) or down has no overlay forwarding to that spoke/hub -- the remote site is unreachable across the WAN even while the tunnel interface and underlay may appear up. Confirm NBMA reachability to the NHS, NHRP registration / authentication, and the IKE/IPsec profile to the peer before relying on the overlay at cutover.

principle.title: Restore the down DMVPN/NHRP spoke before treating the overlay topology as complete
principle.citation: Cisco — Troubleshoot Common DMVPN Issues (NHRP registration/state, 'verify the GRE tunnels work fine without IPsec encryption', show dmvpn detail / show ip nhrp nhs detail)

decisions.recommended_action: Work the dependency chain bottom-up, exactly as Cisco's DMVPN troubleshooting method prescribes — verify GRE/NHRP before blaming IPsec. (1) On the hub, run 'show dmvpn detail' and 'show ip nhrp nhs detail' to confirm whether the spoke is registered and in which state (UP vs NHRP/IKE); a peer that never reaches UP is a registration failure, one that flaps points at holdtime/keepalive or an unstable underlay. (2) Confirm underlay reachability of the spoke's NBMA address and that IKE/IPsec transport (UDP 500/4500, ESP) is permitted end-to-end — a NAT device newly in path or an ACL on the transport is the classic cause. (3) Validate the GRE/tunnel layer in isolation (tunnel source/destination, NHRP network-id, authentication, and the NHS address the spoke is configured to register to); Cisco's guidance is to prove the GRE tunnel works before layering IPsec. (4) Only then descend into the crypto session (see ipsec-crypto-session-down) if NHRP registration is initiating but the protected session will not establish. (5) Re-verify with 'show dmvpn detail' that the peer reaches UP and that NHRP shortcuts re-form before clearing the finding.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to accept the spoke as 'down but covered' — rely on a backup NHS or an alternate WAN/MPLS path and proceed, deferring the fix — or to bounce the tunnel interface to force a fresh NHRP registration without finding the root cause.
decisions.tradeoffs: Deferring saves a maintenance touch now but carries an unresolved single-site fault (and an unverified spoke-to-spoke data plane) into the cutover baseline, so a benign-looking redundancy event during the window can silently isolate the branch.

decisions.title: Characterize egress queue drops and prove they spare sensitive classes before freezing the QoS baseline
decisions.driver: Application performance at runtime: a QoS class dropping its own traffic (especially the LLQ) proves the policy is mis-sized -- the intent exists on paper but fails under load.

evidence.summary: 2 egress QoS class/queue(s) are dropping traffic at runtime (core1 Gi1/0/24 class VOICE 1,840,521 drops (6.9%/LLQ), core1 Gi1/0/24 class BULK-DATA 512,000 drops (5.8%)). 1 of these are PRIORITY/LLQ class(es) -- real-time traffic is being congestion-dropped, which a priority queue must never do. A class shedding a material share of its traffic means the configured QoS is not protecting the traffic its intent classified -- the queue/policer is undersized, the class is misclassified, or the link is oversubscribed. Right-size the priority bandwidth / queue-limit (and the policer) for the real load, and re-verify the drop counters are flat before cutover.

principle.title: Characterize egress queue drops and prove they spare sensitive classes before freezing the QoS baseline
principle.citation: Cisco — Troubleshoot Output Drops on Catalyst 9000 Switches (per-queue 'show platform hardware fed ... qos queue stats/config', Hardmax/Softmax buffers, microburst mitigation via qos queue-softmax-multiplier)

decisions.recommended_action: Diagnose by isolating the queue, not by globally widening buffers. (1) Confirm and rate the drops with 'show interfaces <intf>' (total output drops and trend) — a tiny, stable count on a best-effort class may be acceptable; a growing count or any count on a priority class is not. (2) On Catalyst 9000, attribute drops to a specific queue with 'show platform hardware fed switch active qos queue stats interface <intf>' and inspect the buffer allocation with 'show platform hardware fed switch active qos queue config interface <intf>' (Hardmax/Softmax); on routers/MQC platforms use 'show policy-map interface <intf>' to see per-class queue and drop counters. (3) Determine the cause class — sustained oversubscription (a capacity/topology fix), microbursts (a buffer/queue-limit fix), or a queueing policy that starves a class. (4) For microbursts, raise the shared-buffer headroom first as the low-risk mitigation ('qos queue-softmax-multiplier', default 100, up to the platform maximum) and/or tune the specific queue-limit; for a class being starved, correct the egress queuing/bandwidth policy so priority traffic is protected. (5) For genuine oversubscription, the real fix is capacity (more/faster uplinks, load-balancing, or moving the talker) — buffers only defer the loss. Re-verify per-queue stats after the change and confirm sensitive classes show zero drops.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper alternatives are to accept the drops as normal best-effort behavior and move on (valid only once you have proven no priority/latency-sensitive class is affected), or to bump the softmax buffer multiplier globally as a blanket absorber without identifying the offending queue.
decisions.tradeoffs: Accepting or buffering-over the drops avoids a QoS redesign and a capacity spend now, but deeper buffers add latency/jitter and only mask microbursts — for true oversubscription the loss is merely deferred, so an uncharacterized drop on a voice/control queue can surface as a service outage after cutover concentrates more traffic on the link.

decisions.title: Restore any leaf/spine that is not Active to the registered Active state before relying on the fabric
decisions.driver: Controller-fabric inventory: a node present in the APIC MIT but not active is a ghost asset or an admin-vs-operational divergence that distorts the fabric census and cutover blast radius.

evidence.summary: 1 ACI fabric node(s) are present in the APIC inventory but NOT active (e.g. core2 node 102 leaf-102-OLD (decommissioned)). A decommissioned node still in the MIT is a ghost asset (cutover blast-radius, stale license/serial); an inactive/disabled node is the controller's own admin-vs-operational divergence -- the fabric reports it down while it remains provisioned. Reconcile each node against the intended fabric inventory and fully decommission or recover it before the node census and cutover blast-radius depend on it.

principle.title: Restore any leaf/spine that is not Active to the registered Active state before relying on the fabric
principle.citation: Troubleshoot ACI Fabric Discovery — Initial Fabric Setup (node discovery states, uplink/LLDP/infra-VLAN/TEP/DHCP checks, acidiag avread, show discoveryissues, certificate validation); Cisco APIC Getting Started Guide — Fabric Initialization and Switch Discovery (Undiscovered->Discovered->Active, registration); ACI System Messages — F0110 fltFabricNodeFailed

decisions.recommended_action: Walk the discovery state machine in order — physical, then identity, then trust — rather than re-registering blindly. (1) Confirm the node's current state in Fabric > Inventory > Fabric Membership / Nodes Pending Registration. (2) PHYSICAL: verify the inter-switch cabling and that the leaf port to the spine is an UPLINK (a downlink will not relay the spine's DHCP, a classic discovery blocker); check the LLDP neighbor with 'show lldp neighbors detail' on the peer and confirm both sides run a supported, compatible image. (3) IDENTITY: from the leaf run 'acidiag avread' (or 'avread') to confirm it sees the APICs and an infra TEP from the configured TEP pool over the correct infra VLAN; if it is unregistered, register it with the intended node ID. (4) TRUST: on 4.2+ run 'show discoveryissues' on the node to surface certificate/clock/connectivity failures, and validate the node certificate and APIC cluster reachability ('Fully Fit'). (5) Resolve the surfaced cause, confirm the node transitions to Active and its F0110/related faults clear, and only then admit it to the cutover scope. For a true replacement, follow the documented decommission/replace procedure so the old serial and TEP are cleanly reused.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier alternative is to exclude the dead node from the cut and proceed on the survivors — migrating onto the remaining Active leaf/spine and deferring the inactive one — instead of fixing discovery first.
decisions.tradeoffs: Proceeding on the survivors keeps the schedule but converts a redundant pair into a single point of failure for the duration of the window, and if the not-Active node was a target, you simply have insufficient capacity/landing space and discover it mid-cutover.

decisions.title: Keep every Arista MLAG domain active, connected and config-consistent (the vPC-equivalent dual-active primitive)
decisions.driver: Arista MLAG is the vPC-equivalent dual-active redundancy primitive: an inconsistent / peer-link-down / single-homed MLAG domain has no working standby and can silently suspend VLANs -- the config-present-but-operationally-broken false-health trap, on a non-Cisco platform.

evidence.summary: 1 Arista MLAG domain(s) are configured but operationally degraded (e.g. core2 (config-sanity inconsistent, 2 inactive MLAG port(s))). MLAG is Arista's dual-active redundancy primitive -- the analogue of Cisco vPC -- so a peer that is inconsistent, has its peer-link down, cannot negotiate, or carries Inactive / single-homed member ports has lost (or is silently suspending) the redundancy the downstream devices depend on: a config-sanity mismatch SUSPENDS the affected VLANs exactly as a vPC Type-1 inconsistency does, and a peer-link loss risks a dual-active split. 'mlag' present in the running-config is NOT evidence of working redundancy; only the operational state is. Reconcile the peer configuration (config-sanity), confirm the peer-link and member-port state, and restore the domain to active + connected + consistent before the pair is on the cutover path.

principle.title: Keep every Arista MLAG domain active, connected and config-consistent (the vPC-equivalent dual-active primitive)
principle.citation: Arista EOS User Manual (Multi-Chassis Link Aggregation); Arista Network Test Automation (ANTA) MLAG health tests (VerifyMlagStatus / VerifyMlagConfigSanity / VerifyMlagInterfaces); analogous to the Cisco Nexus vPC consistency model

decisions.recommended_action: Reconcile the peer configuration until 'show mlag config-sanity' is consistent, confirm the peer-link and member-port state, and restore the domain to active + connected + consistent before the pair is on the cutover path. Treat 'mlag' in the running-config as intent, not proof -- verify the operational state.
decisions.alternatives: Single-homed access (no dual-active redundancy -- a switch failure is an outage); a different dual-active technology where the platform supports it. Neither removes the need to verify the chosen redundancy is operationally healthy.
decisions.tradeoffs: MLAG adds a peer-link and a config-consistency burden across two control planes, but is the standard way to give downstream devices a loop-free, non-blocking, dual-homed attachment on Arista -- the same trade as Cisco vPC.

decisions.title: Restore the down BFD session before baselining — its protected protocol has lost sub-second failure detection
decisions.driver: Fast failover: a BFD session in the Down state removes sub-second failure detection for its client protocol, dropping convergence back to slow native timers (AdminDown / Up are not flagged).

evidence.summary: 1 BFD session(s) are in the Down state (e.g. core1 10.0.255.9 (Gi1/0/3)). BFD provides sub-second forwarding-path failure detection for its client protocol (OSPF/BGP/EIGRP/HSRP/static); a session that is Down means that fast-failover is broken and the client has fallen back to its native (multi-second) convergence timers, so a link or next-hop failure no longer converges in milliseconds. Confirm the L1/L2 path and IGP/BGP adjacency to the neighbor, matching BFD interval/multiplier and echo settings on both ends, and any platform BFD-offload limit before the fast-convergence design is trusted at cutover.

principle.title: Restore the down BFD session before baselining — its protected protocol has lost sub-second failure detection
principle.citation: IETF RFC 5880, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) — session states (Down/Init/Up) and diagnostic codes (Control Detection Time Expired / Echo Function Failed / Neighbor Signaled Session Down); BFD reports state change to registered clients which take action. Corroborated by Cisco 'Troubleshoot Bidirectional Forwarding Detection in Cisco IOS XE' (Doc ID 220364) — UDP/3784, async vs echo, ACL-log breakage, `show bfd neighbors details`.

decisions.recommended_action: Work the session from the bottom of the stack up. (1) Confirm the underlying L1/L2 path and IP reachability first — `show bfd neighbors [details]` for the session's last-down diagnostic, plus `show ip interface brief` / line-protocol on the interface; a flapping or down interface is the usual root cause. (2) If the link is up, rule out a configuration asymmetry: BFD must be enabled on BOTH peers, and the operating mode (asynchronous vs. echo) and the negotiated tx/rx/multiplier timers must be compatible — a one-sided 'bfd interval' or an echo-mode mismatch leaves the session stuck Down. (3) Confirm the protocol client is actually registered (e.g. `bfd` under the BGP neighbor / `bfd all-interfaces` under OSPF) — BFD with no client does nothing. (4) Verify nothing is dropping the BFD control packets on the path: an interface ACL that permits BFD but carries the `log` keyword, or that misses UDP/3784 (and the echo-source for multihop), will break the session even though data forwards; check CoPP on the supervisor for BFD-class drops too. (5) Only once the session reaches Up with stable timers do you re-baseline and treat fast-failover as available for the gate.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to proceed without BFD and rely on the routing protocol's native fast-timers (aggressive OSPF/BGP hello/hold), or to simply note the session down and cut over anyway, planning to fix it post-migration.
decisions.tradeoffs: Aggressive native timers cost CPU and risk false-positive flaps under load and have a detection floor far above BFD's, so cutting over with BFD down trades a few minutes of diagnosis now for a real risk of a multi-second (or longer) black-hole during the very failover the change is designed to exercise.

decisions.title: Never expose an admin / database port (or all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0 in a cloud security group
decisions.driver: Cloud exposure: a security group open from 0.0.0.0/0 to an admin / DB / all port puts the host's management or data plane on the public internet -- the highest-signal, vendor-authoritative cloud-segmentation finding (surface OPEN, not vulnerable).

evidence.summary: 1 cloud security-group rule(s) expose a sensitive port to the whole internet (e.g. sg-0bastion (port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0)). A security group that allows inbound from 0.0.0.0/0 (or ::/0) to an admin port (SSH/RDP), a database port, or ALL ports means the host behind it is reachable from anywhere -- the management / data plane is exposed to the entire internet (CIS AWS Foundations 5.2/5.3). This is a surface-OPEN finding, not a proven compromise, but it is the single most common cloud-exposure anti-pattern and a cutover / inheritance risk. Restrict the source to the specific admin/peering CIDRs (or a bastion / VPN / SSM), and re-scope any 'all ports / all protocols' rule, before the workload is migrated or the account is in production.

principle.title: Never expose an admin / database port (or all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0 in a cloud security group
principle.citation: CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark 5.2 / 5.3 (no security group allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to port 22 / 3389); AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar; AWS EC2 DescribeSecurityGroups API

decisions.recommended_action: Restrict the source to the specific admin / peering CIDRs, or front the access with a bastion / VPN / SSM Session Manager; re-scope any 'all ports / all protocols' rule to the minimum required; and verify there is no inherited world-open admin path before the workload is migrated or the account goes to production. Pair with VPC flow logs + a network-exposure analyzer.
decisions.alternatives: A public load balancer / WAF in front of a private subnet (the host has no world-open rule at all); zero-trust access (SSM / Identity-Aware Proxy) instead of network reachability. Both remove the world-open admin port entirely.
decisions.tradeoffs: Locking the source CIDRs (or adding a bastion) adds a small operational step versus leaving a port open to the world, but removes the highest-signal cloud-exposure path -- the same defence-in-depth trade as a least-privilege firewall rule on-prem.

decisions.title: Identify which CoPP class is dropping and why before the cutover — the policer is shielding the supervisor, not failing
decisions.driver: Control-plane protection: a CoPP class dropping punted traffic either clips legitimate protocol packets (convergence/adjacency risk) or signals a control-plane flood; neither should be carried silently into a migration baseline.

evidence.summary: 1 control-plane-policing (CoPP) class(es) are actively dropping punted traffic (e.g. core2 MGMT-RATE-LIMIT) -- 4521 total discarded. CoPP drops mean CPU-bound traffic is being policed: either the policer is mistuned and clipping legitimate control-plane traffic (routing/ARP/management punts -> adjacency flaps, slow convergence) or a control-plane flood/DoS is starving the supervisor. Identify the dropping class, confirm whether the offered rate is legitimate, and re-baseline the policer (raise the CIR) or trace and suppress the source before cutover.

principle.title: Identify which CoPP class is dropping and why before the cutover — the policer is shielding the supervisor, not failing
principle.citation: Cisco 'Verify Control Plane Policing Violations on Nexus Platforms' (Doc ID 217946) — `show policy-map interface control-plane` violated/dropped-bytes and 5-min violate-rate interpretation, and triage of drops as attack vs. misconfiguration; with Cisco Nexus 9000 NX-OS Security Configuration Guide (Configure CoPP) — default 'strict' start point and per-class CIR/BC tuning as an ongoing process; and the Cisco 'Control Plane Policing Implementation Best Practices' note.

decisions.recommended_action: Attribute, then decide — never blindly raise rates. (1) Pin down which class and how hard: on NX-OS `show policy-map interface control-plane` exposes per-class conformed vs. violated/dropped bytes plus the 5-minute violate rate and violated-peak timestamp; correlate the spike with a change/event window. (2) Classify the drop: map the class back to its CoPP ACL and confirm whether the source is legitimate control traffic at volume or anomalous (a single talker, a scan, a loop/glean storm — for glean specifically, fix next-hop reachability and enable `hardware ip glean throttle` rather than widening the policer). (3) If the traffic is legitimate and the rate is simply too small for this fleet, tune that specific class's CIR/BC upward from the appropriate default profile (strict/moderate/lenient/dense) — Cisco's guidance is to start from the default 'strict' policy and then customize per the protocols and scale actually present, treating CoPP as an ongoing baseline that must be revisited whenever devices/services are added (i.e. at every migration). (4) Re-measure to confirm drops for that class fall to zero/transient under normal load before declaring the control plane clean for the gate.
decisions.alternatives: The fast options are to leave the default policy untouched and accept the drops, or to swap to a more permissive profile (moderate/lenient) or bump every class's rate wholesale so the violations disappear from the dashboard.
decisions.tradeoffs: Blanket-loosening CoPP makes the alarm go away but reopens the exact CPU-exhaustion attack surface CoPP exists to close, so the disciplined move is to widen only the one legitimately-saturated class by a measured amount — keeping protection intact while ensuring real BGP/ARP/LISP/BFD control traffic survives the cutover burst.

decisions.title: Re-establish the TrustSec environment-data download before cutover — without it the device has no SGT/SGACL policy to enforce
decisions.driver: TrustSec segmentation: a CTS environment-data set that is not COMPLETE leaves the device with no SGT-to-policy map, so group-based access control is silently unenforced (default-permit).

evidence.summary: 1 device(s) have CTS TrustSec environment-data that is NOT in the COMPLETE/valid downloaded state (e.g. core1 (WAITING_RESPONSE)). The environment-data download distributes the SGT-to-name table and SGACL policy from Cisco ISE; until it reaches COMPLETE the switch holds no group-to-policy map, so group-based (SGT/SGACL) segmentation is blind and unenforced -- traffic between security groups is default-permitted even though TrustSec is configured. Confirm PAC provisioning, RADIUS/ISE (CTS) server reachability and the 'cts authorization list' / 'cts refresh environment-data' before the segmentation policy is trusted at cutover.

principle.title: Re-establish the TrustSec environment-data download before cutover — without it the device has no SGT/SGACL policy to enforce
principle.citation: Cisco TrustSec Configuration Guide (Catalyst 9000) — 'SGACL and Environment Data Download over REST': environment-data contents and server failover (static-IP vs domain, private→public list, mark-dead/retry), TLS-handshake/HTTP-timeout/wrong-domain failure causes, ERS port 9063, and ISE NAD/NAS-IP REST prerequisites; with the Cisco TrustSec Troubleshooting Guide — `show cts environment-data` state=COMPLETE/Successful and the caution against refreshing env-data while ISE is unreachable in critical-auth mode (policies may clear).

decisions.recommended_action: Restore the device→ISE policy channel, then re-pull data — carefully. (1) Read the current state with `show cts environment-data` (and the server list / last-download status) to see whether it never downloaded, is stale, or marked all servers dead. (2) Verify the transport and trust: ISE reachability (the REST/ERS path is TCP/9063), TLS handshake success, correct server IP/FQDN (a wrong or unresolvable domain name is a common cause), and that the device's CTS credentials/PAC match what ISE has under the network device's Advanced TrustSec settings — and that ISE permits REST API calls from this NAD's NAS-IP. (3) Confirm server-selection health: TrustSec prefers a configured static IP, falls back to the domain name, marks a non-responding server dead, fails the private list over to the public list, and only retries on the next request after marking servers alive — so a single dead-server entry can stall the whole pull. (4) Trigger/allow a refresh and confirm state returns to COMPLETE with the expected SGT table populated. Critical ordering caveat: do NOT manually refresh environment data while ISE is unreachable and the 802.1X links are in critical-authentication mode — a refresh that fails can wipe the existing policies; fix reachability first, then refresh. Only a COMPLETE download with the expected SGTs clears the segmentation gate.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to proceed with whatever cached/stale environment data the device still holds, or to lean on the configured fallback/critical-authentication SGT and cut over, deferring the ISE fix to after the window.
