decisions.tradeoffs: Cutting over on stale or fallback policy means the segmentation you designed and certified is not actually enforced for those endpoints — an invisible east-west exposure — so the safe move is to verify a live COMPLETE download per enforcement node first, since fixing ISE reachability/credentials pre-cutover is cheap compared with discovering an unsegmented fabric in production.

decisions.title: Resolve active L2 instability (MAC flapping) before freezing the baseline / cutover
decisions.driver: Active L2 instability: a flapping MAC is a live loop / mis-cabling, so the current state is an unstable baseline and a storm risk to carry into the target.

evidence.summary: 1 switch(es) are logging MAC-address flapping (%SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF) — the same host learned on two ports, i.e. an ACTIVE L2 loop, a mis-cabled / dual-homed host bridging two access ports, or a unidirectional link. This is happening now: every flap re-floods and churns the VLAN's MAC table, and migrating a flapping domain carries the loop straight into the target where a fabric change can escalate it to a broadcast storm. Find and clear each flap before freezing the baseline and cutover.

principle.title: Resolve active L2 instability (MAC flapping) before freezing the baseline / cutover
principle.citation: Cisco MAC-flapping / %SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF troubleshooting (L2 loop, dual-homed host, unidirectional link); Cisco STP / UDLD loop-prevention design guidance.

decisions.recommended_action: For each flapping host, read the logged VLAN + the two ports, confirm STP state on both (a loop is a link that should be blocking but is forwarding -- resolve the root cause, do not just shut a port), check for a mis-cabled or dual-homed end host bridging two access ports, and rule out a unidirectional link (enable / verify UDLD, check the optic). Clear every active flap and confirm the domain is quiet for a sustained window BEFORE freezing its baseline and scheduling its cutover.
decisions.alternatives: Cut over with the flap unresolved and chase it after (cheapest now, but the target inherits the loop / mis-cabling and a fabric change can escalate it to a storm); port-disable the flapping port as a stop-gap (removes the symptom -- and possibly the host's connectivity -- not the cause).
decisions.tradeoffs: Diagnosing an active flap costs pre-cutover field / console time, but a flapping L2 domain is an unstable baseline and a live storm risk -- the only safe order is resolve, then baseline, then cut.

decisions.title: Discover and inventory undocumented (shadow) infrastructure before baselining the design
decisions.driver: Coverage / blast radius: an un-inventoried switch or router in the data path is a migration blind-spot -- you cannot assess the resilience of, or safely cut over around, a device you have not collected.

evidence.summary: 1 undocumented infrastructure neighbour(s) (switch/router) are visible over CDP/LLDP but absent from the assessed inventory: wan-edge-rtr1.lab. Each is an unmanaged device in the production path -- its uplinks, redundancy, software and end-of-support state are UNKNOWN, and a cutover wave that traverses it can fail silently. Add every shadow node to the inventory and collect it (or formally scope it out with the customer) before baselining the design.

principle.title: Discover and inventory undocumented (shadow) infrastructure before baselining the design
principle.citation: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) + IEEE 802.1AB LLDP capability codes (Switch/Router vs Trans-Bridge/Host/Phone); Cisco PPDIOO Prepare/Plan network-discovery & inventory-completeness practice.

decisions.recommended_action: Identify each shadow node from the advertising device+port and its CDP/LLDP platform/mgmt IP, then add it to the inventory and collect it (or formally scope it out WITH the customer and record it). Re-run discovery until every infra neighbour reconciles, then freeze the baseline.
decisions.alternatives: Proceed on the partial inventory and discover the device during cutover (cheapest now, but the wave starts blind to a live dependency).
decisions.tradeoffs: Chasing every neighbour costs discovery time, but it is the only way the inventory -- and the hardening/lifecycle/cutover plans built on it -- is provably complete rather than silently partial.

decisions.title: Make gateway failover deterministic: pair FHRP preempt with interface/object tracking before baselining
decisions.driver: Gateway resilience: an untracked active HSRP/VRRP gateway black-holes traffic on an uplink failure; preemption makes the elected primary deterministic.

evidence.summary: First-hop redundancy is configured but fragile: 1 active gateway(s) with NO interface tracking. An untracked active gateway keeps forwarding to a dead uplink; without preempt the elected primary is non-deterministic after a failover. Wire object/interface tracking to every active gateway and enable preempt with a delay.

principle.title: Make gateway failover deterministic: pair FHRP preempt with interface/object tracking before baselining
principle.citation: Cisco IOS XE First Hop Redundancy Protocols Configuration Guide — Configuring HSRP (standby preempt, standby track / object tracking, preempt delay); Cisco support doc 'Use Standby Preempt and Standby Track Commands'; RFC 2281 Cisco Hot Standby Router Protocol (priority/preemption/Coup, 3s/10s timers)

decisions.recommended_action: Resolve per group, primary side first: (1) Decide intended roles — set explicit priorities (do not leave both peers at the 100 default) so primary > secondary, and document which device should own each VLAN's gateway. (2) Add tracking on the device whose uplink loss should trigger hand-off — prefer enhanced object tracking (track an object for line-protocol or IP-routing state, or an IP SLA/route reachability object) over the legacy 'standby track <if>' so a tracked-uplink failure decrements priority below the peer; size the decrement so the crossover actually occurs (decrement > priority gap). (3) Enable preempt on the higher-priority router so it both reclaims after recovery and so a tracking-driven decrement on its peer results in a real failover. (4) Add 'preempt delay minimum' (and 'standby delay minimum reload') so a recovering/rebooting router waits for its routing table and uplinks to converge before seizing the gateway, avoiding a transient black hole. (5) For dual-supervisor/stacked platforms keep SSO/HSRP-aware redundancy so a switchover doesn't bounce the role. (6) Re-collect and confirm tracking decrements and preempt are present and roles match design before freezing the baseline.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to enable preempt alone (so the primary at least reclaims the gateway after recovery) and skip tracking. This restores predictable role ownership but leaves the worst failure unguarded: an Active router that loses its own uplink still advertises itself as the gateway and black-holes the subnet, because nothing decrements its priority. A second shortcut — raising priority but never enabling preempt on the primary — gives the appearance of a designed hierarchy while guaranteeing the primary never actually takes the role back.
decisions.tradeoffs: Adding tracking + tuned preempt/preempt-delay costs a short design and change-window effort per group and a brief, controlled failover during testing, in exchange for converting an undefined, evidence-blind gateway behavior into deterministic sub-second-to-seconds failover that the cutover acceptance test can actually prove.

decisions.title: A stateful firewall in the path needs an operational HA peer -- config-present is not redundancy
decisions.driver: Stateful-firewall HA: an enabled failover pair with a unit Failed/Disabled or the peer Not Detected has no standby -- a single point of failure in the data path, regardless of what the running-config claims.

evidence.summary: 1 Cisco firewall(s) have failover ENABLED but a unit in a broken state (e.g. core1: peer Secondary Failed). A firewall whose HA pair is Failed, has a unit Disabled, or cannot see its peer (Not Detected) has no working standby -- it is a single point of failure in the data path, and a failover during the maintenance window would drop every stateful connection through it. 'failover' present in the running-config is NOT evidence of redundancy; only the operational state is. Confirm the failover link, unit/interface health and config sync, and restore the standby to Standby Ready before the firewall is on the cutover path.

principle.title: A stateful firewall in the path needs an operational HA peer -- config-present is not redundancy
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall ASA HA / Failover configuration guide (the show failover state machine: Active / Standby Ready / Failed / Not Detected / Disabled); standard stateful-HA practice.

decisions.recommended_action: Treat the degraded pair as a cutover blocker: confirm the failover/state link is up, both units run compatible image + licensing, interface monitoring is healthy and config sync has completed, then restore the standby to Standby Ready BEFORE the firewall is on the cutover path. Where a firewall is intentionally standalone, design and document the accepted single-point-of-failure (or add a peer) -- do not leave a half-built pair.
decisions.alternatives: Active/active (multi-context) or clustering for scale + HA (more complex state/flow management); a single firewall with an explicitly accepted-risk standalone posture for a low-criticality edge.
decisions.tradeoffs: An HA pair doubles firewall cost and adds state-sync / coordinated-upgrade complexity, but removes the in-path single point of failure -- usually mandatory for a perimeter or inter-zone enforcement point.

decisions.title: Size the firewall above its OBSERVED peak -- a box denying or near its resource limits drops traffic
decisions.driver: Stateful-firewall capacity: a resource the box is denying (or peaking near its limit) is dropping or about to drop production traffic -- the replacement must be sized above the observed peak, not the current average.

evidence.summary: 1 firewall resource(s) are exhausted or near their configured limit (e.g. core1: Conns denied 312 (Limit 280000)). A data-plane resource with Denied > 0 means the firewall hit its Limit and DROPPED real connections / translations at peak; a Peak at >= 90% of the Limit means it is one busy interval from dropping. This is a hard sizing signal for the migration: the replacement (or consolidated) firewall must be sized with headroom above the OBSERVED peak, and any per-context / per-class connection limit re-evaluated, or the cutover inherits (and worsens) the drops. Confirm against 'show resource usage' / 'show perfmon' at peak before fixing the replacement's capacity.

principle.title: Size the firewall above its OBSERVED peak -- a box denying or near its resource limits drops traffic
principle.citation: Cisco ASA performance & resource-management docs (show resource usage Denied / Limit); Cisco Secure Firewall sizing / capacity guidance.

decisions.recommended_action: Size the replacement (or consolidated) firewall above the observed peak with headroom for growth AND failover (an HA pair must carry full load on one unit); re-evaluate per-context and per-class connection / embryonic limits; capture 'show resource usage' + 'show perfmon' at a real busy period as the sizing baseline and pin it into the NRFU acceptance.
decisions.alternatives: Raise the configured limits on the current platform if headroom exists (a stopgap, not a fix if the silicon is the bound); distribute load across an additional firewall / context.
decisions.tradeoffs: Sizing to peak + headroom costs more capacity up front, but a firewall that drops at peak is an availability incident a migration should resolve, not carry forward.

decisions.title: Every FMC-managed FTD must stay connected + healthy -- a disconnected device can't be deployed-to
decisions.driver: Controller-reported reachability: an FTD FMC reports disconnected/red is unmanaged and possibly partitioned -- it cannot be deployed-to or monitored during the migration.

evidence.summary: 1 FMC-managed FTD(s) have lost their management channel or are in a red health state (e.g. core1: AJ-FTD-99 (lost mgmt channel)). A device FMC reports not-connected cannot be monitored, templated or deployed-to and may be partitioned from management; a red health status is an active FMC alert. Confirm the device is powered, on-net and not mid-reboot/deploy, restore the FMC<->FTD management channel, and clear the health alert before the device is counted in-scope at cutover.

principle.title: Every FMC-managed FTD must stay connected + healthy -- a disconnected device can't be deployed-to
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center REST API (devicerecords isConnected / healthStatus).

decisions.recommended_action: Confirm the device is powered, on-net and not mid-reboot/deploy; restore the FMC<->FTD management channel and clear the health alert before counting the device in-scope at cutover.
decisions.alternatives: Out-of-band management path for resilience; local FDM management for a small site (loses central policy).
decisions.tradeoffs: A reliable management channel + health monitoring is operational overhead, but a device FMC can't reach is one you cannot safely change during a migration.

decisions.title: Keep the FMC management plane redundant -- a degraded FMC HA leaves the fleet unmanageable
decisions.driver: Management-plane HA: a Degraded / Split-Brain / unsynced FMC pair means a manager loss leaves the FTD fleet unmanageable during the migration -- restore it before cutover.

evidence.summary: The FMC's own high-availability is degraded (core1: FMC HA DEGRADED (sync FAILED)). The management plane that drives the FTD fleet has no healthy standby -- losing the active FMC during the migration leaves the fleet unmanageable (no policy change, no deployment, no monitoring) and risks a split-brain if both go Active. Restore FMC HA sync / reachability (and resolve any split-brain) before relying on the manager through the cutover.

principle.title: Keep the FMC management plane redundant -- a degraded FMC HA leaves the fleet unmanageable
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center High Availability guide + REST API (fmchastatuses).

decisions.recommended_action: Restore FMC HA synchronization and peer reachability (resolve any split-brain) before relying on the manager through the cutover; verify failover/promotion as part of NRFU.
decisions.alternatives: A single FMC with an accepted-risk posture for a small deployment (no manager failover); cloud-delivered management (cdFMC) to offload HA.
decisions.tradeoffs: An FMC HA pair costs a second appliance + sync overhead, but a single management plane is a recovery gap exactly when a migration needs to push and verify policy.

decisions.title: Keep every Fortinet FortiGate HA cluster in-sync and Health-OK (the firewall HA pair)
decisions.driver: Fortinet FortiGate HA: an out-of-sync member holds a divergent ruleset and a not-OK health means a degraded cluster -- a failover would enforce the wrong policy, the firewall config-present-but-operationally-broken trap on a third non-Cisco vendor.

evidence.summary: 1 Fortinet FortiGate HA cluster(s) are degraded (e.g. core2 (config out-of-sync: FGT-B)). FortiGate HA is the firewall HA pair. A member 'out-of-sync' means its configuration checksum no longer matches the primary -- the standby holds a DIVERGENT ruleset, so a failover would silently enforce the wrong policy (or drop sessions the primary permits); an HA Health Status other than OK means a monitored fault has degraded the cluster. 'config-sync enable' present is NOT proof the peers actually match -- only the checksum is. Recalculate / force-resync the checksums (verify identical firmware + ISDB/IPS versions first) and restore Health to OK before the FortiGate is on the cutover path.

principle.title: Keep every Fortinet FortiGate HA cluster in-sync and Health-OK (the firewall HA pair)
principle.citation: Fortinet FortiOS Administration Guide -- HA, 'Check HA synchronization status' (get system ha status; in-sync / out-of-sync configuration checksums); Fortinet KB (HA checksum-mismatch troubleshooting); analogous to the Cisco ASA / FTD failover model

decisions.recommended_action: Identify the divergent objects ('diagnose sys ha checksum cluster' / the GUI HA widget), confirm identical firmware and ISDB / IPS / AV database versions on both units, then recalculate or force a resync until every member reads in-sync and Health is OK -- before the FortiGate is on the cutover path. Treat 'config-sync enable' as intent, not proof.
decisions.alternatives: A standalone firewall (no HA -- a device failure is an outage); FGSP session-sync without full config-sync (you then own config parity operationally). Neither removes the need to verify the chosen HA is actually in-sync.
decisions.tradeoffs: A FortiGate HA cluster adds a heartbeat / sync link and the discipline of keeping firmware + signature databases identical across members, but gives stateful, sub-second firewall failover -- the same trade as a Cisco ASA/FTD failover pair.

decisions.title: Re-establish the down IPsec/IKE session before baselining any traffic that depends on the encrypted path
decisions.driver: IPsec encrypted WAN: a crypto session in DOWN / DOWN-NEGOTIATING has no IKE/IPsec SA, so the tunnel is hard down and the sites behind it are unreachable; UP-ACTIVE / UP-IDLE / UP-NO-IKE are established and are not flagged.

evidence.summary: 1 IPsec crypto session(s) are DOWN / DOWN-NEGOTIATING (e.g. core1 Tunnel1 -> 10.0.255.9). The session status is the IKE + IPsec SA state to that peer; a session that is not in an UP state has no established SA, so the encrypted tunnel forwards no traffic and every site / prefix reachable only across that VPN is cut off. Confirm peer reachability and the ISAKMP/IKEv2 policy, pre-shared key or certificate trustpoint, transform-set / proposal, and the crypto ACL or VTI route match on both ends before the encrypted WAN is relied on at cutover.

principle.title: Re-establish the down IPsec/IKE session before baselining any traffic that depends on the encrypted path
principle.citation: Cisco — Understand and Use Debug Commands to Troubleshoot IPsec (IKE Phase 1/Phase 2 states, proxy-ID/transform/crypto-ACL mismatch, clear crypto, encaps/decaps verification)

decisions.recommended_action: Diagnose top of the stack down, isolating the failing phase before changing config. (1) 'show crypto session [detail]' for a single per-peer view of session status and whether SAs are active; (2) 'show crypto isakmp sa' (IKEv1) / 'show crypto ikev2 sa' to confirm Phase 1 — if it is not MM_ACTIVE/established the problem is Phase 1: verify the peer is reachable and UDP 500/4500 + ESP are permitted end-to-end, then check matching Phase 1 policy (encryption/hash/DH/lifetime), the pre-shared key, and peer identity/PKI; (3) if Phase 1 is up but Phase 2 is not, 'show crypto ipsec sa' and confirm the transform sets match exactly and the crypto ACLs mirror each other on both peers (non-reversible ACLs cause the proxy-ID mismatch that blocks Phase 2); (4) prove the data plane by checking that encaps and decaps both increment — increment in only one direction indicates an asymmetric/return-path or one-sided ACL fault; (5) where state is stale or flapping, 'clear crypto isakmp' / 'clear crypto sa' to force a clean renegotiation, using debug only when the static checks do not localize the fault. Re-verify encaps/decaps before clearing the finding.
decisions.alternatives: Cheaper options are to clear/bounce the SAs to force a renegotiation and hope the session re-forms without finding the underlying mismatch, or to route the affected traffic over an alternate (possibly unencrypted) path and proceed.
decisions.tradeoffs: A blind clear may restore the tunnel transiently but leaves a latent policy/ACL/lifetime mismatch that re-breaks at the next rekey or under load, and an unencrypted detour trades availability for a confidentiality exposure across the migration window.

decisions.title: Resolve the duplicate IPv6 address (and free the DUPLICATE-state interface) before baselining the fabric
decisions.driver: IPv6 dual-stack readiness: an address in the DUPLICATE state is operationally disabled by DAD, so the interface has no working IPv6 -- the stack is asymmetric and IPv6 hosts on it are stranded until the collision is resolved.

evidence.summary: IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection has FAILED: 1 global IPv6 address(es) in the DUPLICATE state (e.g. core1 Vlan30 (2001:DB8:30::1)). DAD (RFC 4862) confirmed another node already owns the address, so IOS set it to DUPLICATE and is not using it -- the dual-stack interface is dark for IPv6 even though its IPv4 still forwards (a silent stack asymmetry). Find and remove the address collision (a mis-typed static, an overlapping SLAAC/EUI-64 clash, or a duplicated SVI), then 'clear ipv6 duplicate address' to re-run DAD before the segment is trusted at cutover.

principle.title: Resolve the duplicate IPv6 address (and free the DUPLICATE-state interface) before baselining the fabric
principle.citation: IETF RFC 4862, IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, §5.4 Duplicate Address Detection (esp. 5.4.4 'When Duplicate Address Detection Fails' / 5.4.5), and Cisco IOS-XR IP Addresses and Services Command Reference, 'clear ipv6 duplicate-address' / DUPLICATE-state behavior

decisions.recommended_action: 1) Identify the offending address and scope with 'show ipv6 interface <intf>' (look for DUPLICATE/dadfailed and whether it is the link-local or a global/anycast address). 2) Find the true owner of the address on the link — check the neighbor table / ND cache and the L2 path (MAC behind the solicited-node multicast); on a switched segment trace the duplicate to a second device or a mis-bridged VLAN rather than assuming a stack glitch. 3) Fix the root cause, not the symptom: correct the typo'd static address, remove the duplicate from whichever device is the imposter, or (for an EUI-64/link-local collision from a cloned MAC or VM) re-base the interface identifier. 4) Only after the conflict is genuinely gone, return the address to service — on IOS-XR/IOS-XE clear the latched state with 'clear ipv6 duplicate-address <interface>' (or shut/no-shut, which re-runs DAD), since the DUPLICATE flag does not self-heal once set. 5) Re-verify with 'show ipv6 interface' that the address is now VALID/up and confirm the dependent routing adjacency re-forms. Tune 'ipv6 nd dad attempts' only as a deliberate design choice (e.g. set to 0 on a known-clean point-to-point link), never as a way to mask a real collision.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier path is to clear the DUPLICATE state (or disable DAD with 'ipv6 nd dad attempts 0') to make the address usable again without first proving the conflict is gone, or to simply renumber the local interface to dodge the clash. This restores the interface in seconds, but if the real duplicate is still live you now have two nodes answering for one address — intermittent black-holing, ND cache thrash, and a defect that moves with whichever host last spoke.
decisions.tradeoffs: Doing it right costs an investigation cycle and possibly a second device's change window, but it removes the actual address conflict so the cutover reachability is real; suppressing DAD trades minutes saved now for a non-deterministic, hard-to-localize outage during or after the migration.

decisions.title: Keep every ISE deployment node Connected to the Primary Admin -- a partitioned node serves no AAA
decisions.driver: ISE deployment health: a node the Primary Admin reports not Connected has lost contact with the deployment -- it cannot serve AAA/policy, so the access layer that depends on it can fail auth at cutover.

evidence.summary: 1 Cisco ISE deployment node(s) are NOT 'Connected' to the Primary Admin node (e.g. ise-psn-2.aj.local (Disconnected)). nodeStatus is each node's reachability/health to the PAN; a node not Connected has lost contact with the deployment -- it cannot serve RADIUS/TACACS+ AAA or policy and may be partitioned, so endpoints that depend on it for 802.1X/MAB/TrustSec could fail authentication. Confirm the node is powered, on-net and time-synced and that the PAN<->node path (and replication) is healthy before the access layer is cut over onto it.

principle.title: Keep every ISE deployment node Connected to the Primary Admin -- a partitioned node serves no AAA
principle.citation: Cisco ISE Administration / Deployment guide (deployment node status, replication); Cisco ISE Open API (GET /api/v1/deployment/node).

decisions.recommended_action: Confirm the node is powered, on-net, time-synced (NTP) and that the PAN<->node path + certificates + replication are healthy; restore it to Connected before the access layer is cut over onto it. Ensure the switches' RADIUS server-groups list a reachable PSN so a single partition does not blackhole auth.
decisions.alternatives: Operate fewer, larger nodes (simpler, less resilient); distribute PSNs across sites behind RADIUS load-balancing (more resilient, more complex).
decisions.tradeoffs: Cluster health/replication adds operational surface, but a partitioned node silently breaks authentication for everything pointed at it.

decisions.title: Deploy >=2 Policy Service Nodes (a node group) -- a single PSN is an authentication SPOF
decisions.driver: ISE policy-plane redundancy: a single Policy Service node is an auth SPOF -- losing it blackholes 802.1X/MAB on every dependent switch at cutover.

evidence.summary: A Cisco ISE deployment has only ONE Policy Service node (PSN) (e.g. core1 (2 nodes, 1 Policy Service node)). The PSN answers RADIUS for 802.1X/MAB and serves the TrustSec environment-data / SGACL matrix the switches download; a single PSN is an authentication single point of failure -- if it is lost or saturated during the maintenance window, every 802.1X/MAB port on every migrated switch blackholes to fail-auth / critical-VLAN. Deploy at least two PSNs behind the RADIUS clients (a node group, with the switches' RADIUS server-groups pointing at both) before the access layer is cut over.

principle.title: Deploy >=2 Policy Service Nodes (a node group) -- a single PSN is an authentication SPOF
principle.citation: Cisco ISE Performance & Scalability / Deployment guide (PSN node groups, redundancy); Cisco TrustSec & SD-Access design guides (redundant PSN plane).

decisions.recommended_action: Deploy at least two PSNs (a node group so session state survives a PSN loss); configure each switch's RADIUS server-group with both PSNs and dead-criteria/deadtime; size PSN count to the authenticating-endpoint scale. Confirm before cutover so the maintenance window cannot orphan the access layer.
decisions.alternatives: A single PSN with an accepted-risk posture only for a small/low-criticality site; RADIUS to a non-ISE fallback for break-glass (weaker policy).
decisions.tradeoffs: A second PSN (and node group) costs a node + sync overhead, but removes the single point of failure for all identity-based access.

decisions.title: Keep every Juniper SRX chassis-cluster redundancy group ready to fail over (both nodes non-zero priority, monitoring clean)
decisions.driver: Juniper SRX HA: a redundancy group with a priority-0 (not-ready) node, a monitoring failure, or a node lost/disabled has no working standby -- a single point of failure in the data path, regardless of what the configuration claims (the second non-Cisco vendor's HA false-health trap).

evidence.summary: 1 Juniper SRX chassis-cluster redundancy-group/node(s) are degraded (e.g. core2 RG0 node1 (priority 0 (not ready))). SRX chassis cluster is Juniper's stateful-firewall HA -- the analogue of the Cisco firewall failover pair. A node at priority 0 is NOT ready to accept traffic (Junos will not even fail over to it), so that redundancy group has no working standby; a monitor-failure means interface/IP monitoring has caught a fault that has (or will) force a failover; a node lost/disabled/ineligible has dropped out of the cluster. A firewall in the data path whose HA is degraded is a single point of failure -- the config-present-but-operationally-broken trap, on a non-Cisco platform. Restore both nodes to non-zero priority, clear the monitored fault, and confirm a primary+secondary pair before the SRX is on the cutover path.

principle.title: Keep every Juniper SRX chassis-cluster redundancy group ready to fail over (both nodes non-zero priority, monitoring clean)
principle.citation: Juniper Junos OS Chassis Cluster (SRX) documentation -- redundancy-group failover & interface monitoring; Juniper KB19431 (priority-0 redundancy groups); analogous to the Cisco Secure Firewall (ASA / FTD) failover model

decisions.recommended_action: Restore both nodes to a non-zero priority, clear the monitored interface/IP fault that decremented the priority, and confirm a healthy primary+secondary pair (plus the control link / fabric link and RG0 dampening) before the SRX is on the cutover path. Treat 'chassis cluster' in the config as intent, not proof -- verify the operational state.
decisions.alternatives: A standalone firewall (no HA -- a device failure is an outage); a different HA model (e.g. routing-based failover). Neither removes the need to verify the chosen HA is operationally ready.
decisions.tradeoffs: An SRX chassis cluster adds a control link, a fabric link and redundancy-group / monitoring tuning to maintain, but gives stateful, sub-second failover for a firewall in the data path -- the same trade as a Cisco ASA/FTD failover pair.

decisions.title: Confirm whether the down LISP session is a real control-plane outage or an expected no-EID node before gating the fabric
decisions.driver: SD-Access LISP control plane: a fabric node with sessions configured but none established to the map-server / map-resolver cannot register or resolve EID-to-RLOC -- the overlay for that VRF is partitioned, independent of underlay link state.

evidence.summary: 1 LISP fabric VRF(s) have control-plane sessions configured but NONE established (e.g. core1 VRF red (2 session(s), 0 established; CP 10.0.255.2, 10.0.255.3)). Each SD-Access fabric node opens a reliable-transport session to every control-plane node (map-server / map-resolver, port 4342) to register its EIDs and resolve EID-to-RLOC mappings; with zero established sessions in a VRF the node cannot register or resolve, so the fabric overlay for that VRF is partitioned (the border/edge blackholes silently rather than erroring). Confirm underlay reachability to the control-plane loopback, the device's map-server/map-resolver configuration, and any LISP authentication-key mismatch before the fabric is trusted at cutover. (A lone Down peer on an idle border/edge is normal and is NOT flagged -- this fires only when a VRF has total>=1 yet established==0.)

principle.title: Confirm whether the down LISP session is a real control-plane outage or an expected no-EID node before gating the fabric
principle.citation: Cisco SD-Access Fabric Troubleshooting Guide — control-plane node = LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver, TCP-based `show lisp session` registration channel, and the note that a Down session is expected on devices with no EIDs to register (non-route-importing border / edge with no endpoints); with Cisco 'Troubleshoot LISP VXLAN Fabric on Catalyst 9000 Series Switches' (Doc ID 220361) for `show lisp session vrf <ip>` detail and registration/passive-open/locator-set/key checks.

decisions.recommended_action: Disambiguate, then chase the underlay. (1) Establish whether this session SHOULD be up: identify the peer's role — a session from an active edge (with endpoints) or a route-importing border to a control-plane node must be Established; a down session from a device with genuinely no EIDs to register is expected and is not a defect. (2) For a session that should be up, inspect it with `show lisp session` and `show lisp session vrf <vrf> <map-server-ip>` (state, message in/out counts, active instances) to see whether it never came up or flapped. (3) Verify the underlay first — the LISP session is a TCP session, so confirm IP reachability/routing to the map-server RLOC and that no ACL/firewall is blocking the LISP control ports; an underlay routing or MTU problem is the common root. (4) Then check the LISP control-plane configuration symmetry on both ends: the map-server's site/EID configuration and `passive-open`, a complete locator-set, and matching authentication keys (a PSK mismatch fails registration for specific EIDs while the session may still form). (5) Once the session is Established and the expected EIDs are registered (verify on the control-plane node), the fabric mapping is healthy and the gate can proceed.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to treat any Down LISP session as benign 'no-EID' noise and move on, or to cut over relying on the redundant/second control-plane node and existing map-cache, fixing the down session afterward.
decisions.tradeoffs: Assuming-benign without checking the peer's role risks shipping a genuine map-server outage into the cutover (new/moved endpoints silently black-holed), so the small cost of confirming role + reachability + registration up front is what separates a true non-issue from an unverified fabric-wide reachability gap.

decisions.title: Separate the attachment-circuit fault from the pseudowire/underlay fault before declaring the L2 circuit cut
decisions.driver: MPLS L2VPN: a pseudowire in the DOWN state is a hard-down customer L2 circuit; STANDBY/UP are healthy and are not flagged.

evidence.summary: 1 MPLS L2VPN pseudowire(s) are DOWN (e.g. core1 VC 300). A pseudowire carries a point-to-point customer L2 circuit (AToM/EoMPLS) across the MPLS core; a VC in the DOWN state means that attachment circuit is broken end-to-end -- the customer service is hard down, not degraded. Check the attachment circuit, the targeted-LDP session to the remote PE, and VC-ID / encapsulation match on both ends before the L2VPN is accepted at cutover.

principle.title: Separate the attachment-circuit fault from the pseudowire/underlay fault before declaring the L2 circuit cut
principle.citation: RFC 4447 (Pseudowire Setup and Maintenance Using LDP) — targeted LDP, PWid FEC/VC-ID match, VC label, PW Status TLV, PSN-tunnel dependency; and Cisco 'Understand MPLS L2VPN Pseudowire' (Doc ID 213238)

decisions.recommended_action: (1) Read the state first: `show mpls l2transport vc <id> detail` (IOS XR: `show l2vpn xconnect detail`) and split the symptom — is the local AC down, is the remote VC label missing (peer/underlay problem), or are both labels present but the PW still down (parameter mismatch)? (2) Fix the attachment circuit if the AC is down — the customer-facing interface/EFP, its encapsulation, and link/line-protocol state — because no PW comes up over a dead AC. (3) Reconcile the signaling parameters end-to-end: the VC-ID/PW-ID and PW type must match on both PEs, and MTU/encapsulation must agree (note IOS XR counts the L2 header in its MTU, a frequent IOS-XE↔IOS-XR mismatch); confirm `encapsulation mpls`/pw-class is present. (4) If the AC is up and parameters match but the remote VC label is absent, drop to the underlay: confirm the targeted LDP session to the peer is up and the transport LSP to the peer loopback is label-switched — `show mpls ldp neighbor`, `show mpls forwarding-table <peer-/32>`, and validate with a VCCV/PW ping (`ping mpls pseudowire …`). (5) Remediate the layer that failed and re-verify the PW shows UP/UP (AC up, PW up) before re-baselining.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper alternative is to bounce the xconnect/AC and watch it re-signal up without confirming the VCCV path, accepting that the data plane is healthy because the control plane went UP. The riskier shortcut is to disable PW status signaling (`no status`) to force the circuit 'up' when a peer seems not to honor it — which can hide a genuine AC fault behind a green light.
decisions.tradeoffs: Walking AC → parameters → underlay and finishing with a VCCV/PW ping costs a few extra minutes versus a blind bounce, but it stops you certifying a circuit that signals UP while silently dropping customer frames, and it correctly attributes a PW-down to its true cause instead of masking an underlay fault.

decisions.title: Triage the L3VPN underlay before the VPNv4 overlay, then prove the two-label path before cutover
decisions.driver: MPLS L3VPN: a VPNv4 PE-PE session that is not Established stops customer VRF route exchange, blackholing remote sites independently of underlay health.

evidence.summary: 1 MP-BGP VPNv4 (L3VPN) neighbor(s) are not Established (e.g. core1 10.0.255.9). VPNv4 distributes per-VRF customer prefixes between PE routers; a neighbor that is not Established exchanges no VPN routes, so every VRF that relies on that PE loses reachability to its remote sites even while the LDP/IGP underlay stays Up. Confirm the BGP session (update-source / loopback reachability, vpnv4 address-family activation, RR-client config) before the L3VPN service is trusted at cutover.
fields: mpls.vpnv4_neighbors[].state (parse_bgp_vpnv4_summary / show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary)

principle.title: Triage the L3VPN underlay before the VPNv4 overlay, then prove the two-label path before cutover
principle.citation: RFC 4364 (BGP/MPLS IP VPNs) — VPNv4 routes, RD/RT, two-level label stack, PE-reachability requirement; and Cisco 'How to Troubleshoot the MPLS VPN' (Doc ID 13734) for the show-command sequence

decisions.recommended_action: Follow Cisco's top-down-then-underlay sequence. (1) Establish the control plane: `show bgp vpnv4 unicast all summary` (IOS XR: `show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary`) — is the PE-PE/RR session Established and is the VPNv4/MP-BGP address family activated with send-community extended? (2) Confirm policy: the prefix is present with the right RD and its RTs match the remote VRF's import list — `show bgp vpnv4 unicast all <prefix>` and `show vrf <name>` for import/export RTs; a one-sided RT edit is the classic silent break. (3) Confirm the route landed in the VRF and carries a VPN label — `show ip route vrf <name>` and `show bgp vpnv4 unicast all tags` / `show ip cef vrf <name> <prefix> detail`. (4) Now prove the UNDERLAY the overlay depends on: is the remote PE's BGP-next-hop /32 reachable AND label-switched end-to-end? `show mpls forwarding-table <nexthop-/32>` on the ingress PE and at each P hop, then validate the LSP with `ping mpls ipv4 <nexthop>/32` (LSP ping). The order is deliberate: a VPNv4 symptom is frequently an LDP/IGP fault one layer down (this is why the LDP-session-down principle is a prerequisite). (5) Remediate the layer that actually failed — re-peer/activate AF, re-align RTs, or fix the transport LSP — and only then re-baseline.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper alternative is to confirm the VPNv4 prefixes are back in the VRF and accept that as 'fixed' without LSP-pinging the next-hop, trusting that the underlay is healthy. The riskier shortcut is to bounce the BGP session or flap the VRF hoping it re-converges, which can churn every customer prefix on that PE and turn a single-VRF incident into a fleet event.
decisions.tradeoffs: Verifying the actual two-label forwarding path with an LSP ping costs one extra command per affected next-hop, but it is the only thing that distinguishes a control-plane-clean VRF from one that is silently blackholing — the difference between a real go and a cutover that fails the moment the maintenance window closes.

decisions.title: Restore the down LDP session before baselining or cutting over the MPLS underlay
decisions.driver: MPLS underlay: an LDP session not in Oper withholds transport labels, breaking every LSP and VPN service that transits the adjacency.

evidence.summary: 1 MPLS LDP session(s) are not in the operational (Oper) state (e.g. core1 10.0.255.9). LDP distributes the transport labels for the MPLS underlay; a session that is not Oper exchanges no label bindings, so every LSP through that adjacency -- and the L3VPN/L2VPN services it carries -- blackholes. Confirm the link and IGP to the peer, LDP router-id reachability, and any LDP authentication / session-protection before relying on the core at cutover.

principle.title: Restore the down LDP session before baselining or cutting over the MPLS underlay
principle.citation: RFC 5036 (LDP Specification) — sessions, KeepAlive/holdtime, label distribution; and Cisco MPLS Configuration Guide — MPLS LDP IGP Synchronization (blackhole prevention)

decisions.recommended_action: Work bottom-up. (1) Confirm the IGP underneath the session is up and the peer's transport address / router-ID loopback is in the RIB — `show mpls ldp neighbor` / `show mpls ldp discovery` (IOS XR: `show mpls ldp neighbor brief`) to see whether you are stuck at Hello/discovery or at session establishment. (2) If discovery is fine but the TCP session won't form, verify L3 reachability to the LDP transport address and that nothing blocks TCP/646 or has lowered path MTU; check `mpls ldp router-id`/transport-address pinning and that label protocol is enabled on the interface. (3) Inspect label exchange with `show mpls ldp bindings` / `show mpls forwarding-table` to confirm bindings return. (4) Bounce only the affected adjacency with `clear mpls ldp neighbor <ip>` (never restart the LDP process under traffic). (5) Harden against recurrence before cutover: enable LDP-IGP synchronization so the IGP advertises max-metric on a link until LDP is converged (prevents the blackhole), and LDP session protection so a backup targeted-hello adjacency holds the session and its label bindings up across a direct-link flap.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to bring the link/session back, see the LSP repopulate, and proceed without enabling LDP-IGP sync or session protection — accepting the IGP/LDP race and a full reconverge on the next flap. The riskier shortcut is to cut over on the assumption that traffic 'is flowing' because the IGP path is up, even though that path is unlabeled.
decisions.tradeoffs: Configuring LDP-IGP sync and session protection costs a few minutes of change and a small amount of targeted-hello state, but it converts a silent labeled-traffic blackhole during link flaps into a graceful, lossless reconvergence — cheap insurance on a path that carries every VPN.

decisions.title: Keep a reachable rendezvous point (RP) for every running PIM sparse-mode domain (or move groups to SSM)
decisions.driver: Multicast resilience: PIM sparse-mode that is running but has no RP cannot build ASM shared trees -- multicast is silently broken and a cutover baseline would carry the fault forward.

evidence.summary: PIM sparse-mode is running on 1 device(s) but no rendezvous point (RP) is learned (core1) -- ASM multicast (*,G) shared trees cannot form, so multicast forwarding is broken. Restore RP reachability/election (static RP, Auto-RP, or BSR), or migrate affected groups to SSM, before the cutover baseline.
fields: pim[].rp_mapping.rp_count (parse_pim_rp_mapping / show ip pim rp mapping)

principle.title: Keep a reachable rendezvous point (RP) for every running PIM sparse-mode domain (or move groups to SSM)
principle.citation: RFC 7761 (PIM-SM); Cisco PIM RP configuration & verification (Auto-RP / BSR / static / anycast-RP); web-verified.

decisions.recommended_action: Restore RP reachability/election (static RP with anycast-RP redundancy, Auto-RP, or BSR), verify each running PIM device learns the RP, or migrate the affected groups to SSM; re-verify before the cutover baseline.
decisions.alternatives: Migrate to SSM (no RP needed) where the application supports source-specific joins; or run anycast-RP / phantom-RP for RP redundancy.
decisions.tradeoffs: RP availability (redundant/anycast RP, Auto-RP or BSR election) and the operational discipline to keep it reachable, vs the simplicity of SSM where the application supports source-specific joins.

decisions.title: Re-point or dynamic-ize static default routes before any gateway/next-hop change (cutover black-hole)
decisions.driver: Cutover black-hole: a static default route has no reconvergence, so a gateway/next-hop change at cutover black-holes the host until the static route is manually re-pointed.

evidence.summary: 1 host(s) ride a STATIC default route (0.0.0.0/0 via a fixed next-hop, no dynamically-learned default to reconverge). A static default does not fail over: at cutover, the moment its next-hop gateway changes (new core, re-addressed transit, VRF/interface move) the route still points at the old hop and silently black-holes all off-subnet traffic until it is re-pointed by hand. Sequence each re-point into the change (or pre-stage a tracked/dynamic default) — don't discover it broken after the window.

principle.title: Re-point or dynamic-ize static default routes before any gateway/next-hop change (cutover black-hole)
principle.citation: Cisco routing design — a static default route does not reconverge; use a dynamic default, or an object-tracked / floating static (IP SLA) for gateway resilience; Cisco migration practice — re-point or dynamic-ize static next-hops before changing the gateway they point at.

decisions.recommended_action: Inventory every static-default host and its next-hop; for each, decide the target default path and SEQUENCE its update into the cutover step for that device (or pre-stage a floating/tracked static + a dynamic default so it fails over instead of black-holing). Prefer migrating edge defaults to a dynamic protocol (or object-tracked static with IP SLA) so a future gateway change reconverges on its own. Validate reachability to the off-subnet world in NRFU after each re-point.
decisions.alternatives: Leave the static defaults and re-point them reactively during the window (cheapest to plan, but every missed host is a silent black-hole and a rollback trigger); blanket-convert to dynamic (cleanest long-term, but a larger change that needs its own validation).
decisions.tradeoffs: Re-pointing / dynamic-izing static defaults adds per-device cutover steps and NRFU checks, but it converts a class of silent post-cutover black-holes into a planned, verifiable step.

decisions.title: Restore the down WAN-edge control connection before freezing the SD-WAN cutover baseline
decisions.driver: SD-WAN overlay control plane: a WAN edge that loses its control connections to the controllers falls out of the overlay (no OMP/policy), isolating the site regardless of transport health.

evidence.summary: 1 SD-WAN control connection(s) are down or below the expected count (e.g. core1 BR13-cedge -> vsmart (down)). A WAN edge holds DTLS/TLS control connections to the SD-WAN controllers (Validator/vBond, Controller/vSmart); losing them drops the edge out of the overlay control plane -- no OMP routes or policy are exchanged, so the site cannot build overlay tunnels even while its underlay transport is up. Confirm controller reachability per transport color, certificate/serial validity, and any control-policy or firewall blocking DTLS/12346 before the overlay is trusted at cutover.

principle.title: Restore the down WAN-edge control connection before freezing the SD-WAN cutover baseline
principle.citation: Cisco — Troubleshoot SD-WAN Control Connections (Doc ID 214509; control connections-history error codes DCONFAIL/CRTVERFL/CTORGNMMIS/SERNTPRES/BIDNTVRFD, DTLS/TLS, certificate + root-CA + WAN-edge-list checks)

decisions.recommended_action: Work the controller's own verdict, outside-in: (1) read `show sdwan control connections-history` and pivot on the LOCAL/REMOTE ERROR mnemonic rather than guessing. (2) Prove underlay reachability and routing to each controller TLOC (ICMP/traceroute, valid RIB next-hop, correct color/public-private mapping, and firewall/NAT pinholes for 12346+/DTLS or the TLS port). (3) Verify time: confirm NTP is synchronized on the edge and controllers (a skewed clock invalidates certificates and breaks the handshake). (4) Validate identity: certificate validity and the enterprise root-CA installed on the edge (`show sdwan certificate root-ca-cert`), the organization-name match, and that the device UUID/serial is authorized — then re-push the WAN-edge list with Configuration > Certificates > Send to Controllers. (5) Re-check that all expected connections (vBond/vManage/vSmart, both transports) are UP and stable, not flapping. Resolve to green and re-snapshot before the cutover gate.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper move is to accept a partial control plane — e.g. one of two transports/controllers up — and proceed, leaning on the fact that the data plane is still forwarding and graceful restart will hold routes for hours. It defers the fix without a maintenance window.
decisions.tradeoffs: Cutting over on a partial or down control connection trades a few hours of certificate/NTP/reachability triage now for an invisible single-point-of-failure that surfaces as an unreachable site the moment a controller blips, a certificate re-keys, or the 12-hour graceful-restart cache expires.

decisions.title: Re-establish the unreachable device's controller reporting before treating its state as known-good
decisions.driver: SD-WAN fabric reachability: a device the Manager reports unreachable has lost controller contact -- unmonitored, unmanageable, and probably isolated from the overlay.

evidence.summary: 1 SD-WAN device(s) are reported UNREACHABLE by the vManage Manager (e.g. core1 BR99-cedge). Reachability is the controller's own verdict on each WAN edge; unreachable means the Manager has lost management/control contact with the device -- it cannot be monitored, templated or pushed policy, and is likely isolated from the overlay. Confirm the device is powered and on-net, its control connections, and any out-of-band management path before the site is counted as in-service at cutover.

principle.title: Re-establish the unreachable device's controller reporting before treating its state as known-good
principle.citation: Cisco — Troubleshoot Connection When Devices Lose Connectivity to vManage (Doc ID 218077; peer-timeout codes VB_TMO/VM_TMO/VP_TMO/VS_TMO, reachability + RIB/TLOC, certificate 'Send to Controllers', NTP/clock sync)

decisions.recommended_action: (1) Read the connection history and identify which peer timed out (VB_TMO/VM_TMO/VP_TMO/VS_TMO) — that names the lost relationship. (2) Establish underlay reachability to the controllers (ICMP/traceroute) and confirm a valid RIB route with the correct next-hop/TLOC; control connections never form over a broken underlay. (3) Check time first — verify NTP/clock sync on the device and controllers, since skew makes a good certificate look expired and silently breaks the handshake. (4) Validate identity: certificate validity, enterprise root-CA present on the device, organization-name match, and the device serial/UUID in the WAN-edge list — then Configuration > Certificates > WAN Edge List > Send to Controllers to re-sync. (5) If reachability/identity are clean but the device is still not reporting, look vManage-side (NMS/DPI load, cluster/disk health). (6) Confirm the device is back to a full, stable control state and re-collect its evidence so the baseline reflects observed — not assumed — state.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper alternative is to carry the device forward on its last-known (stale) inventory and proceed, assuming the data plane is fine because graceful restart is still holding — deferring the reachability/certificate fix instead of taking a window to restore reporting.
decisions.tradeoffs: You trade a reachability/NTP/certificate restoration now for a device that is unmanageable and unverifiable during the cutover: it silently misses every config/software push, its true state stays UNKNOWN, and if its data plane was only surviving on cached OMP state you discover a stranded or mis-built site after the maintenance window has closed.

decisions.title: Recover the down OMP peering to vSmart before its 12-hour graceful-restart cache hides the loss
decisions.driver: SD-WAN overlay routing: an edge with OMP peers down is missing overlay routes (TLOCs / prefixes), blackholing some sites even while the control/transport plane is up -- distinct from a control-connection loss.

evidence.summary: 1 SD-WAN edge(s) have OMP peers DOWN (e.g. core1 BR13-cedge (1 OMP peer(s) down)). OMP (Overlay Management Protocol) runs over the control connections and distributes the overlay routes, TLOCs and service routes; an edge with OMP peers down is missing overlay routing -- it cannot learn or advertise some remote prefixes, so traffic to the affected sites blackholes even while the control and transport planes look up. Confirm the OMP session and graceful-restart/hold timers to the vSmart, that the edge is advertising its routes, and any control policy filtering them before the overlay routing is trusted at cutover.

principle.title: Recover the down OMP peering to vSmart before its 12-hour graceful-restart cache hides the loss
principle.citation: Cisco — Routing Configuration Guide, Catalyst SD-WAN Releases 17.x: OMP and OMP graceful restart (OMP over DTLS/TLS, ACTIVE/STALE route states, default GR timer 43,200s/12h, EOR marker; recommended 300s hold time)

decisions.recommended_action: (1) Confirm the OMP state and scope with `show sdwan omp peers` — read the peer state (Up vs init-in-gr) and the R/I/S (received/installed/sent) counters; a peer stuck in graceful restart with stale routes is living on borrowed time. (2) Since OMP rides the control connection, first rule out a control-connection fault to that vSmart (history error code, reachability, certificate, NTP) — fix that and OMP typically re-establishes. (3) If the control connection is up but OMP is not converging, check OMP-layer health: hold-time/timer mismatch (Cisco recommends 300s hold time), graceful-restart configuration, and `send-path-limit` / route-count limits that can starve advertisement. (4) Use OMP vDiagnostics (auto-captures a snapshot on peering loss) to root-cause hello/timer/flap behavior. (5) Verify both vSmarts in the cluster are peered (redundancy restored) and that received/installed counts match the expected prefix set before re-baselining.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper path is to rely on the surviving vSmart peer plus the 12-hour graceful-restart cache and proceed — accept reduced control-plane redundancy temporarily rather than schedule the fix.
decisions.tradeoffs: You trade an OMP/control-connection investigation now for a fabric running non-redundant on a stale-route cache: a second vSmart hiccup, or simply the 12-hour timer expiring, flushes the cached overlay and blackholes the site — and any route/policy you pushed during cutover quietly never reached the edges behind the dead peer.

decisions.title: Restore the BGP L2VPN EVPN control plane before baselining or freezing the overlay fabric
decisions.driver: VXLAN control plane: BGP-EVPN distributes the MAC/IP and prefix routes; a down route-reflector session blinds the fabric to every endpoint behind that peer.

evidence.summary: 1 BGP-EVPN neighbor(s) are not Established (core2 10.255.0.253). VXLAN MAC/IP and prefix routes are not being exchanged with these peers -- the overlay control plane is dark even if the NVE data-plane peers are Up; check the EVPN route-reflector and the iBGP L2VPN-EVPN session.
fields: overlay.evpn_neighbors[].state (parse_evpn_summary / show bgp l2vpn evpn summary)

principle.title: Restore the BGP L2VPN EVPN control plane before baselining or freezing the overlay fabric
principle.citation: IETF RFC 7432, BGP MPLS-Based Ethernet VPN (EVPN route types: Type-2 MAC/IP Advertisement, Type-3 Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag; control-plane MAC learning) — corroborated by Cisco Nexus 9000 Series NX-OS VXLAN Configuration Guide, Configuring VXLAN BGP EVPN, and Cisco support doc 'Troubleshoot EVPN/VXLAN in Multi-Site Environment' (show bgp l2vpn evpn summary; rewrite-evpn-rt-asn)

decisions.recommended_action: Work the control plane top-down only after the underlay is confirmed clean. (1) Verify the underlay/loopback reachability the BGP session rides on — a flapping or unreachable spine/RR loopback presents as an EVPN session problem. (2) Run 'show bgp l2vpn evpn summary' on the leaf and its route reflectors/spines; confirm the neighbor is Established and PfxRcd is non-zero. If the session is down, inspect the BGP neighbor state/last-error (AS number, update-source loopback, missing 'address-family l2vpn evpn', RR client config, password/TTL). (3) If the session is up but no routes import, compare route-targets between sites and apply 'rewrite-evpn-rt-asn' where ASN-auto RTs differ; verify Type-2 and Type-3 routes are present with 'show bgp l2vpn evpn'. (4) Re-validate that L2RIB MAC routes are being redistributed into EVPN and that remote VTEPs now see them. For large-scale fabrics, extend BGP graceful-restart (e.g. toward 300s) so a high VNI-count reconvergence does not itself trigger a flap. Only re-snapshot the fabric once EVPN is Established and exchanging routes fabric-wide.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier path is to treat one down EVPN adjacency as redundant (a second RR/spine still carries routes) and proceed to cutover, accepting degraded route diversity and slower convergence rather than pausing to root-cause; viable only if you positively confirm full Type-2/Type-3 coverage via the surviving path and the down session is genuinely a redundant peer, not the device's only route source.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fixing it first costs a maintenance-window detour and possibly an RR/ASN-policy change, but baselining or cutting over on a blind control plane risks an overlay-wide outage and a worthless pre-migration baseline — the cost is trivial against the blast radius.

decisions.title: Restore the down NVE (VTEP) peer before treating the affected segments as migratable
decisions.driver: VXLAN data plane: a VTEP peer down partitions the overlay for every VNI it carries; the underlay or the remote NVE is the fault domain.

evidence.summary: 1 VXLAN VTEP peer(s) are DOWN (core2 10.255.0.2). Hosts behind a down VTEP are unreachable across the overlay; check the underlay (NVE source loopback reachable via the IGP, and PIM or ingress-replication for BUM traffic) and the remote NVE configuration.

principle.title: Restore the down NVE (VTEP) peer before treating the affected segments as migratable
principle.citation: IETF RFC 8365, A Network Virtualization Overlay Solution Using EVPN (VTEPs as NVEs depend on IP reachability between NVEs; VXLAN UDP encapsulation; VNI as segment identifier) — corroborated by Cisco support doc 'Configure VXLAN' (118978) and Cisco Nexus 9000 NX-OS VXLAN Configuration Guide (show nve peers State/LearnType; source-interface loopback; vPC NVE source-loopback hold-down vs delay-restore)

decisions.recommended_action: Diagnose bottom-up, since the NVE peer is a symptom of the underlay. (1) From 'show nve peers', identify the peer IP (the remote VTEP loopback) and its State. (2) Confirm underlay reachability to that loopback: ping/traceroute the remote VTEP source-interface from this VTEP's source-interface, and verify the /32 is present via the underlay IGP/BGP (route present, correct next-hops, no flaps). (3) Verify both ends' NVE config: 'show nve interface' for the correct 'source-interface loopback', host-reachability protocol bgp, and that the two VTEPs share at least one configured VNI. (4) For vPC VTEPs, confirm the NVE source-loopback hold-down timer is set below the vPC delay-restore timer so the VIP is not advertised before the overlay is ready, and check the anycast/secondary-IP configuration. (5) Once the loopback is reachable and config matches, the peer should transition to Up with LearnType CP; re-verify before clearing the segment for migration.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier alternative is to bring the peer up by forcing data-plane discovery (e.g. sourcing host traffic / a ping across the overlay to populate the peer) and move on without fixing the underlay root cause — it can flip the state Up transiently but leaves a fragile tunnel that will drop again under load or reconvergence, so it is only acceptable as a diagnostic confirmation, never as the fix.
decisions.tradeoffs: Properly restoring underlay reachability to the VTEP loopback may require touching IGP/ECMP or vPC timers in the window, but skipping it means the affected leaf/vPC's endpoints are dark over the overlay at cutover — a localized fix versus a per-leaf outage.

decisions.title: Restore the down NVE VNI (segment) before declaring that L2VNI/L3VNI ready for cutover
decisions.driver: VXLAN segment health: a VNI that is not Up strands its VLAN/VRF on the local VTEP -- no overlay reachability for that segment.

evidence.summary: 1 VXLAN VNI(s) are not Up (core2 VNI 50000). The VLAN or VRF behind each is not extended across the fabric (stranded on the local VTEP); check the VLAN-to-VNI / VRF-to-L3VNI binding and the NVE member configuration.

principle.title: Restore the down NVE VNI (segment) before declaring that L2VNI/L3VNI ready for cutover
principle.citation: Cisco Nexus 9000 Series NX-OS VXLAN Configuration Guide, Configure VXLAN / Configure VXLAN BGP EVPN (show nve vni State Up/Down, Type BD vs VRF; VLAN-to-VNI mapping and member vni; L3VNI SVI 'ip forward' and member vni associate-vrf; drive L3VNI via VRF shut/no-shut) — RFC 8365 corroborates VNI-to-broadcast-domain mapping and EVPN carriage of the VNI

decisions.recommended_action: Resolve from the local binding outward. (1) From 'show nve vni' (or 'show nve vni <id> detail'), confirm the VNI's State, Mode (CP), and Type (BD for L2VNI / VRF for L3VNI). (2) For an L2VNI Down: verify the VLAN exists and is active, the VLAN-to-VNI mapping is correct, and a matching 'member vni' is present under the NVE interface; bring the VLAN/bridge-domain up. (3) For an L3VNI Down: verify the tenant VRF, that the L3VNI VLAN/SVI is up and uses 'ip forward', and that 'member vni <id> associate-vrf' is configured — drive state by shut/no-shut on the VRF, never on the VNI interface. (4) Confirm the segment's evidence end-to-end: the VLAN/SVI is up, the VNI shows Up, and EVPN is advertising that VNI's Type-2/Type-3 routes to peers. (5) Only then mark the L2VNI/L3VNI ready and re-baseline that segment.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier alternative is to exclude the single down VNI from the move group and cut over the rest of the leaf, deferring that one tenant segment to a follow-up window — acceptable only if that tenant can tolerate staying on the legacy fabric temporarily and the exclusion is explicitly tracked, because the easy mistake is to assume the VNI will 'come up on its own' post-cutover when its VLAN/SVI dependency is unmet.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fixing the VLAN/SVI/VRF binding is a small, well-scoped change, whereas shipping a down VNI strands one tenant's subnet at cutover behind an otherwise-green fabric — a few minutes of remediation against a tenant-isolating, hard-to-spot outage.

decisions.title: Right-size availability to the application and place in the network, not 5x9 everywhere
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Redundancy posture is observable, but right-sizing it (which tiers warrant which availability) needs a per-class availability/SLA target.

principle.title: Right-size availability to the application and place in the network, not 5x9 everywhere
principle.citation: CCDE In Depth Ch.2 High Availability ('not every network needs 5x9/6x9'); CCDE Designer Skills (availability=MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR))

decisions.recommended_action: Classify sites/modules by criticality and assign an availability target per class; invest redundancy where MTBF/MTTR and app sensitivity justify it, and explicitly accept lower availability where the business does not require it.
decisions.alternatives: Single uniform SLA fleet-wide (simpler, mis-allocates spend); per-application SLA contracts; geographic/DR-tiered availability for cost-sensitive cases.
decisions.tradeoffs: HA vs cost and HA vs simplicity — each added nine multiplies redundancy, hardware and operational burden; a datacentre and a retail store legitimately warrant different SLAs, and too much redundancy raises MTTR.

decisions.title: Choose the DC fabric operating model: standalone NX-OS VXLAN-EVPN (default) vs Cisco ACI policy fabric
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Once a DC spine-leaf fabric is the target, its OPERATING MODEL -- standalone NX-OS VXLAN BGP-EVPN (controller-less, open-standards, Nexus Dashboard/NDFC-managed; the 2026 default for new builds) vs Cisco ACI (APIC-controlled, application-centric EPG/contract policy fabric) -- is a top-down operating-model CHOICE, not a brownfield observable. Both deliver the same distributed-anycast-gateway VXLAN outcome; the difference is how the fabric is policed and operated. Needs the fabric_operating_model requirement (plus any existing-ACI-estate / identity-micro-segmentation mandate).

principle.title: Choose the DC fabric operating model: standalone NX-OS VXLAN-EVPN (default) vs Cisco ACI policy fabric
principle.citation: Cisco AS ACI Design & Deployment (Telco DC) + NRG / EXPO2020 ACI HLD/LLD operating model, cross-checked with the current Cisco Nexus 9000 VXLAN BGP-EVPN design guide + Nexus Dashboard (2026).

decisions.recommended_action: Default to standalone NX-OS VXLAN BGP-EVPN for new builds (open RFC 7432 EVPN / RFC 8365 VXLAN / RFC 9135 IRB standards, portable multivendor skills, Nexus Dashboard / NDFC operations including IP Fabric for Media for broadcast/media estates, BGP-EVPN policy + VXLAN GPO group policy for segmentation). Choose Cisco ACI when an existing ACI estate, or an application-centric end-to-end identity micro-segmentation operating model, justifies a single declarative APIC controller. Note the 2026 trajectory: ACI is converging into the unified Nexus Dashboard / open-VXLAN-EVPN model (APIC federation + VXLAN GPO), which narrows ACI's once-unique segmentation advantage.
decisions.alternatives: A hybrid managed by Nexus Dashboard (NDO / NDFC) that federates ACI and NX-OS-EVPN domains where both already exist, presenting one policy and segmentation model across them.
decisions.tradeoffs: manageability (single declarative controller + intent-based policy) vs simplicity & portability (open standards, no controller dependency, multivendor-transferable EVPN skills); security (controller-native identity micro-segmentation) vs operational familiarity; capex/opex and existing-investment lock-in.

decisions.title: Interconnect EVPN fabrics as isolated sites (Multi-Site at the border-leaf), not one stretched Multi-Pod fabric
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Once the estate spans multiple rooms/buildings/fabrics, whether to interconnect them as ISOLATED Multi-Site domains (a Border Gateway per site re-originates the overlay, eBGP between sites, per-site BUM/storm-control -- a fault, storm or gray failure is contained to one site) or stretch one fabric (Multi-Pod -- simpler, but one shared failure domain) is a scale/containment CHOICE, not an observable. Needs the growth horizon (site count / multi-building reach / fault-containment intent) to decide.

principle.title: Interconnect EVPN fabrics as isolated sites (Multi-Site at the border-leaf), not one stretched Multi-Pod fabric
principle.citation: ipSpace.net 'Multi-Site and Multi-Pod Fabrics' / 'Using VXLAN and EVPN in Multi-Pod and Multi-Site Fabrics' (Krattiger/Pepelnjak); Cisco VXLAN EVPN Multi-Site Design (c11-739942); IETF draft-ietf-bess-dci-evpn-overlay

decisions.recommended_action: Target a Multi-Site interconnect: terminate each site's overlay on a redundant Border-Gateway (anycast) cluster at dedicated border-leaf nodes, keep underlays per-site (no underlay extension between sites), run eBGP between site overlays, and enforce per-site BUM/storm-control at the gateway; terminate the IGP at each site boundary so a control-plane fault is contained per site; design and test the total-inter-site-link-loss and split-brain scenarios. Reserve a single stretched (Multi-Pod) fabric for pods within one facility on reliable links where shared fate is acceptable.
decisions.alternatives: A single stretched (Multi-Pod) fabric for tightly-coupled pods in one facility; full spine-to-spine meshing IF interconnecting at the spine (never partial); Super-spine for very large east-west scale.
decisions.tradeoffs: Multi-Site adds Border-Gateway hardware, per-site edge state and an extra control-plane hop, but contains a fault, broadcast storm or gray failure to one site; Multi-Pod is simpler and cheaper but makes the interconnected fabrics one failure domain.

decisions.title: Adopt spine-leaf (VXLAN-EVPN) for the modern DC; keep collapsed-core+vPC only for small/static footprints
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Whether the target DC becomes a spine-leaf VXLAN-EVPN fabric or stays collapsed-core + vPC is an east-west-scale / multi-tenancy choice, not an observable: spine-leaf earns its complexity with east-west growth and segmentation; a small/static footprint should not take on EVPN it does not need. Needs the growth horizon + traffic/tenancy profile.

principle.title: Adopt spine-leaf (VXLAN-EVPN) for the modern DC; keep collapsed-core+vPC only for small/static footprints
principle.citation: CCDE Session 16 (spine-leaf); Cisco Nexus 9000 VXLAN BGP EVPN design guide; VXLAN-EVPN Multi-Site WP

decisions.recommended_action: Design the DC as a leaf-spine CLOS with BGP-EVPN overlay (anycast gateway on leaf, endpoints only on leaves, ECMP) and VXLAN-EVPN Multi-Site for DCI; keep collapsed-core+vPC only for small/static DCs.
decisions.alternatives: Traditional 3-tier for small footprints; FabricPath/TRILL/SPB as an L2 multipath fabric where an IP/overlay fabric is not yet justified.
decisions.tradeoffs: Scale/determinism/multi-tenancy + segmentation vs the operational-maturity step to L3/overlay (ECMP, EVPN, automation/NDFC) and more inter-switch links; collapsed core is simpler/cheaper but STP-bounded with no overlay mobility/segmentation and a larger blast radius.

decisions.title: Use a three-tier hierarchy for scale (or full-mesh the distribution if collapsing the core), and tier for blast-radius + RBAC
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: The current core/distribution collapse is observable, but a dedicated core vs a collapsed core is a SCALE choice: a dedicated core earns its cost past ~3 distribution blocks, multi-building reach, or tighter fault-isolation; collapsed core suits a small, single-site, low-growth footprint. Needs the growth horizon + closet/block count to right-size.

principle.title: Use a three-tier hierarchy for scale (or full-mesh the distribution if collapsing the core), and tier for blast-radius + RBAC
principle.citation: CCDE Session 16 (3 tiers = scalability, full-mesh distribution if no core); CCDE scenario (tiering = blast radius + RBAC)

decisions.recommended_action: Introduce a dedicated fast core so distribution blocks attach and scale by addition; if core-less, fully mesh the distribution with root/FHRP there; tier the network (with per-tier flooding domains and summarization) to bound blast radius and align RBAC.
decisions.alternatives: Collapsed core for small/cost-bound sites (accept wider blast radius); two-tier spine-leaf for the DC; keep flat where the network is small and stable.
decisions.tradeoffs: Scale/fault-containment/operational separation vs cost and end-to-end path length — more tiers add devices/hops/design effort but localize faults and SPF scope; collapsing tiers is cheaper and lower-latency but widens the blast radius. Cisco scopes the collapsed core to smaller locations only.

decisions.title: Gather the decision-driving requirements before designing — never assume, never re-ask what's given
decisions.driver: A design is good only if it meets requirements; gather them before deciding.

evidence.summary: No requirements register supplied. Decisions that depend on SLA / application / growth / constraints are surfaced as questions, not assumed -- supply the register to right-size the blueprint.

principle.title: Gather the decision-driving requirements before designing — never assume, never re-ask what's given
principle.citation: CCDE MilkaTurka & Ornio scenarios (requirements-gathering, no-assumptions); CCDE Scenario 1/2 (SLA + app matrix + device utilization first)

decisions.recommended_action: Before committing a design choice, confirm the specific decision-driving inputs (existing/partner equipment capability, data security level, convergence/SLA target, application matrix, provider coverage/feature support); design to stated requirements, not reflexive best practice, and never re-ask facts already given.
decisions.alternatives: Assume sensible defaults and proceed (fast, risks redesign); capture requirements iteratively where a full up-front gather is infeasible.
decisions.tradeoffs: Correct, requirement-grounded design vs the time of a discovery round-trip; assuming saves time at the risk of a costly redesign or an over/under-built network.

decisions.title: Size redundancy (second path, BFD, fast timers) to the application's actual convergence requirement, not reflexive best practice
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Convergence posture is observable, but whether it is over- or under-built needs the per-application convergence budget (e.g. voice/video tolerance).

principle.title: Size redundancy (second path, BFD, fast timers) to the application's actual convergence requirement, not reflexive best practice
principle.citation: CCDE MilkaTurka scenario (one-vs-two tunnels per store; BFD/feasible-successor under loose convergence)

decisions.recommended_action: Provision a single path/default timers for loose convergence targets; reserve dual-homing/BFD/feasible-successor/aggressive timers for apps with tight recovery needs; record the convergence target as the design basis.
decisions.alternatives: Dual tunnels + BFD everywhere (textbook HA, unjustified at scale); single path with monitoring only.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast convergence/extra resilience vs doubled tunnel/adjacency count and operational load; protecting a rare failure mode at every site rarely justifies the fleet-wide multiplication when convergence is non-critical.

decisions.title: Confirm the storm-control action and recovery policy on edge ports before cutover, so a storm fails predictably
decisions.driver: Broadcast-storm containment must be OBSERVABLE: a storm-control rule that only drops (action None) hides the event from operations and leaves the storming host attached; trap/shutdown make it visible and self-isolating.

evidence.summary: 34 storm-control rule(s) are configured with action 'None' (access1 Gi0/2 broadcast, access1 Gi0/2 multicast, access2 Gi0/2 broadcast, access2 Gi0/2 multicast, access3 Gi0/2 broadcast, access3 Gi0/2 multicast, access4 Gi0/2 broadcast, access4 Gi0/2 multicast). The control caps the storm but sends no trap and does not err-disable the port, so a broadcast/multicast storm is dropped SILENTLY -- operations never learns it fired and the storming host is never quarantined. Add 'storm-control action trap' (visibility) and/or 'storm-control action shutdown' (containment) on the access edge so a storm is observable and self-isolating.

principle.title: Confirm the storm-control action and recovery policy on edge ports before cutover, so a storm fails predictably
principle.citation: Cisco — Configuring Port-Based Traffic Control: Storm Control (action shutdown=err-disable / trap; recover via shut-no shut or 'errdisable recovery cause storm-control')

decisions.recommended_action: (1) Inventory the per-port action and threshold ('show storm-control', 'show running-config interface') and reconcile to intent — access/host edge ports generally warrant tight broadcast suppression (commonly low single-digit percent to cover ARP) with a containment action, uplinks/trunks generally should not carry an aggressive shutdown that could isolate a whole downstream tree. (2) Decide the recovery model explicitly: if 'shutdown' is used, pair it with 'errdisable recovery cause storm-control' and a sane recovery interval so a transient storm self-heals; if a port must never auto-restore (a known-abusive segment), keep manual recovery but document the runbook step. (3) Check 'show errdisable recovery' to confirm the cause is actually enabled and the interval is set. (4) Before the window, identify which edge ports could be transiently storm-tripped by the planned change and pre-stage the recovery (or temporarily relax to 'trap') so the change itself does not err-disable production access. (5) Re-baseline after cutover that no port sits err-disabled by storm-control.
decisions.alternatives: Cheaper alternatives are to leave storm-control at trap-only (visibility without disruption) or to disable the shutdown action for the duration of the change so no port can be err-disabled by a migration-induced transient.
decisions.tradeoffs: Trap-only or disabling the action removes the risk of self-inflicted port-downs during the window but also removes the automatic loop/storm containment exactly when re-cabling and reconvergence make a transient loop most likely — you trade guaranteed availability of a port against bounded blast radius if a real storm occurs.

decisions.title: Size each switch's replacement for its load plus a growth headroom -- don't port a near-full switch 1:1
decisions.driver: Capacity headroom: the few near-full switches must not be ported 1:1 -- design in runway.

evidence.summary: 16 of 23 switch(es) run at >= 85% port utilisation (< 15% free ports) -- size THOSE switches' replacements for current load plus a growth headroom (and the build-before-break overhead), not 1:1, or they are born full.

principle.title: Size each switch's replacement for its load plus a growth headroom -- don't port a near-full switch 1:1
principle.citation: Cisco Enterprise Campus / CVD capacity & oversubscription planning (size for growth, not 1:1); IEEE 802.3af/at/bt PoE power budgeting.

decisions.recommended_action: Size the target from observed port_util/poe_util plus a documented growth headroom (e.g. +30-50%) AND the build-before-break overhead; prefer higher-density or modular platforms where switches are saturated; verify the PoE budget covers the powered-endpoint load with margin. Carry the headroom assumption into the BoM, not just the slide.
decisions.alternatives: Port 1:1 to minimise BoM (cheapest, but the fabric is born full and a near-term upgrade is forced); over-provision uniformly (simple, wastes spend on lightly-loaded tiers).
decisions.tradeoffs: Headroom raises the up-front hardware/BoM cost, but a target born full forces a premature second refresh and leaves no room to execute the migration in parallel.

decisions.title: Move the default gateway (SVI) LAST for any subnet whose endpoints straddle multiple switches
decisions.driver: Cutover order: move the default gateway after the workloads, never before -- gateway-move-last per subnet.
