evidence.summary: 7 gateway SVI(s) across 4 VLAN(s) serve endpoints that straddle >= 2 switches -- the subnet's default gateway must move LAST (keep the legacy SVI live and the target BD flooding/anycast ready until all workloads are across), or trailing endpoints lose their gateway mid-cutover. Sequence each move-group so the SVI is the final step.

principle.title: Move the default gateway (SVI) LAST for any subnet whose endpoints straddle multiple switches
principle.citation: Cisco 'Migrating Existing Networks to ACI' (BD flood on / unicast-routing off until workloads move; gateway last); web-verified.

decisions.recommended_action: In each move-group, schedule the SVI/default-gateway move as the final step for every straddling subnet; keep the legacy gateway active and the target BD flooding (ARP/unknown-unicast) on with unicast routing off until all workloads are across; only then move the gateway and enable routing.
decisions.alternatives: Move the whole subnet in a single wave where it fits one switch/move-group (no straddle, no ordering constraint); or use an anycast/distributed gateway so the gateway exists on both sides during the cut.
decisions.tradeoffs: A safe, reversible per-subnet cutover (gateway-move-last, build-before-break) vs a longer window where the subnet's L3 is split across legacy and target and must be kept consistent on both.

decisions.title: Keep the FMC at or ahead of every managed FTD's version -- a manager behind a device can't manage it
decisions.driver: Manager/device version order: Cisco mandates FMC >= every managed FTD -- an FMC older than a device it manages cannot reliably deploy-to or upgrade it.

evidence.summary: The FMC is running an OLDER version than a managed FTD (e.g. core1: FMC 7.0.0 (build 94) < FTD AJ-FTD-01 7.2.5, core1: FMC 7.0.0 (build 94) < FTD AJ-FTD-99 7.2.5). Cisco requires the FMC to run a version equal to or newer than every device it manages, so an FMC behind a managed FTD is an unsupported state -- it can fail to deploy policy to, or upgrade, that device. Upgrade the FMC to at least the highest managed-FTD version (respecting the supported upgrade path) before relying on central management through the migration.

principle.title: Keep the FMC at or ahead of every managed FTD's version -- a manager behind a device can't manage it
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center / Threat Defense compatibility + upgrade guides (FMC version must be >= managed device version).

decisions.recommended_action: Upgrade the FMC to at least the highest managed-FTD version (following the supported FMC->FTD upgrade path) BEFORE relying on central management through the migration; sequence the migration's upgrades manager-first, devices-second.
decisions.alternatives: Roll the over-advanced device back to a managed version (rarely desirable); split management so each FMC stays ahead of its own device set.
decisions.tradeoffs: Keeping the FMC ahead is a sequencing constraint on upgrades, but the inverse is an unsupported state that can block deployment/upgrade of the affected device.

decisions.title: Give the ISE PAN and MnT a Secondary -- a single Admin/Monitoring node loses management or visibility
decisions.driver: ISE management-plane redundancy: a single PAN or single MnT means a node loss leaves the deployment unmanageable or blind -- design a Secondary for each before cutover.

evidence.summary: A Cisco ISE deployment is missing administration/monitoring redundancy: no Secondary Administration node (single PAN); and no Secondary Monitoring node (single MnT) (deployment: core1). The Primary Admin node (PAN) owns configuration + replication and the Monitoring node (MnT) owns logging/reporting; without a standby, loss of the primary leaves the deployment unmanageable (no policy change / no promotion) or blind (no auth logs to troubleshoot the cutover). Add the missing Secondary PAN / MnT so the control and logging planes survive a node loss during and after the migration.

principle.title: Give the ISE PAN and MnT a Secondary -- a single Admin/Monitoring node loses management or visibility
principle.citation: Cisco ISE Deployment / High Availability guide (PAN + MnT primary/secondary, promotion).

decisions.recommended_action: Add a Secondary PAN (config/replication failover + promotion path) and a Secondary MnT (logging/reporting failover) so the control and logging planes survive a node loss; verify promotion and log continuity as part of NRFU before relying on the deployment at cutover.
decisions.alternatives: A single combined PAN+MnT for a small deployment with an accepted-risk posture; external SIEM ingestion to reduce MnT-loss blindness (does not restore management).
decisions.tradeoffs: Secondary PAN/MnT nodes cost hardware + replication overhead, but a single management or logging node is a recovery and visibility gap exactly when a migration needs both.

decisions.title: Migrate through a transit/bridge site with build-before-break, parallel-running old and new until validated
decisions.driver: Migration safety: a parallel target + per-wave validation + rollback beats a big-bang cutover.

evidence.summary: 2 migration move-group(s) span 23 switch(es) -- the cutover must be phased build-before-break (stand the target up in parallel, validate per wave, then cut over and decommission), never a single big-bang change, to preserve rollback.

principle.title: Migrate through a transit/bridge site with build-before-break, parallel-running old and new until validated
principle.citation: CCDE Ornio scenario (MPLS L3VPN migration step ordering); engine --compare/--trend snapshot diff

decisions.recommended_action: Choose a transit site; establish new circuits + routing at transit then remote; set metrics so new is preferred while old remains fallback; enable QoS + monitoring; remove old circuits remote-first/transit-last; keep every step reversible and validate with a pre/post snapshot diff.
decisions.alternatives: Flag-day cutover (fast, cheap, outage-prone); for MPLS-domain merges use Inter-AS Option B/C + BGP-LU or re-address rather than merging IGPs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Zero-downtime, reversible migration (parallel run, ordered teardown) vs a dual-transport cost window and added coordination; a flag-day is fast/cheap but outage-prone with no easy rollback.

decisions.title: Treat a degraded fabric health score as an aggregate alarm and drive the worst contributor to 100 before cutover
decisions.driver: Controller-fabric health: a degraded fabric-wide health score is the APIC's own rollup signal that accumulated faults are impacting the fabric -- a measured value, not an absence.

evidence.summary: The ACI fabric-wide health score is degraded (below 90): core2 fabric health 82/100 (maxSev critical). fabricHealthTotal rolls every node, tenant and fault into one 0-100 gauge, so a sub-90 score (sub-75 is serious) means accumulated faults are materially degrading the fabric. Drive the score back up by clearing the contributing faults -- the raised critical/major fault list is the place to start -- before cutover.

principle.title: Treat a degraded fabric health score as an aggregate alarm and drive the worst contributor to 100 before cutover
principle.citation: Cisco Application Centric Infrastructure Fundamentals — Monitoring/Troubleshooting (system, pod and node health-score computation from per-object fault severity; endpoint-weighted leaf health and spine coefficient); Cisco APIC Faults guide (Ignore Acknowledged Faults / Health Score Evaluation Policies effect on the score)

decisions.recommended_action: Decompose the score top-down to the offending object, then fix the fault — never tune the threshold. (1) From the System/Pod dashboard, drill into the lowest-scoring pod, then the lowest-scoring node, to localize the drag. (2) On that node open Faults and rank by severity; the critical/major faults are what is pulling the number down. (3) Remediate the root-cause faults (this reuses the aci-critical-fault-raised runbook) and watch the node, pod and system scores climb as each clears. (4) Distinguish genuine degradation from health that is artificially suppressed — confirm whether 'Ignore Acknowledged Faults' / squelch / a Health Score Evaluation Policy is hiding faults, because an artificially HIGH score is as dangerous as a low one for a cutover decision. (5) Set and record a go/no-go health floor (e.g. fabric and each in-scope leaf at a defined high score with no unexplained critical/major) and gate the migration on it; capture the pre-cutover score as the baseline for the post-cutover diff.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier alternative is to lower the acceptance bar — declare the degraded score 'good enough', or acknowledge/squelch the contributing faults so the number rises — and proceed without curing the underlying condition.
decisions.tradeoffs: Relaxing the floor or suppressing contributors lets the gate pass immediately and avoids root-cause work, but you migrate onto a fabric whose own health model is flagging an unresolved defect, and you forfeit a trustworthy pre/post health baseline to prove the cutover did no harm.

decisions.title: Resolve an Unenforced tenant VRF to an explicit, contract-based enforced policy before cutover (or record it as an accepted exception)
decisions.driver: ACI segmentation posture: a VRF with enforcement unenforced is default-permit between all its EPGs -- the policy segmentation is off for that routing context; confirm intent before cutover.

evidence.summary: 1 ACI VRF(s) have contract enforcement set to UNENFORCED (e.g. core2 LEGACY/legacy-vrf). An unenforced VRF applies no contracts / SGACLs between its EPGs, so every endpoint group in that routing context can communicate freely (default-permit) -- the policy-based segmentation ACI is meant to provide is off there. Confirm whether each unenforced VRF is intentional (e.g. a shared-services context) or a gap, and design the target segmentation (contracts / SGTs) per move group before cutover.

principle.title: Resolve an Unenforced tenant VRF to an explicit, contract-based enforced policy before cutover (or record it as an accepted exception)
principle.citation: Cisco ACI Contract Guide White Paper (Enforced vs. Unenforced VRF semantics, any-any deny vs. any-any permit, Unenforced disables contract-based QoS/deny/PBR, Preferred Group); How To: vzAny Usage (vzAny provide+consume permit-any == Unenforced; vzAny vs. Preferred Group mutual exclusivity)

decisions.recommended_action: Make the policy explicit and contract-based BEFORE the cutover, and never flip the flag bare. (1) Decide the target posture for the VRF from the migration design (segmented, or intentionally open). (2) Profile the real traffic first — use the fabric's flow/contract telemetry and connectivity/permit logs to enumerate which EPG pairs actually communicate, so you build contracts from evidence, not assumption. (3) If the intent is open-but-enforceable, switch the VRF to Enforced and reproduce the open behavior explicitly with a vzAny construct: have vzAny both provide and consume a single permit-any contract (functionally equivalent to Unenforced but now a real, enforced policy you can later tighten, and which unblocks QoS/deny/PBR). (4) Then progressively replace the permit-any with per-application contracts (or migrate selected EPGs into a Contract Preferred Group), tightening in stages while watching for drops. (5) Honor the constraint that vzAny-contracts and the Preferred Group are mutually exclusive in the same VRF — pick one model. (6) Validate post-change that intended flows still pass and unintended ones are denied; if the decision is to remain Unenforced, record it as an explicit, signed-off risk exception so it never silently becomes 'healthy'.
decisions.alternatives: The cheaper, riskier alternatives are either to leave the VRF Unenforced and migrate the flat posture as-is, or to flip it straight to Enforced in the maintenance window without first discovering and provisioning the required contracts.
decisions.tradeoffs: Leaving it Unenforced is free and zero-outage-risk at cutover but carries an unsegmented east-west blast radius and forfeits QoS/deny/PBR; the bare flip to Enforced achieves segmentation cheaply but, without prior flow discovery and contracts, drops every uncontracted flow the moment it takes effect — turning a policy change into an outage.

decisions.title: Reconcile staged-but-undeployed FMC changes before cutover -- running config must equal intent
decisions.driver: Config drift: an FTD with staged undeployed changes is running a config that differs from FMC's intent -- reconcile before cutover so the running state is known.

evidence.summary: core1: 1 device(s) with staged undeployed changes -- staged, undeployed configuration changes in FMC. The running config no longer equals FMC's intended config: deploying mid-migration changes device behaviour, and not deploying leaves the intended policy un-applied. Reconcile each pending deployment BEFORE the cutover window (deploy and re-validate, or explicitly defer) so the firewall's running state is known and intended at cutover.

principle.title: Reconcile staged-but-undeployed FMC changes before cutover -- running config must equal intent
principle.citation: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center REST API (deployabledevices) + change-management practice.

decisions.recommended_action: Reconcile each pending deployment BEFORE the cutover window -- deploy and re-validate, or explicitly defer with sign-off -- so the firewall's running state is known and intended at cutover; capture the deployment state in the NRFU baseline.
decisions.alternatives: Freeze change windows ahead of the migration so no drift accumulates.
decisions.tradeoffs: Reconciling drift is pre-cutover effort, but cutting over a firewall whose running config differs from intent invites surprise behaviour during the change.

decisions.title: Derive a lean DSCP/PHB class model from the application profile and align it to platform/WAN limits
decisions.driver: Design top-down from the WHY: gather the requirement, then decide.

evidence.summary: Absent/ad-hoc QoS marking is observable, but the target class model needs the application traffic profile (which apps, which delay/loss budgets) -- supplied via the critical_apps requirement.

principle.title: Derive a lean DSCP/PHB class model from the application profile and align it to platform/WAN limits
principle.citation: CCDE Session 10 (RFC 4594, minimize classes, close-to-source); CCDE scenario (1 PQ + N BQ from app matrix)

decisions.recommended_action: Define and roll out an RFC-4594 DSCP/PHB scheme at the edge; consolidate to the lean class set the platform and WAN both support; mark close to source and trust those marks downstream.
decisions.alternatives: Legacy IP-Precedence mapping on old gear; a smaller custom class set negotiated with the SP; collapse business-hi/lo to reduce count.
decisions.tradeoffs: Granularity/precision vs hardware limits, operational simplicity and SP class-count constraints; too many classes hit hardware ceilings, too few starve real-time. Standardization vs per-device drift.

open_questions.title: Defense-in-depth via modular, layered security zones — not perimeter-only
Right-size availability to the application and place in the network, not 5x9 everywhere
Choose the DC fabric operating model: standalone NX-OS VXLAN-EVPN (default) vs Cisco ACI policy fabric
Interconnect EVPN fabrics as isolated sites (Multi-Site at the border-leaf), not one stretched Multi-Pod fabric

Use a three-tier hierarchy for scale (or full-mesh the distribution if collapsing the core), and tier for blast-radius + RBAC
Gather the decision-driving requirements before designing — never assume, never re-ask what's given

requirements_model.note: Design top-down from the WHY: supply this register and the blueprint right-sizes each decision and scores the trade-off axes against it; absent, the engine surfaces the questions rather than assuming an answer.

design_blueprint.methodology:
SENIOR-DESIGNER MINDSET the engine should embody:

1) WHY-FIRST, top-down. A design is good ONLY if it meets requirements; technology is chosen last. The reasoning order is WHY (business intent) -> WHAT (functional/application/technical requirements + fixed constraints) -> HOW (topology/protocol/device). Every target-state recommendation must trace to a stated requirement, never to a default technology preference or to maximizing one property in isolation. The engine, which holds rich current-state but NO requirements model, must therefore present its findings as evidence and explicitly flag the requirement gaps it cannot fill, rather than asserting 'the design should be X.'

2) REQUIREMENTS GATHERING & CLASSIFICATION. Tag every gathered fact into exactly one bucket: business goal, functional requirement, application requirement (traffic profile, criticality, QoS/latency budget, RTO/convergence target), technical/non-functional -ility (availability, performance, scalability, security, manageability), or fixed CONSTRAINT (budget, installed base, skills, vendor/standards, regulatory, geography). Constraints BOUND the solution space and routinely veto the technically-ideal option — the engine must filter candidate recommendations through the constraint first. Maintain bidirectional traceability: requirement -> design decision -> validation test (and backward, decision -> why). Dis

axes.label: High availability & resiliency
axes.intent: Survive component, link and node failure; size redundancy to the requirement, not uniformly.

axes.label: Fast convergence
axes.intent: Restore forwarding quickly after a failure (timers/BFD/summarization), traded against stability.

axes.label: Scalability
axes.intent: Grow without redesign; bound table size, flooding scope and broadcast-domain size.

axes.label: Modularity & hierarchy
axes.intent: Replicable, fault-isolating building blocks with clear tiers; the enabler of the other axes.

axes.label: Security & segmentation
axes.intent: Least privilege, zoning, and control-/management-plane protection.

axes.label: Simplicity vs complexity
axes.intent: Prefer the simplest design that meets the requirement; complexity is a hidden, compounding cost.

axes.label: Optimal routing
axes.intent: Forwarding follows the intended, most-efficient paths; avoid suboptimal/asymmetric routing.

axes.label: Load balancing & efficiency
axes.intent: Use available capacity; avoid idle redundant links (e.g. STP-blocked uplinks).

axes.label: Manageability & operability
axes.intent: Observable, consistent and automatable to operate (time, logging, AAA, baselines).

axes.label: Cost / affordability
axes.intent: The universal counterweight every other axis draws from; spend where a requirement justifies it.

summary.headline: 5 critical recommended target-state design decision(s); leading: Enforce secure management (SSH/SNMPv3), centralized RBAC/AAA least-privilege, and retire plaintext.

coverage.caveat: Design decisions are grounded only in collected evidence; not-collected devices (including any uncollected core) are an explicit unknown -- their role and redundancy are not assumed.

aci.title: Clear or formally accept every CRITICAL APIC fault before freezing the migration baseline
aci.recommended_action: Work the fault by its lifecycle and its delegate chain, not by silencing it. (1) Enumerate critical faults at System > Faults and per-node under Fabric > Inventory > Pod > node > Faults; record the fault code, the affected MO (dn), and the lifecycle state. (2) Follow each fault to its ROOT MO — a fault:Delegate surfaced on a parent points back to a fault:Inst on the object actually in trouble; hide delegated faults to find the true origin. (3) Look the code up in the ACI System Messages Reference and execute its documented remediation (e.g. F1394 -> verify the fabric port cabling/transceiver and that the peer is up; F0110 -> drive the node-not-active runbook; F0321/F0323/F0325 -> restore APIC cluster quorum/'Fully Fit'). (4) Remediate the underlying condition and confirm the fault transitions to raised-clearing then clears on its own. (5) Only after the real fix, if a residual is a known cosmetic/expected condition, ACKNOWLEDGE it (which deletes it immediately when retaining, or marks it expected otherwise) — and document why. Re-run the fault sweep and require zero unexplained criticals before the cutover gate.
aci.citation: Cisco APIC Faults, Events, and System Messages Management Guide — Faults (severity levels, fault lifecycle soaking/raised/clearing/retaining, acknowledge vs. squelch, delegated faults, health-score impact); ACI System Messages Reference Guide — ACI F0x Messages (e.g. F0110 fltFabricNodeFailed); Address ACI fault F1394 (interface-physical-down)

aci.title: Restore any leaf/spine that is not Active to the registered Active state before relying on the fabric
aci.recommended_action: Walk the discovery state machine in order — physical, then identity, then trust — rather than re-registering blindly. (1) Confirm the node's current state in Fabric > Inventory > Fabric Membership / Nodes Pending Registration. (2) PHYSICAL: verify the inter-switch cabling and that the leaf port to the spine is an UPLINK (a downlink will not relay the spine's DHCP, a classic discovery blocker); check the LLDP neighbor with 'show lldp neighbors detail' on the peer and confirm both sides run a supported, compatible image. (3) IDENTITY: from the leaf run 'acidiag avread' (or 'avread') to confirm it sees the APICs and an infra TEP from the configured TEP pool over the correct infra VLAN; if it is unregistered, register it with the intended node ID. (4) TRUST: on 4.2+ run 'show discoveryissues' on the node to surface certificate/clock/connectivity failures, and validate the node certificate and APIC cluster reachability ('Fully Fit'). (5) Resolve the surfaced cause, confirm the node transitions to Active and its F0110/related faults clear, and only then admit it to the cutover scope. For a true replacement, follow the documented decommission/replace procedure so the old serial and TEP are cleanly reused.
aci.citation: Troubleshoot ACI Fabric Discovery — Initial Fabric Setup (node discovery states, uplink/LLDP/infra-VLAN/TEP/DHCP checks, acidiag avread, show discoveryissues, certificate validation); Cisco APIC Getting Started Guide — Fabric Initialization and Switch Discovery (Undiscovered->Discovered->Active, registration); ACI System Messages — F0110 fltFabricNodeFailed

aci-fabric.title: Size the policy-controller (APIC) cluster for quorum: odd >=3, sharded/replicated, minority degrades read-only -- never split-brain
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Deploy an odd cluster of at least three controllers; rely on shard replication + per-shard leader election; spread members across pods/rooms/power and off the forwarding path; document that a minority is read-only-but-forwarding and freeze policy changes until majority recovers; scale the cluster for fabric size, not for HA.

aci-fabric.title: Choose the default-gateway anchor deliberately per tier (firewall vs fabric); an external-service gateway forces that BD into L2-transport mode
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Anchor untrusted/regulated tiers on the firewall for full inspection; for tiers needing efficient intranet reach, place the gateway on the fabric with default-route-to-firewall + more-specific intranet routes; for every BD whose gateway is an external service device, explicitly set the fabric to L2-transport mode (no unicast routing, ARP flood, MAC forwarding) and run device-to-router dynamic routing directly between the appliances.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco AS ACI Design & Deployment (Telco DC) -- Firewall-as-Gateway / Fabric-as-Gateway / iBGP-to-ASR + ACI Architecture (Traditional Services Insertion, MAC forwarding); web-verified against Cisco ACI L3Out/BD docs.

aci-fabric.title: An L3Out external-EPG subnet is a security CLASSIFIER, not a route filter -- scope each flag to one purpose, never 0.0.0.0/0 to classify
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Scope each external-subnet flag to its single purpose: a specific classification prefix per external EPG (avoid 0/0 so the policy tag stays unique), Export/Import Route Control only to advertise/gate routes, Shared Route-Control + Shared-Security for deliberate inter-VRF leaks; advertise BD subnets explicitly, never by default; isolate a peer needing a default classification on its own dedicated L3Out.
aci-fabric.citation: ACI Best Practices: Lessons from the Front Lines (Cisco SEVT) + ACI NIP (External EPGs / BD Subnet Advertisement) + ACI Transit Routing; web-verified against Cisco APIC L3 Networking guide.

aci-fabric.title: Treat the APIC cluster + the VLAN-pool -> domain -> AEP -> EPG access-policy chain as the fabric's single source of truth
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Define non-overlapping static VLAN pools per function, bind each to one domain and AEP, reuse named switch/interface profiles, and freeze a naming convention before scale-out; deploy an odd (three-node) APIC cluster as the policy SSOT.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco AS Secure Multi-Tenant ACI Design (APIC Connectivity; Naming Conventions; Pools/Domains/AEPs); web-verified against Cisco APIC access-policy documentation.

aci-fabric.title: An ACI access edge is STP-transparent: flood external BPDUs within the EPG so outside STP breaks loops, and add MCP / Rogue-EP / port-tracking as the fabric's own safeguards
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Leave BPDU filter/guard DISABLED on ports toward external switches/blade chassis so their STP keeps converging; enable BPDU guard only on host ports; enable MCP (with a key), Rogue-EP control and uplink port-tracking as the fabric's intrinsic loop/mobility safeguards. A clean single L2 handoff that drops BPDUs is appropriate only once the legacy STP domain is retired.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI design doctrine (NIP STP BPDU Filter/Guard + Global Policies / MCP / Rogue-EP), grounded in the D:\ ACI corpus; web-verified that ACI runs no STP and floods BPDUs within the EPG.

aci-fabric.title: Move the L3Out to the spine (GOLF) when per-tenant border-leaf WAN scale runs out -- the WAN edge becomes a logical border-leaf via MP-BGP EVPN + VXLAN
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Where border-leaf L3Out scale is the limit, use GOLF (spine MP-BGP EVPN Type-5 + VXLAN to WAN-edge logical border-leaves, OpFlex-automated per-VRF); on a stretched fabric engineer ingress/egress symmetry (advertise fabric host-routes inbound, prefer the local GOLF for egress, AS-path tuning per pod).
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI GOLF / Layer-3 EVPN WAN design; web-verified.

aci-fabric.title: An ACI L3Out applies ONE uniform routing+security policy to all its peers -- split into separate L3Outs for per-exit policy, don't toggle flags on one
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Provision one L3Out per distinct routing-or-security policy domain; bind contracts between the specific source EPG and the intended external EPG; enable transit explicitly (export only required prefixes); leak inter-VRF/transit routes via an external fusion router (matching VRF per fabric VRF) where native shared-L3Out scale does not fit.
aci-fabric.citation: ACI Best Practices: Lessons from the Front Lines (Cisco SEVT) + ACI Transit Routing + EXPO2020 ACI LLD4 (L3Out / external EPG / fusion route-leak); web-verified against Cisco APIC L3 guide.

aci-fabric.title: Design ACI L3Out route-control around its default asymmetry: inbound import is permit-all (tighten on BGP only), outbound export is deny-all and exact-mask
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Enable import route-control only on BGP L3Outs and enumerate every permitted inbound prefix; rely on the export deny-all default and explicitly add each BD/transit subnet to be advertised (exact-mask); document the L3Out route policy rather than assuming a symmetric filter.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI L3Out route-control design (import permit-all / export deny-all asymmetry); web-verified.

aci-fabric.title: Run the EPG overlay from the ACI leaf to the virtual switch so an intermediate L2 / blade fabric-interconnect carries only the infra VLAN, not per-EPG VLAN sprawl
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Where an intermediate L2 / blade-FI sits between the ACI leaf and virtualized hosts, extend the EPG overlay (VXLAN) to the virtual switch so the intermediate fabric and FI carry only the infra VLAN, rather than trunking every per-EPG VLAN across it.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI virtualization / blade-FI integration design; web-verified.

aci-fabric.title: Extend the fabric policy edge into the hypervisor with a VMM domain (APIC-driven DVS / AVE, OpFlex policy) and choose the micro-seg enforcement locus deliberately
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Integrate a VMM domain so APIC drives the DVS and pushes per-EPG port-groups, with OpFlex as the policy/endpoint plane; use AVE/virtual-leaf local switching where host-proximate east-west filtering is wanted; before enabling the stateful hypervisor firewall, design + monitor the inter-instance state-sync path that vMotion depends on.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI VMM domain / AVE / micro-segmentation design; web-verified.

aci-fabric.title: Build ACI inter-VRF shared services to the leaking rules: provider subnet under the EPG, consumer under the BD, contract scope global, conserve class-IDs
aci-fabric.recommended_action: Flag the provider subnet 'shared' under the EPG with non-overlapping per-EPG carvings; put the consumer subnet under the BD; set contract scope Global (or exported); keep leaked subnets non-overlapping; budget the global class-IDs shared contracts consume.
aci-fabric.citation: Cisco ACI shared-services / inter-VRF route-leaking design; web-verified.

aci-multisite.title: ACI Multi-Pod hinges on a qualified IPN underlay (PIM-Bidir + phantom-RP, jumbo MTU, OSPF, DHCP-relay); a stretched subnet needs host-route advertisement to avoid asymmetric egress
aci-multisite.recommended_action: Qualify the IPN for PIM-Bidir (phantom-RP, hardware Bidir support, P2P OSPF loopbacks), jumbo MTU, DHCP-relay and routed subinterfaces BEFORE committing to Multi-Pod; raise OSPF cost on spine-IPN links so the RP path avoids spines; assign an anycast TEP/ETEP per pod as the next-hop; use spine route-reflector peering for pod scale; and for any cross-pod subnet plan host-route advertisement.
aci-multisite.citation: ACI NIP (Multi-Pod / IPN) + ACI Best Practices: Lessons from the Front Lines (Inter-Pod Network Requirements) + EXPO2020 ACI LLD4; web-verified against Cisco ACI Multi-Pod white papers.

aci-multisite.title: Multi-Pod (one stretched policy domain) vs Multi-Site (isolated domains) is a failure-isolation choice -- and Multi-Pod needs a witness pod for cluster quorum on a site loss
aci-multisite.recommended_action: Select Multi-Pod for one stretched policy domain with per-pod fault isolation (and place a third/witness pod to preserve APIC quorum on a site loss, degrading to read-only -- never two writers); select Multi-Site for independently-failing domains with templated policy and independent upgrades.
aci-multisite.citation: EXPO2020 ACI NIP/LLD4 (Multi-Pod over IPN, 3-node APIC quorum + Witness pod) + ACI Stretched Active-Active WP; web-verified against Cisco ACI Multi-Pod / Multi-Site white papers (c11-737855 / c11-739714).

aci-multisite.title: ACI Multi-Site stretches L2 over a plain routed inter-site network via spine Head-End Replication -- no multicast DCI, but EX/FX+ spines are a hard dependency for VNID/Class-ID translation
aci-multisite.recommended_action: When the target is ACI Multi-Site with any stretched BD, specify the ISN as a unicast-only routed core (OSPF/BGP, jumbo MTU, no PIM required) and explicitly verify the inter-site/spine tier is Nexus 9000 EX/FX or newer; if first-gen spines are present, treat Multi-Site L2-stretch as blocked until those spines are refreshed (or fall back to Multi-Pod, which has its own multicast-IPN cost). Capture the contrast with Multi-Pod's PIM-Bidir IPN so the team picks the DCI underlay deliberately.
aci-multisite.citation: Cisco ACI Multi-Site Architecture White Paper (c11-739609); Cisco ACI Multi-Site Fundamentals Guide (cross-site namespace normalization / O-MTEP head-end replication); Cisco Multi-Site Deployment Guide for ACI Fabrics

aci-multisite.title: Gate Multi-Pod vs Multi-Site on the hard latency + single-APIC scale ceilings, not just fault-isolation taste
aci-multisite.recommended_action: When proposing ACI as the DC target, decide Multi-Pod vs Multi-Site against the measured inter-site RTT and the fabric scale forecast: Multi-Pod inside the ~50ms / single-APIC-domain envelope; Multi-Site once latency, leaf/pod scale, or per-region fault-isolation crosses the line. Forbid back-to-back-leaf dual-fabric interconnect; orchestrate multiple fabrics via Nexus Dashboard Orchestrator/Multi-Site.
aci-multisite.citation: Cisco ACI Multi-Site Architecture White Paper (c11-739609) and Cisco ACI Multi-Pod White Paper (c11-737855)

aci-multisite.title: Localize broadcast by default on a stretched ACI Multi-Site BD: keep per-BD 'Intersite BUM Traffic Allow' OFF unless a flooding driver exists
aci-multisite.recommended_action: For every bridge domain proposed to stretch across ACI sites, require an explicit per-BD decision: default 'Intersite BUM Traffic Allow' (and inter-site ARP flooding) to disabled, and only enable it where a documented driver (L2-multicast clustering, live migration, or a bounded legacy-migration cutover) exists -- then plan to turn it back off once the gateway moves into the fabric. Because the orchestrator defaults these knobs ON, treat them as an active 'turn-off' step in the LLD, not a no-op.
aci-multisite.citation: Cisco ACI Multi-Site Architecture White Paper (c11-739609) and Cisco ACI Multi-Site Fundamentals Guide (Stretched Layer 2 with/without flooding); Cisco Nexus Dashboard Orchestrator Configuration Guide for ACI Fabrics

aci-multisite.title: Organize NDO schemas/templates by object scope (site-local vs stretched) with one owning template per object, not one schema per fabric
aci-multisite.recommended_action: If the target architecture is ACI Multi-Site (or a mixed estate orchestrated by NDO), require the HLD to specify the schema/template organization explicitly: which objects are stretched vs site-local, the networking-vs-application template split, per-tenant schema grouping against the release's Verified Scalability limits, and a single owning template per object with a stated NDO-vs-APIC authority for any brownfield-imported policy. Flag a layout that maps one schema per fabric or co-mingles stretched and site-local objects in the same template as a change-blast-radius and drift risk.
aci-multisite.citation: Cisco, 'Nexus Dashboard Orchestrator Schemas and Application Templates / Templates Overview and Operations for ACI Fabrics, Release 4.3.x' (Schema and Template Design Considerations); Cisco ACI Multi-Site Architecture White Paper c11-739609

aci-policy.title: Segment with the EPG/contract whitelist (default-deny inter-EPG), seeded from the existing firewall policy
aci-policy.recommended_action: Model tenant -> VRF -> Application-Profile -> EPG with provider/consumer contracts as the segmentation layer (default-deny inter-EPG, contracts only where flows are required); seed the initial contract catalogue from the current firewall policy and bind a change process that updates contracts whenever firewall rules change; use vzAny for VRF-wide common policy and micro-EPG/intra-EPG isolation for high-value tiers.
aci-policy.citation: EXPO2020 ACI LLD4 (Tenants/VRFs/EPGs/Contracts/vzAny) + ACI Network Implementation Plan (Contracts) + ACI Security & Service Integration; web-verified against Cisco ACI Policy Model + Contract guides.

aci-policy.title: Migrate to ACI network-centric first (1 VLAN = 1 BD = 1 EPG), then evolve to application-centric
aci-policy.recommended_action: Phase 1: instantiate a 1:1:1 VLAN-to-BD-to-EPG mapping (pervasive anycast gateway on the BD, or external gateways with permit-any) so endpoints move 1:1 and forwarding is proven. Phase 2: regroup EPGs into Application Profiles by tier and replace permit-any with least-privilege contracts as the application dependencies are documented post-cutover.
aci-policy.citation: EXPO2020 ACI NIP/LLD (network-centric 1:1:1 VLAN-EPG-BD) + Cisco AS Secure Multi-Tenant ACI Design (Application-Centric vs Network-Centric), cross-checked with Cisco 'Migrating Existing Networks to ACI'.

aci-policy.title: In a contract fabric, a route is not reachability: validate the programmed contract, not just the RIB
aci-policy.recommended_action: Treat connectivity as route PLUS contract: enumerate the required inter-group flows as explicit contracts and validate the programmed deny/permit zoning rules, not route presence alone; make this an explicit NRFU acceptance item for any whitelist fabric.
aci-policy.citation: Cisco ACI Contract Guide (implicit-deny drops a flow even with a route present; two L3Out external EPGs need a contract); web-verified.

aci-policy.title: Reclassify endpoints below the base EPG with micro-EPGs (uSeg) by IP/MAC/VM-attribute, plus intra-EPG isolation -- knowing IP-uSeg only acts on ROUTED traffic
aci-policy.recommended_action: Reserve plain EPG+contract whitelisting for app-tier/zone separation; escalate to a µEPG only where attribute-based classification is genuinely needed; for IP-µEPG ensure cross-subnet (routed) flows + enable unicast routing/SVI; set explicit attribute precedence; use intra-EPG isolation for same-role mutual isolation.
aci-policy.citation: Cisco ACI micro-segmentation / uSeg-EPG design; web-verified.

aci-policy.title: At extreme overlapping-tenant scale, the VRF ceiling forces legacy-L2 BD mode -- and the loss of fabric policy
aci-policy.recommended_action: Stay VRF-per-tenant while tenant count fits the VRF budget and the fabric gateway/policy is wanted; switch a BD to legacy L2 mode only when segment scale demands it, and explicitly relocate gateway/routing/security to external devices; or partition tenants across multiple fabrics/pods to stay under the ceiling.
aci-policy.citation: Cisco AS ACI Practice (Service-Provider Cloud) -- overlapping networks / legacy BD mode / Tenant-Context-BD scale; web-confirmed against Cisco APIC scale docs.

aci-services.title: Insert L4-7 services via service-graph PBR (redirect BD, symmetric hashing, health-tracking, N+M), not by VLAN stitching
aci-services.recommended_action: Use service-graph + PBR with a dedicated redirect BD (endpoint data-plane learning off), symmetric sip-dip-protocol hashing so a flow pins to one node, health-group tracking that withdraws a node in BOTH directions on any leg failure, resilient hashing so only the failed node's flows rehash, and N+M backup sized so survivors are not overloaded; in Multi-Pod add location-based PBR awareness.
aci-services.citation: EXPO2020 ACI LLD4 (PBR / Firewall integration / Anycast service) + ACI Security & Service Integration (Symmetric PBR, Tracking, Resilient-Hash, N+M); web-verified against Cisco PBR Service-Graph docs.

aci-services.title: Build a multi-node PBR service chain as an ORDERED function list, and govern node failure with the threshold down-action (permit / deny / bypass)
aci-services.recommended_action: In the target HLD, render each L4-L7 insertion as an explicit ordered node list with a per-node threshold down-action rationale (security nodes fail-closed/deny; optional optimization nodes bypass or permit), and require IP-SLA tracking on every PBR destination so the down-action can actually fire.
aci-services.citation: Cisco APIC Layer 4 to Layer 7 Services Deployment Guide, Configuring Policy-Based Redirect (multi-node PBR up to 5 function nodes; Threshold Down Action deny/permit/bypass, bypass added APIC 4.1(2)); Cisco ACI PBR Service Graph Design White Paper (c11-739971)

aci-services.title: Give a PBR service node its own routed BD and disable remote-leaf source-VTEP learning to stop endpoint flapping
aci-services.recommended_action: Allocate a dedicated routed service BD per PBR node, disable remote-leaf source-VTEP learning on it (both directions if return is redirected), register the node IP+VMAC in the redirect policy, and confirm the leaf platform supports the redirect; validate the endpoint table stays stable after insertion.
aci-services.citation: Cisco ACI PBR service-graph design (redirect BD, data-plane learning); web-verified.

aci-services.title: Pick the service-graph device mode (GoTo routed / GoThrough transparent / one-arm) by the flow it enforces, and choose managed vs unmanaged by who owns L4-L7 config
aci-services.recommended_action: Use GoTo (routed) as the default + the prerequisite for PBR/route-peering (enable unicast routing, ensure the fabric knows the far-side subnet); GoThrough only for transparent bump-in-the-wire; default to unmanaged (network-policy) mode unless single-pane APIC control of the appliance is wanted AND a maintained device package exists.
aci-services.citation: Cisco ACI L4-L7 service-graph design (device modes, managed/unmanaged); web-verified.

automation.title: Make network change a Git-reviewed CI/CD pipeline with offline pre-change and post-change validation
automation.recommended_action: Adopt a GitOps pipeline: intent/config in Git (source of truth), every change a reviewed MR with branch-protection + CODEOWNERS; CI runs offline pre-change validation; deploy on merge; run post-change validation and auto-rollback on failure; keep the repo as the audit + rollback source.
automation.citation: NetDevOps / GitOps for network automation (CI/CD, pre/post validation); web-verified.

automation.title: Drive config through model-based interfaces (NETCONF/RESTCONF/gNMI over YANG) applied transactionally -- not screen-scraped CLI
automation.recommended_action: Standardize on a model-driven transport (NETCONF/gNMI for config, RESTCONF where a REST/JSON toolchain fits) bound to YANG; apply via candidate-commit with confirmed-commit/auto-revert for risky in-band changes; default to OpenConfig/IETF models for the portable surface, native YANG only where features demand.

automation.title: Anchor automation on a Network Source of Truth holding intended state; render config from it declaratively and idempotently, never the reverse
automation.recommended_action: Stand up a Network Source of Truth as the authoritative intended-state store; render device config from SoT + templates (config = function of intent); model change as declarative idempotent desired-state (Terraform/NSO/idempotent Ansible) so the tool reconciles the delta; detect drift as SoT-vs-device diff.
automation.citation: Network Source of Truth (NetBox) + IaC (Terraform/Ansible/NSO) design practice; web-verified.

automation.title: Replace SNMP polling with model-driven streaming telemetry: named YANG-path subscriptions, on-change for state and tiered periodic for counters, dial-out by default
automation.recommended_action: Specify telemetry as named subscriptions on explicit YANG paths: on-change for state/events, tiered periodic for counters; default dial-out gRPC for fleets; verify path mode via the device's mdt-capabilities; size a redundant collector + time-series store to the stream rate/cardinality; add flow telemetry (full NetFlow/IPFIX for security, sampled for capacity) for the traffic matrix.
automation.citation: gNMI/gRPC model-driven telemetry + NetFlow/IPFIX design; web-verified (beyond the KB's modern-telemetry principle).

automation.title: Add active/synthetic assurance for paths you don't own, baseline per-network with AI analytics, and close the loop only on verified telemetry + safe rollback
automation.recommended_action: Place active/synthetic agents at user-representative vantage points (branch/DC/cloud) to measure off-net paths; use AI analytics for adaptive per-site baselines/anomaly ranking rather than static global thresholds, owning the inputs; gate any closed-loop remediation on verified telemetry + a tested rollback.
automation.citation: ThousandEyes / Catalyst Center Assurance + closed-loop automation design; web-verified.

bgp.title: Use BGP for a multihomed Internet edge with two providers
bgp.recommended_action: Run eBGP to each ISP, obtain a public ASN + PI block, advertise only enterprise prefixes outbound and filter inbound; use dual CPE to two ISPs for HA and BFD for fast peer detection.
bgp.citation: CCDE Session 5/6 (BGP multihoming); Cisco BGP load-sharing doc; engine parse_bgp_summary

bgp.title: Apply an eBGP edge hardening baseline and pre-arm RTBH/FlowSpec for DDoS
bgp.recommended_action: Enable session auth, GTSM, First-AS, max-prefix and inbound bogon/RFC1918 filters (+RPKI ROV); pre-configure dest/source RTBH via BGP and FlowSpec/scrubbing; never count MD5 as DDoS defense.
bgp.citation: CCDE Session 6 (BGP security, RTBH, FlowSpec); CCDE scenario (MD5-vs-GTSM, CoPP/uRPF/GTSM for DDoS)

bgp.title: Choose the enterprise-core BGP model (iBGP / eBGP / hybrid) by scale and policy needs
bgp.recommended_action: Adopt the hybrid for most large multi-region cores (iBGP per region + eBGP/IGP between); reserve pure iBGP-core for optimality-first and pure eBGP-core for policy-first designs; use RRs for iBGP scale.
bgp.citation: CCDE Session 5/6 (enterprise BGP options); CCDE scenario (BGP-core for scale + control)

bgp.title: Enable BGP PIC plus BFD and next-hop tracking for table-size-independent fast convergence
bgp.recommended_action: Enable BGP PIC (core + PIC-Edge backup) backed by hierarchical CEF; run BFD on BGP next-hops; enable Next-Hop-Tracking on loopback/multihop sessions and Fast-External-Failover on directly-connected eBGP.

bgp.title: Restore the path diversity a route reflector hides before relying on it for PE redundancy or fast reroute
bgp.recommended_action: Where RRs serve clients that need redundancy, deliberately restore diversity and size the remedy against four axes (MPLS-VPN fitness / extra session+RR cost / migration disruption / operational familiarity): BGP Add-Path (RFC 7911) for standards-based per-next-hop diversity, unique-RD-per-PE for MPLS L3VPN, shadow-RR or shadow-session where Add-Path is unavailable; pair with BGP PIC for sub-second reconverge.
bgp.citation: RFC 7911 (Advertisement of Multiple Paths in BGP / Add-Path) + Orhan Ergun CCIE-SP path-diversity comparison (Add-Path vs Shadow-RR vs Shadow-Session vs Unique-RD); complements ibgp-full-mesh-to-route-reflector.

bgp.title: Replace iBGP full mesh with redundant route reflectors as the AS scales, and restore lost path diversity
bgp.recommended_action: Introduce dual RRs per AFI sized in clusters, migrate speakers to clients, keep the RR topology congruent to physical, and re-add path diversity (Add-Path/Best-External/ORR/unique-RD) plus BGP PIC for sub-second reconvergence.
bgp.citation: CCDE Session 5/6 (RR rules, diversity, PIC); CCDE scenario (full-mesh iBGP -> RR)

bgp.title: Pick the BGP attribute by traffic direction and prefer portable over proprietary/local
bgp.recommended_action: Inbound: MED (single-homed)/prepend/communities; outbound: LOCAL_PREF over Weight; for HA get an own ASN + PI block; for dual circuits to one SP, terminate on different PEs or peer from a loopback reachable via two static routes.
bgp.citation: CCDE scenario (inbound vs outbound, LOCAL_PREF vs Weight, hot-potato/idle-uplink)

bgp.title: Right-size the Internet-edge BGP table: default vs default+partial vs full
bgp.recommended_action: Choose the smallest table that meets the goal: default-only for simple/single-exit, default + partial for moderate optimization, full only where outbound TE is genuinely required and the platform can hold it.

bgp.title: Use BGP as PE-CE for self-service TE, and solve same-AS/multihoming loops with AS-override + SoO
bgp.recommended_action: Run BGP PE-CE for self-service TE; use one customer AS everywhere with provider AS-override; assign a unique SoO per multihomed site and unique RDs for path diversity.
bgp.citation: CCDE Session 6 (SoO, AS-override); CCDE scenarios (BGP PE-CE, same-AS-everywhere)

campus-fabric.title: Put wireless on the fabric: WLC keeps the CAPWAP control plane, but distribute the data plane via VXLAN at the fabric APs
campus-fabric.recommended_action: Use fabric-enabled wireless so APs VXLAN-encapsulate client data to the local fabric edge (shared anycast gateway + SGT for wired/wireless), keeping the WLC on the CAPWAP control plane; size WLC/edge for the distributed model.
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access Fabric Wireless Design Guide; web-verified.

campus-fabric.title: Layer SD-Access segmentation: macro-isolate with Virtual Networks (VRF), micro-segment inside with SGTs, ISE as the single policy source
campus-fabric.recommended_action: Define a deliberately small set of VNs aligned to hard trust boundaries; micro-segment inside each with SGTs/SGACLs; onboard endpoints closed-loop with ISE (802.1X/MAB -> VN+SGT via RADIUS, CoA for re-auth); design SGT propagation (inline where supported, SXP where not) and ISE redundancy.
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access / TrustSec Design Guide (VN=VRF, SGT in VXLAN-GPO ~64K, ISE/SGACL); web-verified.

campus-fabric.title: For multi-site SD-Access, prefer SD-Access transit to keep VN+SGT intact end-to-end; use IP transit only to hand off to a non-fabric WAN
campus-fabric.recommended_action: Where the inter-site path can carry LISP/VXLAN and meet RTT/MTU, use SD-Access transit (dedicated transit control-plane node, no edge/border) so VN + SGT stay intact end-to-end; use IP transit when you must hand off to a non-fabric WAN, and then explicitly re-map the VN (VRF-lite) and re-carry the SGT (SXP/inline tagging) across the boundary.
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access multi-site design (SD-Access transit vs IP transit); web-verified.

campus-fabric.title: Adopt SD-Access only for a concrete driver (identity-segmentation / automation / mobility); else keep routed-access -- and design the border/fusion handoff
campus-fabric.recommended_action: Adopt SD-Access only when a named driver (segmentation / automation / mobility) earns the complexity; otherwise keep routed-access. If fabric is chosen, explicitly design the border node + fusion device that leaks/terminates VNs and propagates SGTs to the non-fabric world.
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access (Software-Defined Access) Design Guide; web-verified (Catalyst Center, ex-DNA Center).

campus-fabric.title: Place SD-Access fabric roles (edge / border / control-plane / intermediate) by site size: separate for HA, collapse to Fabric-in-a-Box only for the smallest sites
campus-fabric.recommended_action: For medium/large/critical sites, distribute edge, border and control-plane onto separate (and redundant) devices; reserve Fabric-in-a-Box (collapsed roles) for small sites that accept no redundancy; use a stack/SVL where chassis redundancy at a collapsed role is wanted.
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access Design Guide (fabric roles, Fabric-in-a-Box, HA placement); web-verified.

campus-fabric.title: Treat SD-Access as four decoupled planes (Catalyst Center / LISP / VXLAN / TrustSec) on a routed underlay; kill flood-and-learn
campus-fabric.recommended_action: Document four named planes with owners/failure-modes; build a routed L3 underlay (LAN Automation / IS-IS, MTU >= 9100, loopbacks + transit only); deploy >= 2 control-plane nodes per site (their own devices on medium/large sites); standardize on LISP Pub/Sub for new fabrics (image 17.6+).
campus-fabric.citation: Cisco SD-Access Design Guide (LISP control plane, VXLAN, LAN Automation, Pub/Sub); web-verified.

campus-sda.title: Confirm whether the down LISP session is a real control-plane outage or an expected no-EID node before gating the fabric
campus-sda.recommended_action: Disambiguate, then chase the underlay. (1) Establish whether this session SHOULD be up: identify the peer's role — a session from an active edge (with endpoints) or a route-importing border to a control-plane node must be Established; a down session from a device with genuinely no EIDs to register is expected and is not a defect. (2) For a session that should be up, inspect it with `show lisp session` and `show lisp session vrf <vrf> <map-server-ip>` (state, message in/out counts, active instances) to see whether it never came up or flapped. (3) Verify the underlay first — the LISP session is a TCP session, so confirm IP reachability/routing to the map-server RLOC and that no ACL/firewall is blocking the LISP control ports; an underlay routing or MTU problem is the common root. (4) Then check the LISP control-plane configuration symmetry on both ends: the map-server's site/EID configuration and `passive-open`, a complete locator-set, and matching authentication keys (a PSK mismatch fails registration for specific EIDs while the session may still form). (5) Once the session is Established and the expected EIDs are registered (verify on the control-plane node), the fabric mapping is healthy and the gate can proceed.
campus-sda.citation: Cisco SD-Access Fabric Troubleshooting Guide — control-plane node = LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver, TCP-based `show lisp session` registration channel, and the note that a Down session is expected on devices with no EIDs to register (non-route-importing border / edge with no endpoints); with Cisco 'Troubleshoot LISP VXLAN Fabric on Catalyst 9000 Series Switches' (Doc ID 220361) for `show lisp session vrf <ip>` detail and registration/passive-open/locator-set/key checks.

cloud.title: Never expose an admin / database port (or all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0 in a cloud security group
cloud.recommended_action: Restrict the source to the specific admin / peering CIDRs, or front the access with a bastion / VPN / SSM Session Manager; re-scope any 'all ports / all protocols' rule to the minimum required; and verify there is no inherited world-open admin path before the workload is migrated or the account goes to production. Pair with VPC flow logs + a network-exposure analyzer.
cloud.citation: CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark 5.2 / 5.3 (no security group allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to port 22 / 3389); AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar; AWS EC2 DescribeSecurityGroups API

cloud.title: Build the cloud from standardized pods sized to measured workload, each pod an independently-survivable availability zone
cloud.recommended_action: Define a standardized pod (fixed compute/storage/network recipe, ideally hyperconverged) and grow by replicating it; build the capacity model first -- measure cores/RAM/IOPS and per-host/per-VM bandwidth, apply a growth factor, and translate to total edge ports by media, transport class (IP vs lossless/FCoE) and the east-west/north-south split (quoting real one-direction bandwidth); make each pod an independently-survivable availability zone with its own redundant access and its own (or an automatically-failing-over) instance of the management/orchestration/DHCP/DNS services it depends on; never run a single critical service instance across racks (and especially not across data centres); keep inter-zone connectivity routed (L3) and isolate any required stretch behind an overlay with storm-control; reject storage-replication/clustering that mandates end-to-end L2 between zones.
cloud.citation: ipSpace.net 'Designing a Private Cloud Infrastructure' / 'From Traditional Silos to SDDC' / DC Design Case Studies ch.6 & ch.11 'Cloud Infrastructure Failure Domains' (Pepelnjak); RFC 2119 requirement levels

cloud.title: Carry segmentation identity across the on-prem/cloud boundary as shared dynamic tag-group objects -- not as static IP ACLs that drift with autoscaling
cloud.recommended_action: For site-to-cloud segmentation, model each zone/tier as a dynamic tag-based group shared between the on-prem firewall and the cloud enforcement point (one common object, not two hand-synced lists); avoid static IP/CIDR allow-lists for any group whose membership autoscales, and confirm the tag-to-membership resolution is provider-aware on each side.
cloud.citation: Cisco Hybrid Mesh Firewall / Multicloud Defense 'Hybrid Segmentation' + dynamic tag-based address objects (blogs.cisco.com/security/cisco-hybrid-mesh-firewall...; Cisco Multicloud Defense User Guide - Rules and Rule Sets)

cloud.title: Decouple the virtual network from the physical: a stable IP underlay plus overlay removes the maintenance-window tax
cloud.recommended_action: Architect the physical network as a stable IP underlay whose only job is fast, simple, loop-free transport, and move all tenant/application segmentation into an overlay provisioned by the orchestration system; keep the underlay configuration small and change it rarely; let the overlay (and self-service) absorb the churn so segment adds/moves need no physical change or maintenance window. Where heavy manual VLAN sprawl is observed, surface decoupling-via-overlay as a design option.
cloud.citation: ipSpace.net 'From Traditional Silos to SDDC' / 'Designing a Private Cloud Infrastructure' (Pepelnjak); corroborated by VXLAN/EVPN overlay design literature

cloud.title: East-west traffic now dominates: flatten to non-blocking multipath, and treat the hypervisor vSwitch + server NIC-teaming as a first-class, STP-less access edge
cloud.recommended_action: Treat east-west bisectional bandwidth as a first-class requirement: eliminate STP-blocked uplinks by moving to active-active multipath (MLAG at small scale, a leaf-spine VXLAN fabric beyond two switches) and size leaf uplinks to the real oversubscription target; treat the server trunk as an edge facing an unmanaged STP-less bridge -- pre-provision the VLANs on the ToR (or automate via orchestration), use a distributed vSwitch with LACP where a bundled uplink is wanted so the MLAG pair sees one LAG not orphan ports, apply storm-control and don't rely on STP toward the server; for all-active dual-homed servers use server-to-switch LACP LAG on an MLAG ToR pair, but for single-homed/non-LAG servers do NOT MLAG/stack the ToRs (dedicate the ports to uplinks); always use LACP, never static port-channels.
cloud.citation: ipSpace.net 'Data Center 3.0 for Networking Engineers' / 'Server Virtualization Overview' / 'Redundant Server-to-Network Connectivity' / DC Design Case Studies ch.7 (Pepelnjak); VMware vSphere networking design; IEEE 802.1AX (LACP)

cloud.title: Engineer the hybrid-edge BGP path-attribute plane explicitly -- the cloud's LPM/relative-cost overrides AS-path prepend
cloud.recommended_action: For each cloud attachment, document the intended primary/secondary and active-active behavior, then choose the steering lever per direction: more-specific prefix or provider LocalPref community for cloud-side ingress, on-prem LocalPref for egress; treat AS-path prepend as advisory only and verify it is not overridden by LPM/relative-cost. Flag any hybrid edge that relies solely on prepend for failover.
cloud.citation: AWS Direct Connect User Guide -- Routing policies and BGP communities (Local Preference community tags 7224:7100/7200/7300 evaluated before AS_PATH; prepend ineffective across regions / unequal relative cost); Azure ExpressRoute routing (LPM) guidance

cloud.title: Normalize segmentation to a provider-neutral intent model, then render per-cloud -- never lift-and-shift a security-group rule set
cloud.recommended_action: When the target spans more than one public cloud, define segmentation as provider-neutral intent (tier-to-tier flow rules) and generate each cloud's SG/NSG/firewall config from it; document the per-primitive semantic gaps (allow-only vs allow+deny, instance vs subnet vs VPC scope, stateful vs stateless NACL) so a normalized rule cannot be assumed to behave identically everywhere.
cloud.citation: Cisco Multicloud Defense White Paper (cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/security/multicloud-defense/multicloud-defense-wp.html); AWS/Azure/GCP access-control documentation (SG allow-only stateful instance-scoped; NSG allow+deny instance/subnet; GCP firewall stateful VPC-scoped)

cloud.title: Pin per-flow AZ affinity (appliance mode) when inserting a centralized inspection VPC behind a cloud transit hub
cloud.recommended_action: For any hybrid on-ramp that hairpins inter-VPC/inter-spoke traffic through a centralized inspection VPC, mandate appliance-mode / per-flow AZ affinity on the inspection attachment and document the single-hub and same-attachment constraints in the HLD; never assume a multi-AZ firewall fleet inspects symmetrically by default.
cloud.citation: AWS Transit Gateway documentation, 'Example: Appliance in a shared services VPC' and 'Stateful appliances and appliance mode' (docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)

cloud.title: Respect the cloud gateway's prefix-advertisement ceiling -- summarize on-prem, because over-advertising idles the whole BGP session
cloud.recommended_action: Build an advertisement plan per cloud attachment: aggregate on-prem prefixes to a small summarized set sized under the provider ceiling (with growth headroom), and explicitly account for any more-specifics injected for traffic-symmetry. Never let the interior IGP/BGP table redistribute unfiltered toward the cloud edge.
cloud.citation: AWS Direct Connect quotas / User Guide (100-prefix per-VIF limit on private & transit VIFs -> BGP session goes idle when exceeded; 1000 on public VIF; ~200 per TGW-to-DXGW association); Azure ExpressRoute advertised/learned-route limits

cloud.title: Size the VPN-based cloud on-ramp by tunnel quantization: aggregate only via ECMP with dynamic BGP, then scale out horizontally
cloud.recommended_action: Compute required on-ramp bandwidth, divide by per-tunnel capacity to get tunnel/instance count, mandate dynamic BGP + VPN-ECMP (never static) for aggregation, plan horizontal scale-out past a few tunnels, and pin the VPN MTU/MSS expectations; treat VPN as backup to a dedicated circuit when sustained throughput matters.
cloud.citation: AWS Site-to-Site VPN / Transit Gateway docs (per-tunnel ~1.25 Gbps; ECMP requires dynamic BGP + VPN-ECMP option) + Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Cloud OnRamp for IaaS/Colocation design guides (horizontal data-plane scale-out)

cloud.title: Treat the cloud transit hub's route domains as the segmentation SSOT, and resolve overlapping CIDRs before on-ramp attachment
cloud.recommended_action: Author the hub route-domain map (association + propagation + blackhole routes) as a first-class HLD artifact sized against the route-table/route quotas; gate on-ramp attachment on an addressing-overlap check and require re-addressing or NAT for any overlapping prefix before it joins the fabric.
cloud.citation: AWS Transit Gateway documentation, 'Routing' / 'Isolated VPCs' / 'Equal Cost Multipath routing' (VPC CIDRs cannot overlap) and AWS Transit Gateway Quotas (docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html)

cloud-native.title: Connect on-prem to cloud over a dedicated circuit (Direct Connect/ExpressRoute) as primary with a diverse second path + BGP, IPsec VPN as backup; extend an existing SD-WAN via Cloud OnRamp
cloud-native.recommended_action: Make a dedicated private circuit the primary hybrid path, provision a second on diverse paths/locations (redundant edges, dual VIFs) with BGP for failover, keep an IPsec VPN as backup; where an SD-WAN fabric exists, extend it with Cloud OnRamp for Multicloud so segmentation + app-aware policy reach the cloud uniformly.
cloud-native.citation: AWS Direct Connect / Azure ExpressRoute resiliency + Cisco SD-WAN Cloud OnRamp design; web-verified.

cloud-native.title: Make pod-network reachability a deliberate overlay-vs-BGP-native choice with a managed IPAM plan, and pick the CNI data plane (eBPF vs iptables) by scale
cloud-native.recommended_action: Plan pod/Service CIDRs as coordinated, non-overlapping enterprise prefixes sized for real scale; on a BGP-capable fabric prefer non-overlay BGP-native routing (peer each node to its ToR) so pod IPs are routable/inspectable; default to an eBPF data plane (Cilium kube-proxy replacement) past a few hundred Services or where DSR/socket-LB/identity policy is needed.
cloud-native.citation: Kubernetes CNI design (Calico/Cilium, overlay vs BGP, eBPF vs iptables, IPAM); web-verified.

cloud-native.title: Segment pods by workload identity (labels), default-deny -- never by ephemeral pod IP/CIDR -- and front north-south with stable ingress/egress gateways
cloud-native.recommended_action: Adopt namespace default-deny; author NetworkPolicy/CiliumNetworkPolicy by pod/namespace labels (identity), reserving CIDR selectors only for genuinely external endpoints; expose inbound only via an HA ingress/Gateway-API gateway and route compliance-sensitive egress through a pinned egress gateway.
cloud-native.citation: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy + CiliumNetworkPolicy + Gateway-API design; web-verified.

cloud-native.title: Split the service mesh into always-on L4 mTLS and opt-in L7 (ambient ztunnel + waypoint), rather than an Envoy sidecar in every pod
cloud-native.recommended_action: Default new meshes to ambient: per-node ztunnel for cluster-wide L4 mTLS/identity, add namespace-scoped waypoint proxies only for services needing L7 routing/retries/authz; or a Cilium eBPF mesh where the CNI already provides it -- reserving sidecars for cases that genuinely require per-pod Envoy.
cloud-native.citation: Istio Ambient (ztunnel/waypoint) + Cilium Service Mesh (eBPF, sidecarless) design; web-verified.

cloud-native.title: Design cloud VPC/VNet as AZ-striped subnet tiers, interconnect via a transit hub (not full-mesh peering), and centralize egress/inspection per-AZ
cloud-native.recommended_action: Draw a hierarchical non-overlapping IP plan first (distinct CIDRs per on-prem/region/account); stripe each tier across >= 2-3 AZs; layer stateful instance rules under stateless subnet ACLs; interconnect via a transit hub once VPC count/transitive needs appear; route spoke egress through a shared egress/inspection VPC instantiated in every AZ; resolve hybrid private DNS via hub resolver endpoints.
cloud-native.citation: AWS/Azure cloud network design (Transit Gateway / vWAN, AZ subnets, centralized egress, Route 53/DNS); web-verified.

dc-compute.title: Run UCS Fabric Interconnects in end-host mode by default; carry disjoint upstream L2 by VLAN-to-uplink pinning, not switch mode
dc-compute.recommended_action: Default the FI pair to end-host mode, bundle uplinks to the upstream (vPC) pair as port-channels; for multiple disjoint upstream L2 domains use non-overlapping VLAN-to-uplink pinning with one vNIC per domain; reserve switch mode for genuinely upstream-incapable cases.
dc-compute.citation: Cisco UCS Design Guide (end-host mode, disjoint L2, uplink pinning); web-verified.

dc-compute.title: Abstract server identity into stateless service profiles from pools/templates (UCS Manager per-domain vs Intersight), and engineer a lossless no-drop class if converging FCoE
dc-compute.recommended_action: Derive every identity from non-overlapping pools, stamp service profiles from templates (updating templates for fleet change); operate via UCS Manager (single domain) or Intersight (multi-domain); if converging FCoE, define one no-drop CoS engineered end-to-end (PFC on the FCoE priority, ETS bandwidth, DCBX auto-negotiation), keeping the storage VLAN distinct from LAN.
dc-compute.citation: Cisco UCS / Intersight + FCoE DCB design; web-verified.

dc-compute.title: Extend L2 between DCs with a control-plane DCI (OTV-style): advertise MACs, suppress unknown-unicast/ARP across the interconnect, and multihome with per-VLAN AED
dc-compute.recommended_action: Extend only the VLANs that truly need it over a control-plane DCI (OTV or equivalent) that advertises MACs, suppresses unknown-unicast + ARP, and filters BPDU/FHRP per site; deploy >= 2 edge devices per site with per-VLAN AED election + a dedicated site-VLAN and unique site-ID.
dc-compute.citation: Cisco OTV DCI design (IS-IS overlay, AED, unknown-unicast suppression); web-verified.

dc-compute.title: Build two air-gapped SAN fabrics (A/B) that never merge with single-initiator zoning; pick the storage transport (NVMe/FC or NVMe/TCP before RoCE; iSCSI as legacy) by loss-sensitivity
dc-compute.recommended_action: Provision two physically+logically separate fabrics; dual-attach every host/array (one port per fabric) with multipathing; never connect A to B; zone single-initiator-to-target by pWWN; NPV/NPIV at the edge; default the transport to NVMe/FC where FC exists or NVMe/TCP for standard Ethernet, RoCEv2 only with a verified lossless fabric.
dc-compute.citation: Cisco MDS / SAN design + NVMe-oF (NVMe/FC, NVMe/TCP, NVMe/RoCE) guidance; web-verified.

dc-fabric.title: Choose the DC fabric operating model: standalone NX-OS VXLAN-EVPN (default) vs Cisco ACI policy fabric
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Default to standalone NX-OS VXLAN BGP-EVPN for new builds (open RFC 7432 EVPN / RFC 8365 VXLAN / RFC 9135 IRB standards, portable multivendor skills, Nexus Dashboard / NDFC operations including IP Fabric for Media for broadcast/media estates, BGP-EVPN policy + VXLAN GPO group policy for segmentation). Choose Cisco ACI when an existing ACI estate, or an application-centric end-to-end identity micro-segmentation operating model, justifies a single declarative APIC controller. Note the 2026 trajectory: ACI is converging into the unified Nexus Dashboard / open-VXLAN-EVPN model (APIC federation + VXLAN GPO), which narrows ACI's once-unique segmentation advantage.
dc-fabric.citation: Cisco AS ACI Design & Deployment (Telco DC) + NRG / EXPO2020 ACI HLD/LLD operating model, cross-checked with the current Cisco Nexus 9000 VXLAN BGP-EVPN design guide + Nexus Dashboard (2026).

dc-fabric.title: Size a leaf-spine Clos by an explicit oversubscription ratio and keep the fabric control plane deliberately dumb
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Adopt a folded 3-stage Clos sized to the edge-port count on uniform fixed-config switches; state the target oversubscription ratio and derive leaf/spine port and device counts from it (tighten the ratio or add spines for bandwidth-heavy workloads); run one protocol fabric-wide (eBGP-as-IGP: single-AS spines + per-leaf AS), avoid areas/summarization/redistribution, prefer point-to-point routed (optionally unnumbered/IPv6-LLA) core links, and design so no inter-spine/inter-leaf links are required.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'Leaf-and-Spine Fabric Designs' workshop (Clos 101; Physical Design Process; Routing Protocol Selection; Unnumbered Interfaces) and 'Data Center Network Reference Architecture'; Charles Clos (1953) multistage switching theory | RFC 7938 (BGP for large-scale DC); oversubscription is the downlink:uplink BANDWIDTH ratio (port-count N:M equals it only at uniform speed).

dc-fabric.title: Prefer a distributed anycast gateway with symmetric IRB over centralized spine routing
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Specify a distributed anycast gateway (same gateway IP/MAC on all leaves) with symmetric IRB so subnets are confined to leaves with active endpoints; enable ARP (and, where supported, ND) suppression per VNI; before turning off or dropping BUM flooding, verify there are no silent hosts and confirm vendor support; avoid centralized spine/external gateways unless an external service (firewall/LB) genuinely must sit in the inter-subnet path.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'Routing in EVPN Fabrics' / 'EVPN Basics' (Pepelnjak/Dutt); RFC 7432 / RFC 9135 (EVPN integrated routing and bridging); Cisco/Arista distributed-anycast-gateway design guides

dc-fabric.title: An EVPN/VXLAN fabric silently drops STP BPDUs -- the legacy L2 handoff must be one logical link per VLAN, with the VTEP as STP root
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Enforce exactly one logical L2 connection per VLAN between legacy and fabric; configure the VTEP as STP root for all its L2 segments and enable BPDU Guard on all edge ports plus MAC-move violation logging on every leaf; enable South-Bound Loop Detection; verify STP root per VLAN before bridging.
dc-fabric.citation: AJ SDD Migration Approach ('only a single logical layer 2 connection per VLAN ... the EVPN VXLAN fabric is not forwarding any STP BPDUs'), 'Dot1Q VLAN and Spanning Tree Design', 'MAC Move Violation'

dc-fabric.title: For a media fabric, get the underlay multicast (PIM-ASM + Anycast-RP + IGMP-snooping) right at cutover even when Tenant Routed Multicast is deferred
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Ensure every active multicast VLAN is instantiated in the fabric WITH IGMP snooping; configure the underlay with PIM-ASM and PIM Anycast-RP; plan an external-RP-to-fabric-Anycast-RP coexistence for the TRM phase; for mixed/non-TRM platforms consider L2-mode TRM.
dc-fabric.citation: AJ SDD 'Underlay Multicast (PIM-ASM & PIM Anycast RP)', 'Tenant Routed Multicast' ('considered for the future Deployment'), 'L3 TRM PIM RP Placement'; RFC 4610 (Anycast-RP) | TRM routed-multicast control plane is ngMVPN (RFC 6513/6514).

dc-fabric.title: A VXLAN fabric needs a BGP-EVPN control plane built on L3VPN machinery, not flood-and-learn
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Specify BGP-EVPN (l2vpn evpn AFI) as the fabric control plane with RD per VTEP/loopback and RT-based tenant membership (auto-derived from loopback+VNI where supported); reuse the customer's existing BGP operational model and route reflection rather than a new protocol; treat multicast-underlay flood-and-learn as a flooding/scaling risk to call out in the HLD.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'VXLAN and EVPN 101' (Pepelnjak) / 'EVPN Basics' (Dutt); RFC 7348 (VXLAN), RFC 7432 (BGP MPLS-Based EVPN), RFC 8365 (NVO/EVPN-VXLAN), RFC 4364 (BGP/MPLS L3VPN) | standards note: RFC 7432 is BGP-MPLS EVPN (route types 1-4); the VXLAN data-plane binding is RFC 8365 (NVO), and EVPN IP-Prefix (RT-5) is RFC 9136.

dc-fabric.title: Default BUM replication to ingress replication; reserve a multicast underlay for heavy multi-destination load
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Default the EVPN target to ingress replication for BUM; only specify an L3 (PIM) multicast underlay when measured multi-destination/multicast load or VTEP scale makes head-end replication inefficient, and document the per-VNI group mapping if so.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'EVPN Basics' (Dutt) multi-destination-frame section; RFC 7432 (Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag / BUM handling), RFC 8365 (NVO replication options)

dc-fabric.title: Keep fabric ECMP equal-capacity: no LAG/parallel-slow uplinks and never summarize in the Clos core
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Use single higher-speed leaf-to-spine links (40/100GE) rather than LAGs or parallel slower links so a member loss is visible to routing as a path loss; carry full fabric reachability with NO core summarization so every spine has a specific route to every leaf; rely on wide per-flow ECMP on the ingress switch.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'Leaf-and-Spine Fabric Designs' workshop ('Link Aggregation On Leaf-to-Spine Links Is Bad', 'Parallel L3 Leaf-to-Spine Links Are Bad', 'Route Summarization is Bad')

dc-fabric.title: Separate a simple IP underlay from the EVPN overlay; let one eBGP session carry both
dc-fabric.recommended_action: Specify an IP-only underlay for VTEP reachability plus an EVPN overlay; where the underlay is eBGP, run a single eBGP session per leaf-spine adjacency carrying both AFIs, keep next-hop-unchanged for EVPN routes, and let spines act as RR-equivalent transit with auto-derived RD/RT.
dc-fabric.citation: ipSpace.net 'EVPN Basics' (Dutt) BGP-models section / 'VXLAN and EVPN 101'; RFC 7938 (BGP for DC routing), RFC 8365 (EVPN-VXLAN NVO)

dc-multisite.title: Drive DR/active-active from business RTO/RPO and failover headroom, not from stretched-L2 heroics
dc-multisite.recommended_action: Capture business RTO/RPO/budget and per-app downtime tolerance FIRST; choose the replication tier from RPO (synchronous only where a near-zero RPO truly justifies its cost/distance limits, otherwise async / DB-replica / log-shipping); keep warm data and minimal warm infrastructure already running at the DR site; prefer restart-at-DR with DNS/service-discovery endpoints (or VIP-per-site behind global DNS/anycast with a drain-and-shift migration) over stretched-L2 live mobility; cap steady-state per-site utilization near 50% (N+N) or commit to an automated load-shed step; keep latency-coupled tiers co-located; avoid stretched firewall/LB clusters across the DCI; test automated failover under realistic conditions.
dc-multisite.citation: ipSpace.net 'From Disaster Recovery Sites to Active-Active Data Centers' / 'Designing Active-Active and Disaster Recovery Data Centers' / 'Active-Active Application Deployment' (Pepelnjak); standard N+N capacity-planning; CAP-theorem limits on distributed databases

dc-multisite.title: Interconnect EVPN fabrics as isolated sites (Multi-Site at the border-leaf), not one stretched Multi-Pod fabric
dc-multisite.recommended_action: Target a Multi-Site interconnect: terminate each site's overlay on a redundant Border-Gateway (anycast) cluster at dedicated border-leaf nodes, keep underlays per-site (no underlay extension between sites), run eBGP between site overlays, and enforce per-site BUM/storm-control at the gateway; terminate the IGP at each site boundary so a control-plane fault is contained per site; design and test the total-inter-site-link-loss and split-brain scenarios. Reserve a single stretched (Multi-Pod) fabric for pods within one facility on reliable links where shared fate is acceptable.
dc-multisite.citation: ipSpace.net 'Multi-Site and Multi-Pod Fabrics' / 'Using VXLAN and EVPN in Multi-Pod and Multi-Site Fabrics' (Krattiger/Pepelnjak); Cisco VXLAN EVPN Multi-Site Design (c11-739942); IETF draft-ietf-bess-dci-evpn-overlay

dc-multisite.title: A stretched/mobile subnet must engineer ingress, egress and statefulness deliberately, or accept trombones and split-brain
dc-multisite.recommended_action: Localize egress with an anycast gateway or active-active FHRP plus FHRP filtering on the DCI so each site forwards via its local gateway; engineer ingress explicitly (host-route injection or DNS/anycast), or prefer DNS/anycast-reachable scale-out services over a single mobile IP; keep stateful firewall/LB clusters within a single site as independent pairs -- do not stretch them across the DCI -- and provide inter-site continuity at the application layer; if stateful services must front a stretched subnet, document the split-brain and flow-symmetry failure modes as accepted risk.
dc-multisite.citation: ipSpace.net 'Designing Active-Active and Disaster Recovery Data Centers' / 'Data Center Interconnects' (Pepelnjak) -- ingress/egress flows, anycast gateway, stretched stateful services / split-brain; FHRP localization/filtering

dc-multisite.title: Prefer L3 DCI; if a VLAN must stretch, bound its flooding at the LAN-WAN edge and never attach it through a switch
dc-multisite.recommended_action: Default to L3 DCI with path isolation (multi-VRF for a few zones, MPLS-VPN/EVPN to scale) and a distinct IP prefix per site; use routers/routed interfaces as the attachment point to any any-to-any L2 service so each site keeps its own STP/broadcast/security/multicast domain; where a VLAN must stretch, place one forwarding device or MLAG pair per VLAN at the boundary, do not extend STP across the WAN, enable storm-control and unknown-unicast suppression, and prefer VXLAN/EVPN-with-ARP-suppression (split-horizon) over raw bridging; treat stretched-VLAN DCI as a last resort with an explicit split-brain mitigation.
